item.title: Things To Do in Sydney in December: A One-Day Itinerary
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Have one day in Sydney? This itinerary takes you from sunrise at Bondi Beach to dinner on Sydney Harbour, with famous sights, Christmas shopping, and food stops along the way. It's a full day, so choose the stops that interest you most instead of trying to fit everything in. The city grew around its harbor, so the Opera House, The Rocks, the arcades, and the gardens are all close to the waterfront. If you plan well, you spend the day seeing things instead of traveling between them. Sydney in December sweetens the deal. The water is warm, the sun sets late, and the city lights up with decorated trees and market stalls. Christmas party cruises in Sydney put the harbor into the festive mood. Here's a full December itinerary, from sunrise at Bondi Beach to dinner on the harbor, packed with some of the best things to do in Sydney in December. Start where Sydney starts its mornings. Bondi is a wide curve of pale sand about 0.6 miles (1 km) long, facing east, so the sun rises straight over the sea. The water is clear and turquoise, and a Bondi Beach sunrise is worth setting an alarm for. Arrive early for a swim at Bondi Icebergs, a saltwater pool cut into the rock where waves break over the wall. Otherwise, swim between the red and yellow flags, which go out when patrols start around 8 am. Finish with breakfast on Campbell Parade, where cafes open early, and tables face the water. Bondi is about 5 miles (8 km) from the city: 30-45 minutes on the 333 bus from Circular Quay, 20 minutes by taxi. - Best for: ocean sunrise, an early swim and beachfront breakfast - Time needed: 2 to 3 hours, including travel - Cost: free for the beach, $10 for the Icebergs pool - Good to know: Thursdays are normally reserved for cleaning, though summer opening depends on tides. Check current pool hours before visiting. Circular Quay is the harbor's front door, where ferries, trains, and city streets meet. Two of Circular Quay's best-known attractions sit side by side a few minutes away. Ten minutes east of the Quay, the Royal Botanic Garden Sydney stretches along the water's edge: lawns, old fig trees, more than 27,000 plants, and curving paths with the harbor peeking through. Entry is free; it opens at 7 am, and the paths are flat. Follow the path around the point to Mrs Macquarie's Chair, a bench convicts carved into sandstone in 1810 for Elizabeth Macquarie, the governor's wife. From there, the Opera House and the Harbour Bridge line up in one frame, making it a well-liked spot to visit. - Best for: free harbor views, shade, and the best photo spot in the city - Good to know: the Chair sits at the far end of the point, so allow for the walk The garden path leads straight to it. You have seen the Sydney Opera House a thousand times in photos, and it still surprises up close: the white shells are far bigger than they look, and the surface is covered in small tiles that shift color with the light. It opened in 1973 and now carries UNESCO World Heritage status. You can walk around the forecourt and wide steps outside, and guided tours take you inside the concert halls. Walk around to the back toward the ferry wharves for a stunning view of the Harbour Bridge. - Best for: close-up views of the sails and a free harbor walk - Time needed: 30 minutes outside, 1 hour with a tour - Good to know: book the tour ahead, as popular slots go early A ten-minute walk back around the Quay takes you from the oldest part of Sydney to the middle of the modern city. The Rocks is where the city began; Martin Place is where it keeps Christmas. Between them sit lunch and the first sign of the season. Walk a few minutes west of the Quay and the streets narrow fast. The Rocks is a cluster of sandstone lanes, stairways, and courtyards below the Harbour Bridge, now filled with pubs, cafes, and galleries. The First Fleet landed here in 1788, so European settlement in Australia started on this shoreline. Of all the things to do in The Rocks Sydney, lunch in one of the country's oldest pubs comes first. Several sit within ten minutes of each other and still argue over which came first. On weekends, markets fill the streets with food and craft stalls. - Best for: colonial history, old pubs and lanes worth getting lost in - Time needed: 1.5 to 2 hours with lunch - Good to know: markets run only on weekends, so weekdays are quieter with fewer stalls. Ten minutes from The Rocks on foot, Martin Place is a long pedestrian square lined with banks, offices, and old stone buildings. In December, it becomes Sydney's Christmas centerpiece. The tree here is the tallest in New South Wales, lit by more than 110,000 lights, and the Martin Place Christmas markets fill the square below it with food, drinks and handmade gifts. - Best for: Christmas shopping, street food and the biggest tree in the state - Cost: free to walk through, stalls priced individually - Good to know: In 2026, markets run November 28 to December 24 on selected days, generally Wednesday to Saturday, with daily trading in the final week. Check the schedule before visiting. The tree lights up after dark. Afternoon - Shopping Arcades and Gardens If you still have energy, choose the Queen Victoria Building for shopping and architecture or the Chinese Garden of Friendship for a quieter break. Alternatively, return to your hotel to rest and change before taking a dinner cruise. Locals call it the QVB. Opened in 1898, the Queen Victoria Building fills a city block on George Street and features five floors of stained glass, iron railings, and a central dome under a glass ceiling. It's now a shopping center, with boutiques, jewelers, and cafes on every level, so come for the building as much as the shops. In December, an enormous Christmas tree hangs through the atrium. - Best for: shopping, Victorian architecture, and a cool break from the heat - Good to know: the upper galleries give the best view of the dome and tree. A ten-minute walk south from the QVB takes you to the southern end of Darling Harbour where a high wall hides one of the city's quietest places. The Chinese Garden of Friendship opened in 1988 and is modeled on private gardens from southern China. Inside, you'll find lakes with koi carp, waterfalls, and pavilions, while the walls block much of the traffic noise. A teahouse serves tea and dim sum. - Best for: quiet, shade, and photos unlike anything else that day - Good to know: open daily 10 am to 5 pm, with free 35-minute tours twice daily. Closed on Christmas Day. Darling Harbour is the waterfront on the city's western side. In December, the whole precinct lights up with a Christmas tree floating on Cockle Bay. For things to do in Darling Harbour at night, start with the light tunnel, then board a dinner cruise. A few minutes from the water, Darling Square sets up a light tunnel each December, lit every night until Christmas. The lights arch over the path so you can walk the whole length and stop for photos. More than 50 places to eat and drink line it, making it a great spot as the sun drops toward the horizon. - Best for: Christmas lights, waterfront bars and a sunset walk - Good to know: time it for dusk, when the tunnel shows up best End the day aboard one of the Sydney dinner cruises, departing from King Street Wharf a few minutes from Darling Square. This is the signature Sydney way to wrap up an evening: dinner and a live show on a boat cruising Sydney Harbour. Christmas versions run through December and are ideal for groups. - Best for: a signature Sydney dinner cruise with live cabaret - Time needed: around 3 hours on the water - Cost: ticketed, with dinner and the show included - Good to know: book ahead, as December evenings fill early That's a full day in Sydney, from first light at Bondi to an evening on the harbor. Skip a stop or two for a slower pace, and leave enough time to reach King Street Wharf before your cruise's boarding time. This article was published in partnership with Sydney Showboats.

item.title: The world's top 'cities to watch' in 2026
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Toulouse to Ho Chi Minh City: Five fast-rising cities that should be on travellers' radars right now A new global report spotlights the world's emerging urban hotspots. From thriving cultural scenes to changing neighbourhoods, locals reveal what makes them worth exploring now. New York, London and Paris have once again topped Oxford Economics' annual ranking of the world's leading cities. But beyond these familiar names, its 2026 Global Cities Index has identified 28 "cities to watch" – places whose rapid growth and rising fortunes could see them become increasingly influential in the years ahead. These cities aren't just growing economically. New neighbourhoods, thriving cultural scenes and improved transport links are already reshaping the visitor experience and making them increasingly interesting places to visit. We selected five from the list and spoke to people who know them well to find out what's changing – and why they're worth exploring now. With its population forecast to grow by 57,000 over the next four years – more than anywhere else in France – Toulouse is one of Europe's fastest-growing cities and is attracting younger, skilled newcomers with its mild climate, relatively affordable cost of living and high quality of life. "Here, you don't have to choose between slow life and fast life," said Elodie Paramelle, who recently returned to Toulouse after 10 years in London. "You get the energy of a big city, with an incredible food scene, independent cafes, cocktail bars and a growing cultural offering, alongside a much slower pace of life." Toulouse has changed significantly in recent years, according to Mélodie Tyler, who moved back here after seven years in Paris. She says the city is much more walkable and bike-friendly, while its food and wine scene has expanded dramatically. And she notes that the buzz is spreading beyond the historic centre. "Ponts-Jumeaux where I live hosts a bunch of festivals, guinguettes [open-air bars] and skateboarding competitions," she said. "The Toulousains love to party and be outside as much as possible!" Beyond its thriving neighbourhoods, Toulouse is also major aerospace hub, home to hundreds of companies, including Airbus's global headquarters. Visitors can explore that heritage at the Cité de l'Espace space-themed discovery centre or Aeroscopia aviation museum beside the Airbus runways. For something more unusual, La Halle de La Machine brings art and engineering together through giant mechanical creatures created by a local street theatre company. Vietnam's largest city is on a remarkable trajectory. Oxford Economics predicts Ho Chi Minh City will be among the world's 50 fastest-growing cities over the next five years, with an economy that could rival Berlin's by 2050. Tourism is booming too, with more than eight million international visitors last year, exceeding projections. "The first metro line only opened at the end of 2024, and it's one of the most tangible symbols of how quickly the city is changing," said Meaghan Yash, a travel specialist at tour operator Timbuktu Travel who frequently designs trips here. The 20km (12.5 mile) line runs from Ben Thanh Market in the city centre to the Suoi Tien theme park, with single fares costing less than £1 ($1.33). Yet, Ho Chi Minh's appeal lies in how it balances change with continuity. Chris Buchart, commercial director at Vietnamese hotel company Fusion Group, suggests travellers visit the French-colonial Central Post Office and Opera House, and then the War Remnants Museum for context on the country's history, before turning to one of the city's greatest strengths: its food. Buchart recommends trying bánh mì (Vietnamese baguette sandwich), cơm tấm (broken rice) and bánh xèo (crispy pancakes), while Yash suggests venturing beyond the usual tourist circuit in central District 1 to quieter, more residential neighbourhoods where leafy streets are ideal for wandering and cafe-hopping. He also suggests Chợ Lớn, the city's historic Chinatown, for its markets, temples and medicine shops, while across the river in Thảo Điền, independent boutiques, galleries and home-grown Vietnamese brands make for excellent shopping. The Polish capital has made one of the fastest jumps in the Global Cities index, climbing more than 100 places to 61st. Its quality-of-life score now surpasses London, New York and Tokyo, while its economy is projected to expand by around 3% annually – nearly twice the European city average. For Konrad Warzecha, a Polish-Australian whose family home is in Warsaw's Wola district, the transformation has been remarkable. "From our balcony you can see the skyline, and watching the roads, highways and towers go up over 20 years has made the city almost unrecognisable," said Warzecha, who blogs at House Sitters Guide. The biggest changes, he says, are on the streets. "As a kid I rode the trams and did not feel safe, and I saw many robberies happen," he said. "Now I have never felt safer. People walk around at night, the streets are clean and trouble gets dealt with quickly." For first-time visitors, Warzecha recommends a walk that takes in both the old and new city. He starts at the Soviet-era Palace of Culture and Science and follows Nowy Świat boulevard into the Old Town, painstakingly rebuilt after World War Two. Along the way, he stops for pączki (Polish doughnuts) and a meal at a bar mleczny, one of the city's traditional, no-frills milk bars. "It tastes like home cooking," he said. "A three-course meal with drinks comes to around £13 ($17). Warzecha once wanted to leave Poland and move back to Australia, but today his feelings have changed. "These days Warsaw is one of the places I recommend most, and not because I am from there. I am proud to have a Polish background." Medellín's remarkable transformation is reflected in its economic fortunes. Employment in business and financial services has more than doubled over the past 20 years, and Oxford Economics predicts that the Colombian city's average income will overtake Buenos Aires and São Paulo by the 2040s. "In the 10 years I've lived here, Medellín has gone from a curiosity for only the most daring to a hub for travel," said Patrick Quinn, who runs the Colombia Writers Retreat in nearby El Peñol. "Once blighted or overlooked places like Comuna 13, Perpetuo Socorro and Ciudad del Río have become cultural and economic centres." The city's Metrocable, the first urban cable car system designed for mass public transport, carries commuters and visitors up the surrounding hillsides, while emerging creative districts are giving travellers new reasons to explore. "There is enough happening in its food, art and design scenes to warrant several days in its own right," said Joanna Rigby Jones, a travel specialist at Timbuktu Travel who has planned trips here for years. She recommends the creative district, Perpetuo Socorro, for design shops, galleries and speciality coffee. Comuna 13, once one of the city's most dangerous districts, now draws some of Medellín's biggest crowds. "Go with a local guide who can provide the context behind the murals, escalators and music rather than treating the neighbourhood simply as an Instagram backdrop," said Rigby Jones. Quinn also recommends exploring the Poblado and Laureles neighbourhoods, seeking out local creators and curators. "That way, you can go home and tell stories that will dismantle outdated misconceptions about this place," he said. Once heavily dependent on oil, Abu Dhabi has transformed its economy through investment in technology, renewable energy, property and finance. The UAE capital now ranks sixth in the Global Cities index for the skills and education of its workforce, ahead of Paris and Boston, while its non-oil economy and job market are projected to surpass neighbouring Dubai. "Abu Dhabi feels a little slower and more relaxed than Dubai or Sharjah," said Muna Abu-Hijleh, an American who has lived in both Abu Dhabi and Sharjah. "There's more of a sense of space, and you can go from a very modern city to the beach, the mangroves or quieter neighbourhoods quite easily." That slower pace is part of the appeal for Jeremy Savory, a longtime UAE resident and frequent visitor to Abu Dhabi, "It's a city that's been engineered to be the stable alternative next to Dubai's flash," he said. "In this region right now, boring is a selling point." Yet, Abu Dhabi is making an enormous cultural statement. On Saadiyat Island, the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi and Zayed National Museum both opened in 2025, while the Frank Gehry-designed Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is scheduled to open on 11 December 2026. Abu-Hijleh also suggests at least one day at a slower pace, such as having breakfast at a local cafe or browsing at the mall. "The UAE can look incredibly futuristic from the outside, but everyday life is much more ordinary and human than the skyscrapers and luxury hotels might suggest." – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: Whatever happened to big, boozy wine?
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink
For decades, wines grew more potent as hotter summers met a taste for strong, ripe flavours. Now drinkers want freshness without sacrificing character — and winemakers are finding new ways to give it to them

item.title: Why don't Scandinavians say please?
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Why is there no word for please in the Nordic languages? It has never been more important to be a polite and respectful traveller. But how do you ask nicely when there is no equivalent word for "please"? I'm in a Copenhagen bakery, standing in line for sugar-dusted slices of lemon cake, delicately plaited cardamom buns and golden-brown cinnamon swirls. When I reach the front of the queue, I'm ready to order in simple Danish. But then I hit a snag: in this country, there is no single word that works quite like the English "please". Like a lot of people, when I travel I learn the basics of hello, goodbye, yes, no, please and thank you. But that's just not possible in Danish, Swedish, Norwegian, Icelandic or Finnish, where there is no catch-all word that works in quite the same way. So, what's going on? Are Nordic speakers simply more direct, or is politeness being expressed in ways outsiders may not immediately recognise? For travellers, understanding the difference can make everyday interactions much easier to navigate. The first thing to understand, says linguist Dr James Puchowski, a researcher at the Nynorsk Kultursentrum (The Norwegian Museum of Written Culture), is that looking for a direct translation of "please" may be the wrong place to start. Danes, for example, might ask for a pastry in a bakery using the words må jeg bede om – "may I ask for" – as a way to signal manners. In Sweden, a speaker might add tack (thank you) on to the request; while in Norway, politeness might be conveyed with an uplift to the end of the request and a smile. There are also words that translate as "please", including the Swedish snälla and Norwegian vennligst, but these tend to be used in more specific contexts – snälla often conveys pleading, while vennligst is more commonly used in formal requests or instructions. Neither functions quite like the everyday English "please". Danish language teacher Daniela Hummelgren says directness is part of the communication style. "Efficiency is valued here and communication is generally direct," she says. Being extra polite might be seen as annoying if it slows a process down. But are they being rude? Puchowski sees these differences as a reflection of societal structure. In Nordic countries, he explains, egalitarianism is prized and distinctions between people are less strongly marked in everyday speech. For example, more formal forms of address like Herr and Frue (Sir and Madam) have largely fallen out of everyday use – a reflection of how they see themselves as more equal and less defined by class. This egalitarian streak is often associated with Jante's Law, the Scandinavian idea that nobody should consider themselves more special or important than anyone else. In everyday interactions, Puchowski says, that can mean less emphasis on signalling status. Politeness may therefore rely less on a deferential word like "please", and more on phrasing, tone and context. Similar social norms extend across the region, including Finland, despite Finnish belonging to a separate language family from Danish, Swedish, Icelandic and Norwegian. "Language is more than words," Puchowski said. "It's also about how you present an idea." Hummelgren says visitors should take their cues from the people around them. "You need to calibrate the level of politeness of where you are," she said. "Observe the situations around you, so you can get accustomed to the level of what is polite and what is not." Even without speaking the language, travellers can pay attention to tone, body language and how people address service staff and strangers. In Sweden, one simple option is to add tack – "thank you" – to a request. Research into the Swedish tack links its use to equality and reciprocity, rather than deference. The same basic word is used across much of the region: tak in Danish and takk in Norwegian and Icelandic, while Finnish speakers use kiitos to say thanks. But visitors needn't worry too much about getting it wrong. Nobody will tut or give you a dark look if you order a coffee without saying "tak". In fact, Hummelgren says that being excessively polite can itself seem unusual – and even read as suspicious. "I've never heard of anyone sending a physical thank you card after a job interview or something similar," she said. "It would read as a bit over the top and perhaps like you are looking for favours." For travellers, the lesson is that politeness does not always depend on the same words or rituals. You may not hear "please" – but that doesn't mean politeness is missing. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: Lufthansa gives Columbus, Ohio, its first-ever nonstop route to Europe
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Lufthansa gives Columbus, Ohio, its first-ever nonstop route to Europe Columbus, Ohio, will get its first nonstop flight to Europe in May 2027, when Lufthansa launches service between John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH) and Frankfurt Airport (FRA). Lufthansa will launch the service May 5, 2027, the airline said Monday. The new flights will operate three times a week on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays. Bookings are scheduled to open Oct. 20, 2026. The service will provide Columbus-based travelers with nonstop service to Germany and access to Lufthansa's Frankfurt hub, which offers connections to hundreds of destinations. The Star Alliance carrier will fly a Boeing 787-9 with 28 Allegris business class suites, 28 premium economy seats and 197 economy seats on the new CMH route. "The new service will provide both business and leisure travelers with a convenient nonstop connection to Germany, as well as onward destinations across our Lufthansa Group network," Dirk Janzen, vice president of passenger sales for the Americas at the Lufthansa Group, said in a statement. "The launch of this route is an important step in our continued expansion in the United States, our most important market outside the Lufthansa Group's home markets." The new route adds Columbus to a growing list of central U.S. airports gaining transatlantic service: Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS), Nashville International Airport (BNA) and St. Louis Lambert International Airport (STL) are also seeing new European connections announced for next summer on Delta Air Lines, Air France and Icelandair, respectively. American Airlines and United Airlines also plan to add new destinations in Europe from their transatlantic gateways at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) and Washington's Dulles International Airport (IAD). CMH — unlike its Ohio peers Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport (CVG) and Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) — has never boasted a nonstop service to Europe. This was even true when the airport was a hub for America West Airlines, which itself never flew across the Atlantic; America West merged with US Airways in 2005. CVG was previously a hub for Delta Air Lines, and CLE was previously a hub for Continental Airlines. The new Lufthansa flight benefits from revenue guarantees provided by the state agency JobsOhio. Members of Lufthansa's Miles & More loyalty program can earn and redeem miles on the new route, as can those in partner United's MileagePlus loyalty program. Related reading:

item.title: Amtrak Guest Rewards guide: How to earn and redeem points
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Amtrak Guest Rewards guide: How to earn and redeem points Whether you take Amtrak for a quick trip along the Northeast Corridor or a cross-country train journey, it's worth joining Amtrak Guest Rewards. This free loyalty program lets you earn points on paid train tickets and redeem them for future travel, upgrades, lounge access and more. But there's more to Amtrak Guest Rewards than earning points on train tickets. You can also earn points through cobranded credit cards and partners, while frequent riders can unlock additional perks through elite status. Here's what you need to know about earning and redeeming Amtrak points and getting the most from the Guest Rewards program. You can earn Amtrak Guest Rewards points in many different ways, ranging from traveling on Amtrak to spending on Amtrak credit cards and even completing online surveys. Members earn 2 points per dollar spent on Amtrak travel. Plus, you'll get a 25% point bonus when traveling in business class and a 50% point bonus when traveling in Acela first class. That means you'll earn 2.5 points per dollar spent on business-class tickets and 3 points per dollar spent on Acela first-class tickets. U.S. residents can earn Amtrak points with two cobranded credit cards as follows: Both cards offer a 5% rebate on points when you redeem them for Amtrak travel and have no foreign transaction fees. Plus, your points won't expire as long as your card account remains open. You may want to get the Amtrak Guest Rewards Mastercard if you ride frequently enough to benefit from the onboard food-and-beverage rebate but don't want to pay an annual fee. Meanwhile, the Amtrak Guest Rewards Preferred Mastercard is a better option for frequent Amtrak riders who want extra perks and the ability to earn tier qualifying points with their card. The information for the Amtrak Guest Rewards Mastercard and the Amtrak Guest Rewards Preferred Mastercard has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. You can transfer Bilt Points to Amtrak Guest Rewards at a 2:1 ratio in increments of 1,000. This means that for every 2,000 Bilt points that you transfer to Amtrak, you'll get 1,000 Amtrak points. Bilt Blue members must transfer at least 2,000 points, while other Bilt members can transfer as few as 1,000 points. However, you'll want to consider whether the value you'd get when transferring Bilt points to Amtrak is better than what you'd otherwise get when redeeming Bilt points. - Buy Amtrak points: Amtrak members can buy or receive up to 50,000 points per calendar year, while elite members can buy points without an annual cap. - NRG Home: Earn Amtrak points when you choose NRG Home as your energy provider and enroll in an eligible plan; earn 10,000 bonus points after two months as an active NRG customer on an eligible plan, and then continue earning 2 points per dollar spent on the supply portion of your bill. - Rail Passengers Association membership: Earn 100 to 10,000 points each time you enroll in or renew. - Survey Points Club: You can earn Amtrak points by completing online surveys, including a special bonus of 250 points after you complete your first survey. - Teleflora: Earn 750 Amtrak points on every bouquet you order. Once you earn Amtrak points, you have several options for redeeming them. Amtrak doesn't have a fixed award chart, and redemption rates generally vary with paid fares. Amtrak says redemptions start at just 400 points, but I found this ticket for the 16-minute ride from New York to Newark for just 188 points. In general, the number of Amtrak points you'll need to redeem scales directly with the ticket's current cash price. So, you can generally expect to get around 2.6 cents per Amtrak point when redeeming for train travel. For example, I found a train from New York to Washington, D.C., for 750 points or $20 per ticket. As such, you'd get 2.67 cents per point on this redemption. You can also book Points & Cash rates. You'll see this option on the final payment screen when booking a train ticket with points. For example, here are the Points & Cash options Amtrak gave me for a ticket that would otherwise cost 2,175 points or $58. I could use my entire Amtrak balance (1,568 points) on a Points & Cash booking, which is appealing since I don't travel on Amtrak all that frequently. However, I'd only get 1.54 cents per point while doing so, which is much less than the 2.66 cents per point you'd get when redeeming the full 2,175 points for the $58 ticket. As such, you'll usually want to avoid Points & Cash tickets unless you can get close to 2.6 cents per point or have no other way to use the points. You can redeem 2,500 Amtrak points for a one-class space-available upgrade on a one-way paid ticket. This means you could upgrade from coach to business, or business to first class on Acela, using an upgrade coupon. You can redeem for an upgrade coupon on the Amtrak website or in the Amtrak app. Then, you can apply the coupon to an eligible one-way ticket within 12 hours of departure, subject to availability. Each upgrade coupon can only be used once and expires 12 months after you redeem points for it. You can also redeem 1,500 Amtrak points on the website or in the app for a single-visit lounge pass valid at participating Amtrak lounges at eligible stations. Lounge passes are generally accepted at Metropolitan Lounges in New York (Moynihan Train Hall), Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles, Philadelphia, Portland and Washington, D.C. You can buy a single-visit lounge pass for $35 ($50 in New York), so you'd get 2.33 cents per point (3.33 cents per point in New York). You can only use a lounge pass at your departure station or scheduled layover station up to three hours prior to your scheduled departure time. Lounge passes expire 12 months after you redeem points for them. You can also redeem Amtrak points for various gift cards, including Amazon, Chipotle and Grubhub. Redemptions are usually 2,500 points for a $25 gift card or 5,000 points for a $50 gift card. Unfortunately, you'll only get 1 cent per point when redeeming Amtrak points for gift cards. You can pay $10 per 1,000 points to transfer your points to another member's account. This is a poor-value way to redeem your points, especially since you can skip the sharing fees and book awards for other travelers directly from your account. Amtrak Guest Rewards has its entry-level member tier as well as three elite tiers that you can reach based on the tier qualifying points you earn each calendar year. Here's an overview of the four tiers and some of the perks members at these tiers get each membership year: Once you earn a status, you'll keep that status for the remainder of the calendar year you earned it in, all of the next calendar year and through the end of February of the following year. If you want to secure Amtrak elite status, you'll need to earn tier qualifying points each calendar year. Elite points-earning bonuses don't affect the amount of tier qualifying points you'll earn on train tickets. But here's how you can earn tier qualifying points: - 2 tier qualifying points per dollar spent on Amtrak travel - 25% bonus for business class, so 2.5 tier qualifying points per dollar spent on Amtrak business-class fares - 50% bonus for first class, so 3 tier qualifying points per dollar spent on Acela first-class fares - 1,000 tier qualifying points each time your Amtrak Guest Rewards Preferred Mastercard purchases reach $5,000 (up to 4,000 tier qualifying points per year) So, you could earn Select status by spending $2,500 on nonpremium Amtrak travel, $2,000 on business-class fares or $1,667 on Acela first-class fares. You can also earn up to 4,000 tier qualifying points per year through spending on the Amtrak Guest Rewards Preferred Mastercard at a rate of 1,000 tier qualifying points per $5,000 in qualifying purchases. Amtrak Guest Rewards is worth joining, even if you only travel by train occasionally. You can earn points on paid Amtrak tickets and redeem them for future travel, often getting about 2.6 cents per point. Frequent Amtrak travelers may also find value in one of the cobranded credit cards or through elite status. But regardless of how often you ride, you'll generally get the most value from your Amtrak points by redeeming them for train tickets rather than gift cards or Points & Cash bookings. Amtrak Guest Rewards is free to join for U.S. and Canadian residents. Members can earn at least 2 points per dollar spent on eligible Amtrak travel and redeem their points for train tickets and other rewards. Amtrak Guest Rewards points are generally worth around 2.6 cents each when redeemed for train tickets. Other redemption options, such as gift cards and Points & Cash bookings, often provide less value. Amtrak Guest Rewards points expire after 24 months without qualifying earning or redemption activity. However, your points won't expire as long as you have an open Amtrak Guest Rewards Mastercard or Preferred Mastercard account. Bilt members can transfer points to Amtrak Guest Rewards at a 2:1 ratio. However, Amtrak isn't a direct transfer partner of other popular programs like Chase Ultimate Rewards or American Express Membership Rewards. Amtrak Guest Rewards awards points to the person traveling, regardless of who purchases the ticket. Make sure your Amtrak Guest Rewards membership number is attached to your reservation to earn points. If your Amtrak points haven't posted within seven days of travel, you can submit a missing points request within 120 days of your trip. New members can also claim points for eligible travel taken up to 21 days before joining the program. You can redeem Amtrak Guest Rewards points to book train tickets for another traveler, even if you aren't traveling with them. This lets you avoid the fees associated with transferring points directly to another member's account.

item.title: 14 Bears Were Euthanized at One Montana Home. Wildlife Experts Explain What Went Wrong.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Montana wildlife officials euthanized 14 black bears near Bozeman in September after determining the animals posed a public safety risk. (Photo: Peter Zenkl/Group via Getty Images) Montana state officials euthanized 14 black bears at a property in Bozeman in September after wildlife wardens found the animals had become so accustomed to human food that they posed a public safety risk. According to a September 29 announcement from Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks (FWP), staff responded to a report of suspected illegal bear feeding at a residence north of Bozeman. During their investigation on September 24 and 25, officials found 15 bears that were severely food-conditioned and habituated to humans. Fourteen of the bears were captured and euthanized, while one cub was transported to Montana FWP’s Montana WILD facility in Helena for possible placement at an accredited zoo. The number of animals involved was highly unusual, according to Morgan Jacobsen, communications and education program manager at Montana FWP. Jacobsen told Outside that the investigation remains ongoing and officials have yet to determine how long the alleged feeding occurred, what the bears were eating, or why whether or not the feeding was intentional. “This case is different from typical incidents involving bears getting into unsecured garbage or other food sources. It involves the possibility of deliberate feeding,” Jacobsen said. Montana law prohibits intentionally providing supplemental food to bears. The investigation into what happened at the Bozeman property remains ongoing, and officials have not publicly identified anyone responsible for the alleged feeding. What officials have established is that the bears were severely food-conditioned, meaning they had learned to associate people with an easy meal. And according to Chris Servheen, president of the Montana Wildlife Federation, who spent 35 years as the grizzly bear recovery coordinator for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, it doesn’t take much for a bear to remember where it found food. “One feeding is all it takes, if there’s a significant amount of food there,” Servheen told Outside. “Bears are information vacuums, and so every time they get food in a certain place, they’re going to remember that.” A single substantial meal doesn’t necessarily make a bear dangerous, but it can teach the animal to return to a particular location Severheen said. When food remains available, bears may begin regularly visiting the property and eventually seeking food around other nearby homes. Black bears regularly move through Bozeman and other Montana communities without causing problems, but wildlife managers become concerned when the animals repeatedly find food around people. What begins with a bear tipping over a garbage can can eventually escalate to damaged property or attempts to enter vehicles, garages, and homes. Bears seeking human food can also become aggressive toward people, although Montana FWP has not reported any attacks involving the 14 bears euthanized near Bozeman. In this incident, Jacobsen said the bears showed no fear of humans, no longer foraged, and caused property damage. Their behavior had become so established that wildlife managers determined they could not safely be returned to the wild. Relocating bears with these behaviors presents several problems, Servheen explained. Adult bears have strong homing instincts and may travel considerable distances to return to familiar territory, including places where they’ve previously found food. “Adults have a tremendous homing ability,” Servheen said. “We can take them 40 miles, and they’ll be back in a couple of days.” Even if a relocated bear remains in its new habitat, it faces another challenge. Bears learn where to find food and how to survive within their home ranges, often beginning as cubs following their mothers. Moving them into unfamiliar territory can leave them struggling to find natural food sources while competing with bears already living there. Placement at an accredited zoo is another possibility, but Jacobsen explained that Montana FWP must first find a facility with the space and resources to accommodate the animal. In this case, officials had coordinated with a zoo that potentially could accept a cub, but did not have room for an adult bear. That opportunity allowed Montana FWP to hold one cub at its Montana WILD facility rather than euthanize it alongside the others. The cub’s age and the zoo’s available space, rather than evidence that it was less food-conditioned, determined why it was spared. Jacobsen did not have an update on its placement as of October 19. The Bozeman incident comes amid an unusually busy year for wildlife managers responding to bear conflicts in parts of the West. In south-central Montana, wildlife officials reported roughly 400 bear conflicts by late September, compared with about 175 during all of 2025, according to Montana Public Radio. More than 200 conflicts had been reported in Red Lodge alone by late August, where officials were also investigating suspected intentional feeding. Colorado has also experienced a sharp increase in reported bear activity. According to preliminary figures released by Colorado Parks and Wildlife, the state received 8,672 reports of bear sightings and incidents through August 31, compared with 3,680 during the same period in 2025. Those figures include sightings, not just dangerous encounters. Poor natural food availability can contribute to these encounters, particularly in the fall, when bears enter a period of intense feeding known as hyperphagia. During this time, they seek out as many calories as possible to build fat reserves before hibernation. Servheen cautioned against assuming that bears seeking human food are necessarily starving. He compared the appeal of an easily accessible, calorie-rich meal to walking into an ice cream store. “It’s like putting yourself or myself in an ice cream store,” he said. “It’s not that you’re starving, it’s just that you’re near such a good, concentrated thing to eat. Why should you go anywhere else to get food when it’s right in front of you? Even during years when natural food is plentiful, bears will take advantage of an easy meal.” Preventing these situations requires more than reminding people not to feed wildlife, according to Alexander Metcalf, a University of Montana researcher who studies the human side of wildlife management. In a 2021 study published in the Journal of Wildlife Management, Metcalf and his colleagues examined why Montana landowners do or don’t secure garbage and other food sources that attract bears. They found that people who had spoken with wildlife professionals were more likely to take precautions, while neighbors’ behavior and expectations also influenced whether residents secured attractants. “Most of them already want to do the right thing, but they’re also busy people,” Metcalf told Outside. “Securing all of the attractants around your property, whether they’re put there intentionally or not, takes a lot of work, and fitting that into your busy life can be hard.” Metcalf said communities can help by making it easier for residents to secure garbage, pick up fallen fruit, and remove other attractants rather than relying on public warnings alone. Julie Golla, a conflict prevention specialist with the Montana nonprofit People and Carnivores, works with residents to prevent bears from accessing garbage, chicken coops, bird feeders, and other food sources around homes. Her organization helps people identify potential attractants and install preventive measures such as electric fencing. “Just because there are bears doesn’t always mean that there’s a problem,” Golla told Outside. Montana FWP recommends reporting bears that begin accessing food near homes as soon as possible. Jacobsen said early intervention can sometimes prevent food-seeking behavior from becoming habitual, giving wildlife managers options beyond euthanasia.
