item.title: DOT delays rule change on airline maintenance delays
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
DOT delays rule change on airline maintenance delays A new federal rule that could change what passengers are owed after certain flight delays will be on hold for a couple more months. The new regulation could leave airlines off the hook to pay for passengers' expenses like meals and hotels due to some maintenance disruptions. The measure, which was part of a sweeping aviation bill passed by Congress in 2024, had been slated to take effect this week. But the U.S. Department of Transportation now plans to wait until the 2027 to implement the change. Once in place, passengers stranded because of a mechanical delay or cancellation could have less luck getting the airline to pay for expenses that pile up. Airlines 'off the hook' to pay after some flight disruptions Today, some airlines reimburse passenger expenses when a maintenance-related cancellation or long delay pops up. Those disruptions have historically been deemed "within the airline's control." Under the changes greenlit by Congress in 2024, certain unscheduled maintenance incidents would no longer be considered "controllable" by the airline. Among them: Unscheduled maintenance issues that can't wait until after the flight to be addressed. In those situations, airlines may no longer be on the hook to fulfill consumer guarantees, like paying for meals, hotel stays or ground transportation. "The number of delays and cancellations for which air carriers provide amenities and compensation to consumers is expected to be reduced," the DOT wrote in its final rule implementing the changes. Several other types of flight disruptions would also no longer be counted as within the airline's control, including: - Aircraft cleaning because of a passenger death - Aircraft damage due to extreme weather - Cybersecurity attacks, assuming the airline was in compliance with cyber regulations. - Airport closure due to volcanic ash, wind or wind shear - Overheated brakes due to a safety incident that required emergency procedures - A baggage- or cargo-loading delay due to an outage to a system not controlled by the airline or its contractor Airlines would still be on the hook for other "controllable" delays and cancellations like crew scheduling. And not all maintenance issues will be exempt, so passengers should err on the side of requesting reimbursement if they get stranded — as the saying goes, "You can always ask." You can find the full list of promises carriers have made at FlightRights.gov. Flight trouble due to bad weather or air traffic control issues have historically counted as "uncontrollable," and passengers must typically pay for their own expenses if they get stuck. However, some credit cards have built-in travel insurance that can help offset those expenses. This rule change does not affect federal refund rules. Passengers are owed a refund if their flight is canceled or significantly delayed — regardless of the reason — if they ultimately choose not to fly. The DOT had expected to implement the maintenance-related changes on Oct. 19. However, the agency now plans to go live with the new regulation to start the new year, beginning with flights departing on Jan. 1. You can read more about what these changes mean for consumers and the best way for travelers to protect themselves in our full breakdown of this issue. Related reading:

item.title: How a Missed Turnaround on Mt. Shasta Turned a Dayhike into a 36-Hour Survival Situation
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
How Backpacker reported this story: Writer Sam Anderson spoke with the Forest Service program manager for Shasta’s climbing rangers and the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office to learn about how two dayhikers ended up spending 36 hours stuck high on California’s Mt. Shasta and the mission to rescue them. Two hikers from Salt Lake City had a close call on Mt. Shasta this week after a missed turnaround and a wrong turn forced them to spend an unplanned night exposed to 15-degree weather. The Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office (SCSO) received a distress call at 10:20 p.m. on Monday, October 12. A 19-year-old male and 20-year-old female were underequipped to safely wait out the night at their location, about 11,000 feet up Avalanche Gulch. They’d begun their day at 4 a.m. at the Bunny Flat Trailhead with no plans to summit, alongside a male companion who did plan to summit. According to Sage Milestone, public information officer for the SCSO, the group had been on their way to Mt. Rainier when they made the spur-of-the-moment decision to climb Shasta. Their route was dangerous from the beginning: Avalanche Gulch’s terraced scree ramps are loose and crumbly without snow and ice to consolidate them. Along with that advisory, the pair had also ignored a recommended turnaround time posted at the trailhead. On their way up, Milestone said, the pair ran into their friend who had summited as he descended; he advised them to turn around at Red Banks, located at 12,800 ft. Unfortunately, the pair did not reach that point until around 5 p.m., five hours past the posted turnaround of noon. Now separated from their companion and stuck in rapidly-dropping temperatures with inadequate clothing, they followed officials’ advice to keep descending to maintain body heat. The group again contacted emergency services at 2 a.m. to report that they had reached Helen Lake at approximately 10,400 feet. Shortly thereafter, their phones died. Rescuers scrambled in a first-light operation involving air and ground operations. Ground searchers and air crews with CHP Air Operations first scanned the upper reaches of Avalanche Canyon. Around 9 a.m., they located two hikers, who turned out to be unrelated to the search and in no need of help. On the ground, crews tried another approach. Beginning at Horse Camp, a large cabin at 7,880 ft. on one of the mountain’s most prominent trails, which the hikers had already passed on their way up, they descended into nearby Cascade Gulch. While rescuers didn’t necessarily think Cascade Gulch was the most likely place to find the missing climbers, searching it was a matter of diligence, Nick Meyers, program manager for the Forest Service’s Mt. Shasta climbing rangers and avalanche center, said. “Cascade Gulch is a common place for people to end up if they get lost on Avalanche, but it’s usually only when the trails are covered,” Meyers said. “When trails are exposed like they are now, you can just follow the main drainage to hit any of the trails back to Bunny Flat.” However low-percentage, the decision paid off. Rescuers in Cascade Gulch heard shouting around 4 p.m. Soon they had located the two hikers, who were uninjured and managed to descend safely with help. According to rescue crews, the hikers confirmed they had passed Horse Camp on their way down. How they got lost from there remained unclear. “The trail from the cabin to Bunny Flats is a superhighway,” Meyers explained. “It’s the baseline recommended day hike for anyone of any experience level on that area of the mountain, so it’s really well-marked and very wide. We’re still scratching our heads about how they missed it.” While Milestone said “there were red flags from the get-go on [the hikers’] attempt,” he noted that officials were grateful the climbers followed rangers’ advice to keep moving down the mountain to stay warm, and that they believed the pair had learned from their experience. The rescue follows multiple similar incidents on Mt. Shasta during the past month. One badly injured hiker was airlifted from Horse Camp on Sept. 11 after attempting a glissade at high altitude, injuring his feet, and crawling back down most of Avalanche Gulch. And three young hikers endured a long rescue in early September after using AI to plan their summit bid via the Clear Creek route.

item.title: United adds new easternmost city in Canada in 6-route expansion with partner Air Canada
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
United adds new easternmost city in Canada in 6-route expansion with partner Air Canada United Airlines and Air Canada have agreed to expand their partnership on routes between the U.S. and Canada. And the two carriers are planning to launch a half-dozen new routes between the two countries for next summer. As part of the cross-border expansion, United on Friday announced it would return to St. John's in Canada's easternmost province of Newfoundland and Labrador for the first time in more than a decade. Plus, the airline on Friday announced service to two additional Canadian cities from its hub at Denver International Airport (DEN). Meanwhile, Air Canada is adding three additional U.S. routes: Louisville, Indianapolis and Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) will get new service to destinations north of the border. However, the Canadian flag carrier also plans to cut several U.S. routes from its schedule as part of the shakeup, TPG has confirmed. In all, United plans to add three new routes to Canada: - Newark to St. John's International Airport (YYT) — summer seasonal - Denver to Ottawa International Airport (YOW) - Denver to Quebec City's Jean Lesage International Airport (YQB) This expansion will mark the first time United has offered service from Newark to St. John's since 2016. The EWR-YYT route will give the airline a new easternmost destination in Canada. Today, that label belongs to Halifax, which United already serves from three U.S. cities. WestJet is currently the only carrier flying between the U.S. and St. John's. As part of its U.S. network shakeup, Air Canada announced three routes it'll launch for summer 2027. - Louisville, Kentucky's Muhammed Ali International Airport (SDF) to Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ) — Flights between April 28 and Oct. 31, 2027. - Indianapolis International Airport (IND) to Montreal Trudeau International Airport (YUL) — Daily service between June 1 and Sept. 30 - Newark to Edmonton International Airport (YEG) — Four weekly flights between June 1 and Oct. 17 Beyond these new routes, United and Air Canada also announced plans to add additional flights or larger planes on a handful of existing routes. However, Air Canada will also cut five U.S. routes from its schedule, as first reported by Ishrion Aviaton. Routes getting the axe include: - Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) to Billy Bishop Toronto International Airport (YTZ) - Charleston International Airport (CHS) in South Carolina to Toronto Pearson - Nashville International Airport (BNA) to Vancouver International Airport (YVR) - Raleigh-Durham International Airport (RDU) to Vancouver - Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Montreal In a statement to TPG, the carrier cited "commercial reasons," saying it "regularly reviews its schedule to ensure capacity is aligned with customer demand and travel patterns." Friday's route announcement between Air Canada and United came as the carriers announced an agreement to expand their cooperation on service between the U.S. and Canada. The proposal is currently under review by Canadian regulators. On top of partnering through the Star Alliance, the two airlines share a joint venture that allows them to coordinate on schedule and pricing. That aspect of the tie-up dates back to 2022. "The new routes and flights we're announcing today further underscore our commitment to investing in Canada and making travel between our two countries easier," United's chief network planner, Patrick Quayle, said in a statement shared by Air Canada Friday. Travel demand between the U.S. and Canada has seen some volatility over the past couple years, and that's led to a host of airline route adjustments during that stretch. Across all airlines in 2026, the total number of flights and seats between the two countries is down roughtly 6% versus two years ago, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. Related reading:

item.title: The Plaza is closing, Dallas will welcome a beautiful new hotel and other hospitality news from this week
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
The Plaza is closing, Dallas will welcome a beautiful new hotel and other hospitality news from this week As TPG's hotel reporter, I spend a lot of nights each year in hotel rooms. But this week I traded in the hotel for a stay at my friend's farm out in west Tennessee. It's been a good reminder that while satin sheets and made-to-order omelets are always great, hospitality comes in many shapes and forms. But while I've been out taking it slow in the country, the world of hotel news has kept on spinning. The most exciting news this week is that World of Hyatt has finally made it possible to transfer points between members online — and without having to fill out a PDF and email it in. The loyalty program also launched some new offers with Air Canada, like the chance to temporarily earn points between the two programs. We also reported on a social-forward new hotel opening in Silicon Valley. Here's the other hotel news you need to know about this week. Earlier this year, I stayed in my first Hilton LXR property, Ka La'i Waikiki Beach, LXR Hotels & Resorts, in Hawaii. I really enjoyed how the brand gives independent, luxury hotels a proper place in the points-and-miles world. Now, in Bengaluru, India, LXR is planting a new flag with the opening of The Den Bengaluru, LXR Hotels & Resorts. The resort features 226 rooms and suites, a rooftop Mediterranean and Indian restaurant, The Sanctuary Spa, a pool and even a game room called The Playhouse. How to book: Rates at The Den Bengaluru start around $176 per night or 66,000 Hilton Honors points per night. The most exciting new hotel in Dallas is taking reservations As a native Texan, I pass through Dallas quite a bit while visiting my family up in the Panhandle. Next year, I'll be sure to spend an extra night or two at the highly anticipated new Auberge Collection hotel, The Knox. Now accepting reservations from Jan. 29, 2026, the Martin Brudnizki hotel in the Knox Street district is a design-lover's dream. Set right off the Katy Trail, the hotel is close to nature, great shopping, popular restaurants and everything else Dallas has to offer. Once open, the hotel will feature bars and restaurants, a spa and a pool to help beat the fierce Texas heat. How to book: Cash rates start around $800 per night. When my corgi Splenda got invited to stay at The Plaza, NYC's most iconic hotel, a few years ago, we jumped at the chance. If a stay at The Plaza is on your bucket list, you'd better go soon; The Plaza will close for four years starting in January "for a restoration of the 18-story building's landmark facade," according to The New York Times. Luckily for folks heading to the city for holiday celebrations, there's one more chance to visit the hotel, which opened back in 1907, before the renovations start. This hotel in Rome is helping guests experience "what dreams are made of" Hilary Duff inspired a whole generation of millennial travelers with the 2003 film "The Lizzie Mcguire Movie." Specifically, it had every tween with a television hoping to visit Rome (and maybe fall in love with an Italian superstar). In the Eternal City, Generator Rome is now offering the "What Dreams are Made of" package, which includes — on top a stay at the hotel — a day exploring Rome on a Vespa for two, a Lizzie McGuire-themed map of filming locations, a one euro coin to make a wish at the Trevi Fountain and two Lizzie McGuire-inspired cocktails at the end of the day.

item.title: 11 Types of Vinegar: A Guide to Cooking With Them and More
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
There are an awful lot of vinegars in the worldâwhich ones you cook with depends entirely on your favorite flavors and what youâre making. Maybe you favor red wine vinegar for the punchy tang it brings to salad dressing. Or you canât imagine a bowl of white rice without the gentle acidity of seasoned rice vinegar running through it. Perhaps you fall asleep at night dreaming of bowls of vanilla ice cream covered in ripe summer strawberries dripping with balsamic vinegar. Whether youâre the kind of cook who has a favorite vinegar for every occasion or simply grabs whichever bottle is closest to the stove, it pays to know what youâre working with. You can often substitute one vinegar for another, but it's worth being strategic. âEach vinegar contributes its own flavor and character rather than just adding acidity,â says Sathish Kumar, the head chef of Indienne in New York and Chicago. So which bottles deserve a spot in your pantry? Weâre breaking down 11 types of vinegar, what to use them for, and substitutions that work in a pinch. What makes one vinegar different from another? Vinegar starts with alcohol, which bacteria convert into acetic acid. The starting ingredientâwine, apples, rice, malted barley, or sugarcane, for exampleâhelps determine the flavor, as do the fermentation and aging processes. That's how you get everything from the crisp, fruity tang of apple cider vinegar to the rich, savory complexity of Chinese black vinegar. There are countless varieties of vinegar; these are just the ones we reach for most often. Apple cider vinegar starts withâyou guessed itâapples. The fruit is fermented first into hard cider and then into vinegar. The result is bright, fruity, and pleasantly tart, with enough character to stand up to bold ingredients. Itâs also the subject of some debatable health claims. We like it in salad dressings, quick-pickled onions, and anything that could use a little fruitiness. It's a natural partner for pork and chicken, particularly in apple-cider braises, and its acidity cuts through the richness of cheeseburger fried rice or braised collard greens. And not for nothing, it makes a heck of a pie. White wine vinegar is the closest everyday substitute, though Champagne vinegar or unseasoned rice vinegar can also work when you want a lighter touch. Clear, inexpensive, and unapologetically sharp, distilled white vinegar is the pantry's most straightforward source of acidity. Made by fermenting distilled alcohol, often derived from grains, it has a relatively neutral flavor that lets other ingredients shine. Tom Carlin, the chef of Burl in Evanston, Illinois, likes adding a dash to braises at the end of cooking. It brightens them âwithout changing the flavor at all,â he says. That same clean tang makes distilled white vinegar a natural choice for classic dill pickles. Itâs also a great base for homemade flavored vinegars, especially those infused with chiles, herbs, or spices. In many cooked dishes and dressings, you can substitute rice, apple cider, or white wine vinegar. Each will bring its own flavor to the party, so taste as you go. Red wine vinegar is bold, fruity, and assertive. You canât dress a classic Greek salad or splash oysters with mignonette without it. Like white wine vinegar, it begins with wine that undergoes a second fermentation, but the red wine base gives it a more robust fruit flavor. Red wine vinegar brings welcome acidity to BAâs Best Gazpacho, coq au vin, a pot of hearty lentils, and rich meat marinades. If you're making a vinaigrette for a salad loaded with tomatoes, olives, or cheese, this is a good bottle to reach for. You can use white wine or apple cider vinegar in its place, but Chicago-based Sifr culinary director Sahil Sethi favors sherry vinegar. He says its nutty, aged character gives it a depth that mirrors red wine vinegarâs body and acidity. Fermented from white wine, white wine vinegar has a lighter, more delicate flavor than red wine vinegar. Its gently fruity acidity makes it particularly useful when you want to brighten a dish without overpowering it. Reach for it to use in salad dressings, seafood marinades, braised chicken, brothy steamed mussels, or a buttery pan sauce like beurre blanc. Conor Dalton, head chef at Smyth in Chicago, calls white wine vinegar âthe most versatileâ option and likes infusing it with herbs, such as lemon verbena, to sharpen creamy sauces for shrimp and balance richer preparations. Champagne vinegar is an especially good substitute. Sherry, apple cider, and unseasoned rice vinegars can also stand in, depending on the dish. Light, fruity, and delicately tangy, Champagne vinegar is typically made from wines produced using the same grape varieties as Champagne, such as Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. That doesnât mean itâs necessarily made from Champagne wine, nor does it enjoy the same strict regional protections. Its subtle fruit and floral notes give it a gentler flavor than many white wine vinegars, though it isnât necessarily less acidic. Some producers age Champagne vinegar in barrels to develop a rounder, more complex flavor. Itâs a particularly good choice when a more assertive vinegar might steal the show. Sethi calls Champagne vinegar his favorite for salad dressing, thanks to its subtle fruitiness. Try it in a vinaigrette for tender greens, drizzled over seafood, or in a dressing for spring vegetables. It can bring a little lift to richer dishes, too, without contributing much competing flavor. White wine vinegar, though slightly more assertive, is the most straightforward substitute. Unseasoned rice vinegar also works when a mild flavor is the primary goal. If red wine vinegar is bright and brash, sherry vinegar is its smoother, more nuanced cousin. Made from sherry wine and aged in wooden barrels, this amber-hued vinegar develops a rounded acidity with nutty, sometimes caramel-like notes. That complexity makes sherry vinegar especially good at finishing sauces, dressing roasted vegetables, and brightening stews. Try it in a classic leeks vinaigrette, braised chicken escabÃ¨che, or a glaze for ribeye. Dalton also likes using it to deglaze a pan or brighten a sauce at the end of cooking. Vinagre de Jerez comes from the area around Jerez, Spain, and must age in wooden barrels for at least 6 months. Itâs worth keeping a bottle around if you like a vinegar with a little more depth, but red or white wine vinegar works in many of the same applications. Malt vinegar has a more robust flavor, but can contribute some of the same woody, caramel undertones. Dark, rich, and sweet-tart, balsamic vinegar can be a finishing touch or an essential ingredient, depending on the bottle. Traditional balsamic vinegar, made in Modena or Reggio Emilia, Italy, starts with cooked grape must (freshly crushed grape juice), and ages in wooden barrels for at least 12 years. The result is intensely concentrated, syrupy, and complex. The balsamic vinegar youâre more likely to find at the supermarket is different. Commonly made by combining grape must with wine vinegar, it's generally thinner, tangier, and far less expensive than traditional balsamic. Thatâs not a bad thing: It's the kind we reach for when making balsamic dressing, roasting brussels sprouts with honey and garlic, or adding sweet-tart depth to Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta. For a thicker finishing sauce, you can also simmer everyday balsamic into a balsamic reduction, concentrating its sweetness and acidity. Save especially good aged balsamic for drizzling over Parmesan, ripe tomatoes, or even strawberries and vanilla ice cream. What about white balsamic vinegar? Made with grape must processed to minimize browning, white balsamic is paler, lighter, and fruitier than traditional dark balsamic. Use it to brighten a melon salad, dress roasted peppers, bring a little sweetness to a pan sauce without turning everything brown, or to make a sweet-and-tangy custard for a fruit tart. Both varieties of balsamic are tricky to substitute because their sweetness is as important as their acidity. For dressings or cooked sauces, try sherry or apple cider vinegar with a little honey or brown sugar. It won't have the same depth, but it'll get you closer to the sweet-tart balance. Mild, gently sweet, and endlessly versatile, rice vinegar is a staple in Japanese, Korean, Chinese, and Vietnamese cooking, among other cuisines. It's made by fermenting rice into alcohol and then vinegar, though its flavor and production vary by region. At the grocery store, youâll usually encounter two kinds: seasoned and unseasoned. âUnseasoned rice vinegar has a clean, mild acidity with a subtle sweetness,â says Jae Seong Ha, head chef at Jeong Yuk Jeom restaurant in New York. That makes it a natural fit for Korean dressings, marinades, and pickled vegetables. We also like it in this Crispy Rice Salad with Spicy Tahini Dressing, tomato-basil salad, Salt and Pepper Fish, and miso-caramel glazed salmon. Seasoned rice vinegar contains added sugar and salt, making it especially convenient for sushi rice and certain dressings. Wondering about rice wine vinegar? âThe terms ârice vinegarâ and ârice wine vinegarâ are used interchangeably,â Ha says. âWhen shopping, I pay more attention to the ingredient list and whether the vinegar is seasoned or unseasoned.â To substitute unseasoned rice vinegar, try Champagne or white wine vinegar. If you need seasoned rice vinegar, start with unseasoned and add a little sugar and salt to taste. You can do the same with another mild vinegar in a pinch. Dark, earthy, and deeply savory, black vinegar brings considerably more than acidity to a dish. There are several styles, including Chinkiang vinegar from China, but theyâre generally made from fermented grains, such as rice, wheat, or sorghum. âIt has a little sweetness, a malty character, and more fermentation flavorâ than milder rice vinegar, says Cheng Lin, chef-owner of Shota Omakase in Brooklyn. He likes it with dumplings, noodles, âand other dishes where you want the vinegar to have a stronger presence.â Try black vinegar in dipping sauces for scallion pancakes, splashed into a cabbage stir-fry or Black Vinegar Chicken With Radishes, or whisked into a punchy dressing. A little goes a long way. Thereâs no substitute for black vinegar's complex, distinctive flavor. If youâre in a pinch, Lin suggests combining balsamic and unseasoned rice vinegar. âIt wonât be exactly the same, but it gives you some of that darker, sweeter, aged character.â If youâve eaten fish and chips, youâve probably tasted malt vinegar. Made from malted barley, it can range from amber to dark brown, and has a sweet, nutty tang and a toasted flavor. Itâs hard to beat on french fries, but we'd happily splash it over roasted or steamed potatoes, or stir it into mayonnaise for dipping sweet potato wedges too. Malt vinegar can also lend depth to Sweet-and-Sour Tomato Chutney and other sauces. Reduce it with chiles and molasses for a sticky glaze for roast chicken, or use it in a tangy lamb chop marinade. For fried foods, a squeeze of lemon will provide a similar bright finish, though not malt vinegarâs toasty flavor. Apple cider or sherry vinegar is a reasonable stand-in for sauces and glazes. Made from fermented sugarcane juice, cane vinegar is a staple in many Filipino kitchensâand important in many other cuisines, too, but the category is broad. Sukang maasim is an all-purpose white (clear) cane vinegar, while sukang Iloko is a darker variety hailing from the countryâs north, often made from clay-aged sugarcane wine (basi). Its flavor varies by producer and region, but it generally offers a clean, sometimes subtly sweet acidity. Itâs a key ingredient in Philippine adobo, often balanced with soy sauce and aromatics like black pepper and bay leaf. Kumar also points to cane vinegarâs importance in Northern Indian pickling traditions, including sirka pyaaz, tangy onions commonly served alongside kebabs. It also works well in dipping sauces or infused with chiles for a spicy, tangy condiment. If you can't find cane vinegar, try unseasoned rice vinegar or apple cider vinegar, depending on the dish. Neither is an exact match, but both can provide the acidity you need. Coconut vinegar is another popular option in regions that favor cane vinegar, and can also work well in similar applications. The world of vinegars is vast. Other varieties include honey vinegar, made from mead and vaguely similar to white balsamic; akazu, a beautifully layered red vinegar that comes from aged sake lees; and roasty-toasty beer vinegar, a good swap for malt vinegar. Coconut vinegar, made from fermented coconut sap, is another versatile option, especially in Filipino and South Asian cooking. Kumar says its flavor is âdistinctive and slightly funkyâ and that it works well in dipping sauces, marinades, and rich, savory dishes. Which vinegar has the mildest flavor? Unseasoned rice vinegar and Champagne vinegar are good choices when you want acidity without an overpowering flavor. White wine vinegar is another versatile option. Distilled white vinegar has a neutral flavor, but a sharpness that can make it aggressive in some dishes. Can you substitute one type of vinegar for another? Usually, yes. Red and white wine vinegars can often stand in for each other, though red wine vinegar has a bolder flavor. Apple cider vinegar works well in place of white wine vinegar, while unseasoned rice vinegar is a good choice when you want something milder. Balsamic and black vinegars have more distinctive flavors and are harder to replace. For home canning and shelf-stable pickling, follow a tested recipe and use vinegar with the specified acidity rather than making substitutions based on taste alone. Which vinegar is best for salad dressing? You know that old saying: The limit does not exist. And a simple vinaigrette is a great way to taste the nuances of a new-to-you vinegar. That said, red wine, white wine, Champagne, and sherry vinegars are all commonly used in Western-style salad dressings. Red wine vinegar works particularly well with bold ingredients like tomatoes and olives, while Champagne and white wine vinegars complement delicate greens. Reach for sherry vinegar when you want something a little richer and nuttier. Does vinegar need to be refrigerated? Most commercially produced vinegars don't need refrigeration. âVinegar is actually very easy to take care of,â Lin says. He recommends storing bottles tightly closed in a cool, dark cabinet away from sunlight and heat. Some vinegars may become cloudy or develop harmless sediment over time, but that doesn't necessarily mean they've spoiled. Homemade infused vinegars may require refrigeration. What are the essential vinegars to keep in your pantry? The answer depends on what you cook. One way to cover your bases is with something mild and versatile, like unseasoned rice vinegar; something fruity, like red wine or apple cider vinegar; and something distinctive, like sherry or balsamic. But if chicken adobo is in heavy rotation, youâre going to want a steady supply of cane vinegar. Love fish and chips? Don't skip the malt. Whatever your pleasure, thereâs no wrong way to take an acid trip.

item.title: A Rare Super El Niño Is on the Way. Here Is Where Snow Will Fall.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
You’ve probably heard about the weather phenomenon called Super El Niño, which climate scientists predict will impact winter weather. And if you’re a skier, this year’s Super El Niño could bring some pretty good news, with parts of the American West expected to get more snow than usual. According to the 2026-27 winter forecast by AccuWeather, a U.S. weather prediction service, parts of the Sierra Nevada, Great Basin, Wasatch Range, and Central Rockies could see above-average snowfall this season, with parts of the Southern Rockies also expected to get more snow than last winter (which, let’s be real, wouldn’t really be hard to do). Meanwhile, much of the Northeast, Midwest, and Pacific Northwest might not be so lucky. AccuWeather’s lead long-range forecaster Paul Pastelok told Outside that California, Utah, and Colorado should all have favorable skiing conditions this winter, though California could experience more frequent storms and greater travel disruptions. “The West definitely looks like a better bet for skiers hoping to find consistently good snow conditions this winter, largely because of how strong this El Niño is,” Pastelok said. Pastelok told Outside that the term Super El Niño isn’t an official scientific classification. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) categorizes El Niño events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong, depending on how much warmer than normal the tropical Pacific Ocean becomes. “Super” is simply a weatherperson’s way of saying “very strong.” And this year’s El Niño could be one for the record books. Every few years, waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become unusually warm. That extra heat changes where air rises, clouds form and rain falls, which can alter weather patterns thousands of miles away. One of the biggest changes involves the jet stream, a band of fast-moving winds high in the atmosphere that acts a bit like a highway for storms. During an El Niño winter, that highway typically shifts farther south, steering more storms and precipitation toward California and the southern United States. Meanwhile, northern states tend to experience warmer, drier conditions. What makes this year’s El Niño super is the strength of the warming. In its October 8 outlook, NOAA estimated an 83 percent chance that this El Niño would surpass the strength of every event in its historical record dating back to 1950 during the October-to-December period. “The stronger the El Niño gets, the more confident we feel that typical El Niño conditions will occur,” Pastelok told Outside. Here’s where AccuWeather expects the snow to fall, and what that means for skiers. California could see repeated bouts of heavy mountain snow as a series of Pacific storms, including atmospheric rivers, moves inland. Pastelok expects several atmospheric rivers to arrive during the winter, specifically during the middle and latter parts of the season. Those storms could deliver feet of snow in the mountains, although heavy precipitation could also create flooding and landslide risks at lower elevations. “There may be more snow in California,” Pastelok said, comparing the state’s outlook with Utah and Colorado. “But the downside for California is that it could be much stormier, making travel to ski resorts more difficult than in Utah or Colorado.” Utah’s Wasatch Range is also expected to benefit from an active southern storm track, with above-average snowfall possible across the region. AccuWeather predicts Salt Lake City will receive between 50 and 65 inches of snow this winter, compared with just 3.7 inches last season, the city’s least snowy winter on record. Those figures represent snowfall in the city rather than the nearby mountains, where accumulations are substantially greater. That’s good news for skiers hoping to carve turns at Park City, Snowbird, Alta, and the region’s other world-famous resorts. Colorado and the Central and Southern Rockies could also see a significant improvement over last winter. AccuWeather expects an early start to the snow season across the region, with additional storms arriving as winter progresses. By February, the Four Corners region is forecast to experience cooler-than-average temperatures and above-average precipitation, conditions that could support additional mountain snowfall. Pastelok said Colorado might not receive as much snow as California this winter, but should still experience good skiing conditions. The Great Basin, which stretches across Nevada and portions of neighboring states, is another region where AccuWeather expects above-average snowfall. The forecast favors an early start to the snow season across the region, although AccuWeather has not provided specific seasonal accumulation estimates for individual mountain areas. The snow outlook is less promising across much of the Pacific Northwest and Northern Rockies, where periods of snowfall could be interrupted by extended dry stretches. In the Northeast, warmer temperatures and below-average snowfall could create particularly difficult conditions for lower-elevation ski areas. Pastelok said smaller ski areas could struggle to maintain adequate snow coverage as repeated warm spells bring rain and ice. “When people hear that, they assume it’s going to be a bad ski season,” Pastelok said. “And for many smaller, lower-elevation ski areas, that’s probably true. Warmer temperatures, rain and ice are going to make it difficult to keep snow on the slopes.” But higher-elevation resorts in northern Vermont and New Hampshire could fare better, and the region may still experience significant snowstorms in late January or February. He added that three previous Super El Niño winters brought major snowstorms to the Northeast in late January or early February, potentially offering skiers some relief after an otherwise disappointing season. “The season could start out poorly, but a big snowstorm in late January or February could still give skiers a good weekend on the slopes,” he said. Before booking a weeklong ski vacation based on the forecast, there’s one thing worth keeping in mind, Pastelok said. Seasonal snowfall predictions are better at identifying broad weather patterns than predicting conditions at a particular mountain on a particular date. Pastelok said long-range forecasters use historical weather patterns and current atmospheric conditions to identify which regions are most likely to experience active storm periods. But even an exceptionally strong El Niño can throw forecasters a curveball. For example, Pastelok said that during the powerful El Niño of 2015-16, the jet stream shifted farther north than expected, leaving Southern California and the Four Corners region, including Colorado, with less snow than forecasters had anticipated. And even when the storms do arrive, more precipitation doesn’t necessarily mean more snow. If temperatures are warm enough, it could fall as rain instead. AccuWeather plans to update its winter forecast in mid-November, Pastelok said. While a seasonal forecast might help skiers decide which part of the country to visit, figuring out exactly when to book that trip is another matter. “If you’re asking me, should I go on a snow trip on February 2 because we’re going to get a lot of snow right before that?” Pastelok said. “That’s hard for me to tell you right now.”

item.title: Inside the world's last divided capital
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Nicosia: Inside the world's last divided capital Decades after the Berlin Wall fell, Cyprus's capital remains cleaved in two and separated by watchtowers, barbed wire and a UN buffer zone. Moments after passing Nicosia's weathered Venetian walls, I followed a series of chain-link fences topped with barbed wire into a no-man's land. Here, at the checkpoint, I was suddenly surrounded by watchtowers and crumbling buildings in the heart of the United Nations buffer zone – a geopolitical scar cutting directly through Cyprus's capital. A guard inside a pop-up tent eyed our passports before waving us through to the other side. Even though I was in the same city on the same Mediterranean island, I had just left the Republic of Cyprus and the European Union. Now, I was standing in self-declared state of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), in the middle of the world's last divided capital. In 1974, Turkish forces invaded northern Cyprus in response to a military coup backed by the junta ruling Greece, leading to the displacement of 150,000 Greek Cypriots and 50,000 Turkish Cypriots across the island. Ever since, Cyprus, and its capital of Nicosia, has been cleaved in two, with one side ruled by the island's Greek Cypriot majority, and the other run by its Turkish minority. Today, visiting this divided Mediterranean city offers travellers a rare glimpse at a place where residents have been separated from their neighbours for more than 50 years. For the past seven years, I've lived in arguably the world's most famous formerly divided city, Berlin. The scars of the Berlin Wall are a short walk from my home in the former East, and I regularly move across both sides. After learning how the city's decades of division have shaped the place I now call home, I was curious to see the last capital where such a border still remains. Before the war, Cyprus's only international airport was in the heart of Nicosia, but for the last 52 years, its rusting remains have sat abandoned in the middle of the UN buffer zone (known as the Green Line). So I flew into Paphos, a coastal city in south-west Cyprus, and took a two-hour bus ride to Nicosia, where I signed up for the Walk Talk Cyprus tour led by local Greek Cypriot Eleni Ellinas. "I started this journey because I felt that Cyprus, and Nicosia in particular, is often oversimplified or misunderstood by outsiders," she said. "People read about the conflict in history books or news headlines, but they rarely get to feel the living, breathing soul of the city or understand what daily life actually looks like along a crossing." Ellinas was just four years old when years of ethnic and nationalist tensions between Greek and Turkish Cypriots led Turkish forces to invade northern Cyprus. The fighting forced her family out of their home in Famagusta (modern-day Gazimağusa, in the TRNC) and into a refugee camp on the island's south-eastern coast. "Life in the camp was harsh," she recalled. "My mother, sister, and I were ill. When my father came to check on us and saw the dire conditions we were living in, he knew he had to save his family. He managed to drive us to the RAF base in Akrotiri, and we were fortunate to be evacuated by British forces to the UK." Their hearts never left Cyprus, so in 1980, the family returned to the island and relocated in Nicosia. "This city welcomed us, embraced our broken pieces and slowly became the place where we laid down new roots and made a home." In 1983, a separate Turkish Cypriot state was established unilaterally. Yet, it wasn't until 2003 that travellers and Cypriots alike – both Greek and Turkish – were allowed to cross the internationally unrecognised border separating each side. Today, the Republic of Turkey is the only nation to officially recognise the TRNC. Ellinas says she remembers crossing the border for the first time since fleeing like it was yesterday. "Stepping across was like walking straight into a dream," she said. "As I walked through those neighbourhoods for the first time as an adult, it felt like I was stepping back into the 1970s… It felt completely surreal, overwhelming and deeply emotional." In 2019, Ellinas launched her tours "to share the soul of the island I love so dearly" and convey that emotion to travellers. Ellinas' tours start at the Ledra Palace Checkpoint, the first crossing that Turkish Cypriot authorities opened inside the demilitarised UN Green Line in 2003. The Ledra Palace was once Cyprus's most famous hotel, a luxury property that opened in 1949 and frequently hosted politicians and actors like Elizabeth Taylor, Richard Burton and Sophia Loren. It also became the site of intense fighting during the 1974 invasion. Bullet holes can still be seen throughout the exterior, walled off today by UN peacekeeping forces with barbed wire. Following the ceasefire, it was used as a headquarters and barracks for UN peacekeepers until 2019. Today, homes and other buildings caught in the middle of the buffer zone remain abandoned and frozen in time. On the other end of the road near the Ledra Palace, Ellinas pointed out the TRNC border crossing. The word "FOREVER" stands in large, emboldened red letters underneath the name "Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus". Similarly, a giant TRNC flag painted on the hillside north of Nicosia with the message, "How happy is he who says I am a Turk" is visible from the Greek side. Ellinas expressed disappointment over the nationalistic messaging and expressed hope that the island will one day be reunited. "While some [Cypriots] remain stuck in the past, there is an overwhelming longing for unity felt by many," she said. "You see this energy bringing new life to areas like the restored streets around Ermou [the city's premier shopping hub up until the war] where art, youth and community are reclaiming space that was once deserted and dead." To help visitors experience both sides of Nicosia, Ellinas encourages all travellers to cross into the Turkish side following the end of her tour. "You cannot truly understand a divided capital by looking at it through a single window," she said. "You have to feel both perspectives." Plan your trip: The UK and US don't have any travel warnings to Cyprus. Non-EU citizens need a passport to cross the UN buffer zone in Nicosia, whereas EU citizens can simply present a national ID card or passport. Since the Greek side uses the Euro and the Turkish side uses the Turkish lira, most international travellers choose to stay in the southern Greek Cypriot side. For her, Cyprus is still in many ways one place. The two sides have a shared history, architecture, and in her words, pain. "Suffering was experienced by all Cypriots, regardless of background," she said. "When you step across and walk through places like the old Armenian quarter in Arab Ahmet, or stroll down historic Victoria Street, it feels as though time stood frozen in place. Seeing the old homes, breathing in the quiet atmosphere, and connecting the human threads on both sides gives travellers a complete, empathetic picture of what this island truly is." Passing through the checkpoint in the UN buffer zone and stepping foot into the TRNC felt like entering a different country. Whereas the Green Line along the Greek side was marked by abandoned buildings, the Turkish side appeared much livelier. Pedestrians spilled out onto the narrow streets, the savoury aroma of Turkish kebabs filled the air and a domed mosque from a 16th-Century caravanserai soon appeared before me. I visited some of the sights that Ellinas had recommended, namely the 16th-Century Büyük Han caravanserai and the Samanbahçe Evler neighbourhood – a one-of-a-kind social housing estate with geometric mud-brick units. The highlight, though, was my stop at the Rüstem Kitabevi, a bookstore founded in 1937 where I sipped coffee and ate carrot cake after admiring towers of hardback tomes spread across two floors. Ali Rüstem's father started the business out of his grandfather's house in 1937 when Cyprus was under British colonial rule (1878-1960). Born in 1971, Rüstem was too young to remember much of Cyprus before the buffer zone divided it in two. He says that he has good friends from the Greek community, but for people of his generation, it's normal for Nicosia to be segregated between the two communities. "Of course, things could always be better," he said, adding that he hopes for more "common sense" and "logic" between the Greek and Turkish administrations. In the meantime, like Ellinas, he encourages travellers to also visit the Greek side to experience the different cultures firsthand. As Ellinas told me: "Nicosia isn't just a divided city of the past. It is a living, breathing, hopeful city where people are reaching across borders to heal, rebuild and belong to one another again." – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
I havenât made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what Iâd make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if youâre lucky, theyâre also stuffed with a nutty cheese)âthis style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casingâs texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid. Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6â8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1â1Â½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate. Step 2Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and Â½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Â¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6â8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute. Step 3Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1Â½ cups apple cider, 1Â½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, Â½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining Â½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Â¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30â35 minutes. Step 4Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

item.title: The ghost town that almost became Aspen
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
'A fortune of failures': The Colorado ghost town that almost became Aspen On a crisp June day, I wander among the empty log cabins in the ghost town of Ashcroft, 12 miles (19.3km) from Aspen at the base of Colorado's Elk Mountains. The only sounds are the rustling of aspen leaves, the gurgle of Castle Creek and the occasional whistle of a high-elevation warbler. In winter, save for the distant glide of cross-country skiers or the soft clop of snowshoes, the valley is nearly silent. It's hard to reconcile this quiet place with the booming mining town that once stood here – or with the ambitious plan, nearly 100 years ago, to transform it into a major European-style ski resort. "Ashcroft would have been Aspen," says Aspen Historical Society archivist Anna Lookabill. "I don't think Aspen would have happened had the Ashcroft plans come together." Before Aspen became a playground for the rich and famous, home to high-end boutiques and $25m mansions, the two towns were rivals – first for silver, then for skiing. In 1879, prospectors poured into Colorado's Roaring Fork Valley in search of silver, establishing camps at Independence and Aspen. By the following year, Ashcroft had become one of the region's hottest mining towns. "The ore was close to the surface in Ashcroft compared to Aspen," Lookabill says. "It had the potential to be a good investment early on. Aspen was slower to get going because the ore was a little deeper." Walking between Ashcroft's surviving log cabins, it's hard to reconcile the quiet with the town that once stood here. At its peak in 1882, more than 1,000 people lived here, with hotels, mercantile stores, a bowling alley, dance hall, 14 saloons and Pitkin County's first school. But the boom was short-lived. Within a few years, the population had collapsed to around 100, with many residents and businesses relocating to Aspen. By the 1930s, nearly all of Ashcroft's buildings were abandoned. But a group of business associates who had skied in Europe – Ted Ryan, T J Flynn and Olympic bobsled gold medallist Billy Fiske – saw something in the empty valley surrounded by towering peaks: the making of a ski resort. They formed the Highland Bavarian Corporation and brought in Swiss mountaineer André Roch to survey the surrounding peaks on touring skis. He chose Hayden Peak above Ashcroft as the centrepiece. "Mount Hayden was going to be the mountain with the ski area. Ashcroft would be the Bavarian village," Lookabill says. Ashcroft would have been Colorado's first major ski area – and, at the time, the world's highest. Plans included a tram from Ashcroft up Hayden Peak, dozens of ski runs and several chairlifts. Today, visitors can look up from the ghost town to where the ski area would have climbed above 13,000ft (3,962m) and the slopes would have taken skiers directly into town. Why go: For an atmospheric excursion from Aspen that combines ghost-town history with hiking, cross-country skiing and snowshoeing in the Elk Mountains. Best time: February for snow, or June for quieter trails. What to do: Join a snowshoe tour or rent cross-country skis and explore the 22 miles of groomed trails. In summer, explore the ghost town on foot. Where to stay: Experienced backcountry skiers can recreate Roch's stripped-back touring experience at the Markley Hut, reached via a 2.3-mile (3.7km) climb on skis, snowshoes or splitboard. Less rugged travellers can stay in downtown Aspen at The Gant or Limelight Hotel. The Highland Bavarian Corporation secured $650,000 in state and federal funding and development was about to begin. Then, World War Two cancelled the entire plan. "They had the ski area laid out, the tram laid out. Washington was allocating funds to build this ski area, because it was going to be the new tourism driver for the US. They had an order for steel to build the lifts and the tram," Lookabill says. "The US needed the steel to build tanks and fighter planes." While Ashcroft's plans stalled, skiing took hold down the valley. Roch had already begun teaching locals how to ski, launching The Roaring Fork Winter Sports Club (which eventually became today's prestigious Aspen Valley Ski and Snowboard Club), and leading touring groups around Mount Hayden. For easier access, he marked a run on Aspen Mountain – still called "Roch Run" – and Ryan oversaw the installation of the first lift: a "boat tow" built with old mine hoists, a second-hand motor and a pair of sleds. It marked the beginning of Aspen's transformation into a ski resort, and effectively ended Ashcroft's chances of becoming one. What Ashcroft was left with was the landscape itself. Today, rather than luxury lodges, visitors find a handful of preserved cabins surrounded by 22 miles (35km) of Nordic ski trails and snowshoe routes in winter, with horseback riding and hiking taking over in summer. Though Ashcroft is an easy drive from Aspen, there are no chairlifts or cable cars; in winter, human-powered travel is the only way to explore the pristine valley. Johnny Wilcox, whose father bought Ashcroft Ski Touring from Ryan in 1986, runs guided horseback tours and winter skiing and snowshoeing. His family also operates the gourmet Pine Creek Cookhouse. "The ultimate experience is to ski up here at night with a headlamp on," Wilcox says. "That brings you the closest to the mining and ski history, breaking trail through the snow with no chairlift to be seen." That absence is part of Ashcroft's appeal. While just down the road, Aspen buzzes with four ski resorts, fine dining and fashion boutiques, Ashcroft sits along Castle Creek, surrounded by pine forests, aspen groves and empty, treeless summits. "That's largely what makes this valley special," Wilcox says. "It's a step back in time. We don't have snow mobile tours. We have no Wi-Fi, no cell service. We are off the grid. In the winter, it's not easy to get here, so people who come really want to be here." Walking between the ghost town's surviving cabins – one a former dance hall, another a saloon – it is difficult to imagine an Aspen-sized town with thousands of visitors, a tram humming overhead and skiers skidding to a halt amid multi-million-dollar houses. "I always think of Ashcroft as a fortune of failures," Lookabill says. "It was a boomtown and it died off. There was potential of being a ski area, that ended up dying off. Now it's a touristy place, but a large, open, beautiful space. These booms, or fortunes that failed, ultimately preserved it." – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.
