item.title: Make-Ahead Mashed Potatoes
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Thanksgiving dinner can feel like a game of Tetris, but this make-ahead mashed potato recipe gives you one less thing to juggle. It lets you prepare the potatoes up to two days in advance, then reheat them just before serving without sacrificing their rich flavor or velvety texture. The secret is in the technique: Simmer whole, skin-on Yukon Gold potatoes to keep them from absorbing excess water, then pass them through a potato ricer with plenty of butter. Adding the butter before the warm milk and cream coats the potato starches in fat, helping the mash stay smooth and creamy even after refrigeration. A little sour cream adds a welcome tang. For extra flavor, try adding roasted garlic, finely grated Parmesan, or infusing the milk and cream, as we do in BAâs Best Mashed Potatoes, with bay leaves, thyme, or rosemary. Tips and FAQ for make-ahead mashed potatoes How far in advance can you make mashed potatoes? Up to two days. Let the finished mashed potatoes cool slightly, then cover and refrigerate promptly. Need a longer head start? Learn how to freeze mashed potatoes. How do you reheat mashed potatoes without making them gummy? Gently warm them in a saucepan over medium-low heat with the additional milk and cream to restore the proper consistency. Stir often but gently to prevent scorching without overworking the potatoes, which can turn them gluey. Why are my mashed potatoes watery? The potatoes may have absorbed too much water during cooking. For this recipe, simmer them whole, with the skins on, until very tender but not falling apart. Drain well and let them dry in the warm pot before ricing. Add the warm milk and cream gradually, stopping when the potatoes reach your desired consistency. Do you need to peel the potatoes? No. Leaving the skins on while boiling helps prevent waterlogging, and most of the peels will stay behind in the ricer. Clear out the collected skins between batches to prevent clogging. If you prefer to peel the potatoes yourself, do so after cooking, while theyâre still warm. Can you make mashed potatoes without a ricer? A food mill fitted with a fine disk is your best alternative. A potato masher will produce a less uniform texture and requires peeling the potatoes first. Avoid a food processor or blender, which can overwork the starches and make the potatoes gluey. - OXO Good Grips Stainless Steel Potato Ricer $35 At Amazon - Rubbermaid Brilliance Glass Food Storage Containers $80 At Amazon Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Place 4 lb. medium Yukon Gold potatoes, scrubbed, in a large pot and pour in cold water to cover by 1". Add a large handful of kosher salt (water should taste briny, like the ocean) and bring to a boil. Reduce heat and simmer until potatoes are very tender but not crumbly, 30â40 minutes. Drain and return potatoes to warm pot to dry (off heat). Step 2Meanwhile, heat â cup heavy cream and â cup whole milk in a small saucepan over medium until just about to simmer. Reduce heat to low and keep warm until ready to add to potatoes. Step 3Pass hot potatoes and 1Â¼ cups (2Â½ sticks) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, through ricer into a large bowl (this will help combine them quickly; most of the skins should stay behind, but pick out any small pieces that get through if you want); season generously with salt. Mix with a potato masher until butter is melted and combined. Step 4Gradually add half of the warm cream mixture to mashed potatoes, folding with a spatula until combined, followed by Â½ cup sour cream. Gradually add remaining cream mixture until you reach your desired consistency (the potatoes will thicken slightly as they sit). Taste and season with salt and freshly ground black pepper as desired. Step 5Transfer mashed potatoes to a baking dish or other shallow container, let them cool until the potatoes stop steaming, then cover and chill up to 2 days. Step 6To serve, transfer refrigerated potatoes to a small pot and add â cup heavy cream and â cup whole milk; reheat over medium-low, stirring often (but gently) to prevent scorching. Editorâs note: This recipe for make-ahead mashed potatoes was first published in our November 2018 issue; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more great make-ahead Thanksgiving recipes â

item.title: 5 Quick Dishes Our Editors Make With Marinated Artichokes
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Each month in Well Stocked, our staff shares unfussy recipe ideas that you can call upon any day of the week. Because yes, our editors love to cook, but sometimes we need to get dinner on the table 12 minutes ago. Thatâs when we look to pantry and fridge staples that can quickly morph into delicious meals. This month, itâs all about marinated artichokes. Oh, the artichoke: an aloof green globe, made up of scale-like leaves and a fuzzy interior. But the flavor? So vegetal, so buttery. As a member of the thistle family, the raw vegetable takes a fair amount of trimming and coaxing (including removing the spiky part aptly known as the choke) before itâs good to go. And after youâve wrestled it into submission, thereâs not a ton to show for all that effort. Which is part of the appeal of marinated artichokesâthe kind you get in a jar. Tender, tangy, and genuinely ready to eat, theyâre a shortcut worth taking, adding a bright hit of acidity and a satisfying meaty texture to all kinds of dishes. Toss them into a pantry-friendly pasta with speckles of salty pancetta. Mix them into a no-cook antipasto salad. Even nestle them into an unhinged sandwich. Read on for five smart ways our editors put them to work. A last-minute galette happens to be my specialty, and marinated artichokes are the perfect addition. You could make this full recipe, which involves a simple cream cheese filling, those âchokes, and asparagus, plus a vinaigrette-dressed arugula topping. But you could also just toss the artichokes with whatever other veg you have in the fridge and a couple spoonfuls of marinade, maybe some grated parm if you have it, into a rolled out puff pastry crust. âRebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor My team knows my love for a good potato salad, as I sing its virtues all the time. Marinated artichokes are a killer ingredient to add to a French- or German-style potato salad thatâs heavy on the vinaigrette: Add chopped marinated artichokes and their brine to just-cooked potatoes, which will hungrily drink up the juice. Standard marinated artichokes are fine; grilled marinated artichokes (like the jarred ones at Trader Joeâs) are even better. âHana Asbrink, deputy food editor Itâs saved my butt many times: antipasto pantry pasta. (Antipantry pasta? Hm. No.) I raid my cupboard for salty-savory-oily things like olives, capers, roasted peppers, sun-dried tomatoes, chickpeas, and, of course, marinated artichokes. Mix everything in a bowl while the pasta boils. Throw in some mozzarella if thereâs any around. Takes 15 minutes tops and always hits the spot. âEmma Laperruque, cooking director My fanciest 20-minute dinner involves a couple of sheet-pan fish fillets surrounded by frilly burnished artichoke hearts. Iâll simply brush some of the marinating juices over salmon or whatever flaky white fish my seafood share provided that week, then save the rest for a finishing drizzle. The drained artichokes go right on the same pan. Then it goes into the oven for about 15 minutes and dinnerâs ready. For what itâs worth, those crispy âchokes are also great for a vegetarian Italian-style deli sandwich. âJoe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking My bakery days taught me many things, chief among them that ricotta deserves a little fluffing. I loosely follow this recipe and whip it until smooth, then pile it onto pan-fried toast with sizzled artichokes and capers (two dependable ingredients always stationed in my pantry). I like to top the toasts with an herb salad: usually basil and dill dressed in the brine from the artichoke jar. Let no drop go to waste. âNina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

item.title: Why Red Bull Got Into the Ski Business—And Teamed Up with an Austrian Racing Legend to Do It
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Plenty of skiers are gear-obsessed, but Marcel Hirscher is in a league of his own. Over the course of his 15-year racing career, the legendary Austrian skier and founder of VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports would drive his coaches and teammates crazy with constant chatter about tech specs and modifications. Maybe not the guy you want to challenge in gear trivia, but definitely the guy you want designing your skis. Which is why he’s the first person to convince Red Bull to co-own a ski brand. Born in Salzburg and raised in the Austrian Alps, Hischer made his World Cup debut in March 2007 and found himself catapulted into the limelight. In 2008, he bagged his first World Cup podium, and in 2009, his first win. Over the next 10 years, he became the winningest Austrian ski racer of all time, turning heads with masterful racing strategy and unparalleled technique. Credit those skills to his uncompromising perfectionism, a characteristic that drove him to 67 World Cup wins, two Olympic gold medals, and eight consecutive overall World Cup titles. And when he retired from ski racing in 2019, it’s what drove him to start manufacturing his own skis. Hirscher has always been a tinkerer by nature—maddeningly meticulous and chronically detail-oriented. Red Bull already knew that after a decade of working with him as a sponsor and supporter. So, when Hirscher said he was launching his own company in 2021, their ears perked up. Hischer called his brand VAN DEER, a name that plays up his half-Dutch heritage and winks at the fact that hirsch is German for “deer.” The goal was to give the brand some racing pedigree without directly naming it after a pro. After all, Hirscher never set out to make skis just for the elite. Hirscher’s overarching philosophy is that all skiers are equal. It doesn’t matter if you’re a bunny-hill newbie, a weekend warrior, or a champion racer. Everyone can benefit from a ski that fits, and everyone can access the sublime sense of flow and rhythm that only skiing can offer. “Nothing feels quite like a perfectly carved turn,” Hirscher says. “When a ski truly fits its skier, you feel it through a certain naturalness of movement.” He’s honed his sensitivity to that feeling through decades of racing. Now, he’s applying that fine-tuned sensibility to ski design. “For a ski racer, skiing is a constant search for hundredths of a second, where even a tiny change in edge angle or flex can make a huge difference,” says Hirscher. “The real challenge is transferring that knowledge from the racecourse to everyday skiers in a way that makes them better.” That process requires converting raw data and physics into the unquantifiable feeling of human movement. That’s the alchemy Hirscher lives for. He spent the first months of his new project immersed in the all-consuming process of design. Then Red Bull stopped by. After such a longstanding partnership, maybe it’s no wonder that Hirscher and Red Bull had developed a strikingly similar vision for the future of alpine skiing. Regardless, a collab was an easy yes. Red Bull got a peek at what Hirscher was doing, liked what they saw, and came on as a partner in 2022. The result: VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports. Since then, the Alps-based brand has become a beacon of Austrian heritage. The skis are sleek, classic, and no-nonsense. Their craftsmanship is decidedly traditional, but the high-tech materials and rigorous testing are as modern as it gets. The skis get put through their paces on mountains all over the world—including on World Cup courses where they’ve already earned gold medals and dozens of podium finishes. Hirscher even wore them himself when he returned to racing for the 2024/25 season. Better yet, the athletes who ride those skis deliver their feedback to VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports, a tight-knit partnership that continues to drive the pace of innovation. Two of those skis—the FREERIDE SERIES, which is exactly what it sounds like, and the H-POWER SERIES, which is designed for all-day skiing in any terrain—bring Hirscher’s profound knowledge and racing heritage to skiers across a wide range of skill levels. The new launches are also designed to complement the brand’s four existing lines: the PRO SERIES, RACE SERIES, JUNIOR PRO SERIES, and TOURING SERIES. “My mission is to make the feeling I have while skiing accessible to others,” Hirscher says. “With us, there is no racing privilege when it comes to material quality—we build skis with World Cup quality, adapted for free skiing.” Because while World Cup racing will always have a special place in Hirscher’s heart, his primary mission is to help up-and-coming skiers accelerate their mastery of the sport he loves. The goal isn’t only to help that new generation win more medals. It’s to help them fall in love with skiing—with each drop, each pole-plant, each turn—exactly in the same way he did. At VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports, founded in the Austrian Alps by ski legend Marcel Hirscher, we do things differently. We believe in the power of “new” and a no-compromise approach to skiing and equipment. Together with Red Bull, we combine racing expertise with innovation to create world-class skis for a new generation.

item.title: The ultimate guide to Alaska cruise ports and attractions
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
The ultimate guide to Alaska cruise ports and attractions An Alaska cruise is the adventure of a lifetime, offering the promise of frontier towns, impeccable scenery, cold beer, fresh seafood and a world of adventure to enjoy ashore. If you're cruising on a big ship, chances are good you'll be stopping at the "Big Three" ports: Ketchikan, Juneau and Skagway, Alaska. But there are a plethora of smaller — though no less interesting — ports of call that ships big and small can call on during voyages to Alaska from both Vancouver, British Columbia, and Seattle. If you leave from the latter, you're guaranteed to stop in at least one Canadian port of call in order to satisfy U.S. cabotage laws. Here is our ultimate guide to Alaskan cruise ports of call. These are the go-to ports of call. The standards. The "OG" ports, as the kids say. No first-time trip to Alaska is complete without a visit to one of these mainstay ports filled with history and adventure. Sometimes referred to as "Alaska's First City" due to its location on the Inside Passage just north of the Canadian border with the United States, Ketchikan instantly charms visitors with its houses and boardwalks built on stilts along the harbor and historic Creek Street district situated not far from the cruise ships. This former Red Light district is now a tourist and photographer's dream come true. Salmon can frequently be seen spawning here in the late summer and early fall. The town's history is tied inexorably to the sea, fishing and the Tlingit Natives that have called this their land for centuries. There are four main cruise berths in Ketchikan, all within walking distance of the main downtown area. Pack your umbrella: If it's going to rain at any point on your journey, it will be here. Rain is omnipresent in Ketchikan, even during the "dry" months. In fact, it rains in Ketchikan approximately 233 days of the year. But Ketchikan is also home to several amazing sights, including Totem Bight State Historical Park; nearby Misty Fjords; excellent fishing and hiking; and family-friendly diversions like the always-fun "Great Alaskan Lumberjack Show." Bring your rain gear and your sense of adventure. It's not hard to fall in love with this little seaside community, rain or shine. Ketchikan (Ward Cove) If you're sailing with Norwegian Cruise Line, Oceania Cruises or luxury brand Regent Seven Seas, you might see Ketchikan (Ward Cove) stamped on your itinerary. And while you'll indeed see Ketchikan, you won't be docked where the other ships are. Located seven miles west of downtown Ketchikan, Ward Cove is a new development that was inaugurated in conjunction with Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings in 2021. Nestled within a beautiful cove (it's one of our favorite sailaways in Alaska), ships calling on Ward Cove discharge passengers into the remains of a former cannery that now functions as a staging area for shops, quick bites, and shore excursions – some of which operate in the wilderness area close by. Here's the downside: You're a 20-minute bus ride from downtown Ketchikan, which dramatically limits your time in town. Buses, particularly those serving bigger ships, can be hot and crowded. We've had buses break down. We've had buses without air conditioning. We've had buses without heating. You name it. Not to mention, when other passengers can hop back on their ship in the heart of town, Ward Cove guests must line up in the sun — or the liquid sun — for their ride back to the ship. You still get to see Ketchikan, but some preplanning is a good idea if your ship is calling on Ward Cove. The state capital of Alaska, Juneau is present on nearly every itinerary sailing to or from Alaska. And while it lacks the quaint charm of Ketchikan or the Klondike vibes of Skagway, Juneau is the port of call that offers more adventure, food, drinks and options for exploration than any other. Completely inaccessible from the mainland by road, Juneau is one of the few U.S. state capitals that you can only reach by sea or air. Ships dock along South Franklin Street and all, with the exception of the southeasternmost dock, the AJ Dock, are within easy walking distance of town. (You can walk into town from the AJ Dock in about 20 minutes, but if it's raining, we don't recommend it.) While the city of Juneau is worth a wander in its own right, most first-timers to Juneau will likely be exploring farther afield. About a 30-minute drive away, Mendenhall Glacier offers some great trails and an interpretive center. Plus, it's the base for several popular soft adventure excursions, including rafting, hiking and even helicopter landings on its pristine surface. Other popular diversions include whale watching and exploring the Gastineau Channel and nearby Auke Bay, while hiking aficionados will find the trails accessible by the Mount Roberts Tram (situated right downtown) to be the perfect thing. If you opt to stay in town, check out heavyweight tourist-approved stalwarts like Tracy's Crab Shack and Alaskan Brewing Company, or stop into The Hangar Pub to get a quick bite and watch the ships and seaplanes come and go. You'll be glad you did. At the end of the Lynn Canal (the deepest, longest fjord in the U.S.), the gold rush-era town of Skagway still looks much as it did in its 1898 heyday. But don't let its (often faux) Klondike appearance deceive you: This is one of the most fascinating and diverse ports in Alaska. To start with, Skagway is charming. Sure, it's a town that exists much for tourists, but the approximately 800 or so locals who live here year-round are dedicated to offering local wares, artisanal crafts, books and more. There are two great breweries in town, plus a charming local distillery to whet your whistle. And, in terms of Alaska, Skagway perhaps offers the wildest lore, from the gun-toting bandit, Soapy Smith, who briefly reigned over the town in 1898, to the herculean feat that is the White Pass & Yukon Route Railway, which now serves tourists instead of tired prospectors on its steep, narrow grades. If you're the active type, you'll want to hike or cycle to the ghost town of Dyea, just up the road. Little remains here save for some pier pilings and a half-collapsed storefront, but Dyea was once as crucial to the gold rush as Skagway. For hikers, Skagway offers some of the best trails you'll see in Southeast Alaska, all within easy walking distance of your ship. And for those seeking a little more adventure, cruise lines often craft shore excursions that take passengers into Canada's Yukon territory to see, among other things, the Carcross Desert — a desert in the middle of a mountainous rainforest. Alaska cruise ports: Off the beaten path Chances are good that your cruise itinerary includes a visit to one of these more off-the-beaten-path ports of call. While some, like Sitka and Icy Strait Point, are becoming as ubiquitous on itineraries as Juneau and Ketchikan, it hasn't always been that way. Ditto for Haines, which sometimes serves as an overflow port of call for nearby Skagway but is worth visiting in its own right. Think of Haines as Skagway's little brother. Home to less than 2,000 people, Haines is located in Lynn Canal, just a quick 60-minute ferry ride from Skagway, which makes day trips to Skagway and its attractions a reality. Likewise, some shore excursions in Skagway will visit Haines. Haines lacks Skagway's grandeur and railroad but makes up for it with its abundant nature. Plenty of hikes, rafting excursions and backcountry treks are possible from here, and the town itself is also worth your time. Be sure to check out the Hammer Museum at the heart of downtown — there's an enormous, inflatable hammer on the front lawn if you need a landmark. It features a "Hammer of the Month" and a seriously impressive collection of this useful tool. Stop in for a pint at one of the local watering holes, or pay a visit to Fort William H. Seward National Historic Landmark, the last of 12 gold rush-era military outposts built in Alaska. If you're not up on your Alaskan history, Sitka might surprise you. This quaint city on the western end of Baranof Island was under Russian rule from 1799 to 1867, when it was called New Archangel. Sitka was also the site of the Alaska Purchase from Russia in 1867 and served as Alaska's capital city until 1906, when it was moved to Juneau. Today, cruise visitors come ashore at a brand-new, purpose-built terminal on the north side of the island, taking shore excursions or the complimentary shuttle bus into town. Smaller ships still anchor in the main bay from time to time and tender passengers ashore to the center of town. Once in town, Sitka's Tlingit and Russian heritage is on display. St. Michael's Cathedral, the first Orthodox cathedral in the New World, still stands in the center of town (though this version is a replica built after a 1966 fire wiped out the original). The Russian Bishop's House National Historic Landmark, dating back to 1842, still stands, as does the Sitka Pioneer Home that dates back to 1913. Also worth your time here is a bear refuge and education center called Fortress of the Bear and a spectacular raptor rehabilitation center called the Alaska Raptor Center, which has been operating for over 40 years. Situated on the northern end of Chichagof Island, just southeast of the entrance to Glacier Bay National Park and Preserve, Icy Strait Point is a manufactured cruise destination. But don't let that put you off. Icy Strait Point, which began welcoming cruise ships in 2004, is a local success story that is well worth your time. Developed in conjunction with Huna Totem Corporation, this former salmon cannery turned Alaska Native-owned tourist destination is staffed almost entirely with residents from the nearby village of Hoonah (which is also a pleasant and easy walk down the road on a nice day). It has two cruise piers connected by a scenic tram, a mountaintop gondola that rises 1,500 feet in the air, and the world's largest ZipRider, which is 5,495 feet long and reaches speeds of up to 60 mph. But Icy Strait Point is also rustic and beautiful. Restaurants with indoor and outdoor seating serve cold brews made specially for Icy Strait Point, along with local salmon chowder and other eats. Visitors can purchase locally made crafts and wares and find plenty of quiet spots to sit and enjoy nature before heading out on a whale-watching excursion, where magnificent sightings are pretty well guaranteed. The creation of Icy Strait Point has ensured the survival of this beautiful spot and the nearby town of Hoonah, making it a mutually beneficial development. One of the prettiest towns you're likely to see in Alaska, Wrangell is mostly visited now by smaller luxury and expedition cruise ships after a failed attempt by Norwegian Cruise Line to turn it into a big-ship port of call back in 2004 and 2005. There's plenty to do here, and it's all within easy reach of your ship. You can hike (a 20-minute walk, really) to nearby Petroglyph Beach State Historic Site, with its ancient rock carvings and gorgeous shoreline, or hike almost 1 1/2 miles along the Rainbow Falls Trail just outside the city limits. You can also pay a visit to Chief Shakes Tribal House, a faithful replica of the traditional Tlingit house of the Naanya.aayi Clan. You might also enjoy the authentically gritty bars and general whimsy of the town itself; our favorite sighting was a hairdresser along the main drag with the business name "I'll Cut You." If you're looking for big shopping deals or duty-free trinkets, you should know that this is not that kind of port — and that's precisely why we're in love with it. It's an authentically Southeast Alaskan experience. Don't forget these Canadian ports of call If you're leaving on a cruise out of Seattle, you'll be calling on at least one Canadian port of call, thanks to U.S. legislation that requires all foreign-flagged cruise ships (most likely, yours) to call on a "distant foreign port" before returning to Seattle. That's where these little Canadian gems come into play. Conversely, you might call on some of these Canadian ports if you're setting sail on a longer itinerary or if you've chosen a luxury or expedition cruise — smaller ships love smaller ports of call. So close to Ketchikan you could practically reach out and touch it, the port of Prince Rupert is steadily becoming more popular with cruise ships headed to Alaska. Located in the Canadian province of British Columbia, the traditional home of the Coast Tsimshian (shim-shan) people is home to the third-busiest cargo port in Canada nestled within North America's deepest ice-free harbor. There's plenty of natural and Indigenous history to enjoy in Prince Rupert, from hikes along the Butze Rapids Trail to the picturesque Sunken Garden right in the heart of the city. Near the port, a Japanese fishing vessel, the Kazu Maru, has been preserved for years after it washed ashore on the coast of British Columbia in 1987. Its owner, Kazukio Sakamoto, had set out for a fishing trip from the Japanese port of Owase nearly two years earlier and never returned. The vessel has been preserved in Prince Rupert ever since it was found. Victoria, the provincial capital of British Columbia, is best described as a slice of Victorian England on North America's west coast. It's filled with turn-of-the-century buildings, including the gorgeous Parliament Buildings, which are attractively lit every evening. Victoria is home to a number of world-famous attractions, including afternoon tea at the Fairmont Empress hotel, which overlooks the Inner Harbour, and The Butchart Gardens, a sprawling 55-acre, 121-year-old garden in nearby Brentwood Bay. Most big ships call here only from 8 p.m. to midnight on their way back to Seattle, but don't let the short visit put you off. Buses whisk guests from the ships to the Inner Harbour, allowing for visits to local restaurants, pubs or even the acclaimed Fairmont Empress hotel for a nightcap. If you're visiting while it's still light (or don't mind a nighttime stroll), Victoria's downtown attractions are just a 25-minute walk from the piers at Ogden Point. Some luxury cruise brands and lines like Cunard make Victoria an all-day affair, allowing for a wide range of adventures in this charming Canadian city.

item.title: Connecticut's forgotten witch trial past
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Connecticut's forgotten witch trial past Decades before Salem, Connecticut was the centre of America's witch trials. A new statewide haunted history trail connects the towns and sites tied to this overlooked chapter of history. As I wander the tree-lined streets of Windsor, Connecticut's historical Town Green, I'm drawn to a circular patio of red Heritage Bricks – many of which feature inscribed personal tributes to local friends and family. I scan the inscriptions and spot a chilling outlier: "Alice 'Alse' Young: Witch Hanging Victim, May 26, 1647." Young was the first documented person to be executed for witchcraft in the American colonies. While Salem, Massachusetts is intrinsically linked with witch trials, the neighbouring state of Connecticut experienced its own wave of mass hysteria that predates the infamous Salem panic by more than four decades. Now, Young's memorial brick is a stop on Connecticut's new Haunted History Trail, a self-guided statewide route encompassing more than 130 locations – from ancient burial grounds to haunted homes to occult shops – associated with paranormal or tragic stories. Warning: This article contains mentions of hangings that some may find upsetting Boasting a nearly 400-year history, Connecticut is home to an unusual wealth of supernatural sites. But its true witchy past might be scarier than all its ghost stories combined. Occurring between 1647 and 1697, Connecticut's witch trials grew out of the Puritan witch-hunting culture early colonists brought over from England. Salem's witch trials began in 1692 and lasted only 15 months, but during Connecticut's own 50-year witch panic, at least 49 individuals were accused of entering into pacts with the devil or using supernatural powers to cause harm to others. Of those, 34 were indicted and at least 11 were hanged. The last suspected Connecticut witch – Mary Barnes – was executed in 1663 on Hartford's Gallows Hill, but trials continued to be held in the state until 1697. The final American colonial executions for witchcraft took place in Salem in 1692. That Salem held the final witch trial executions helps explain its enduring notoriety – immortalised in films from The Crucible to Hocus Pocus. But why do so few know about Connecticut's dark witch trial past? "We don't know what happened to all those records," says Beth Caruso, co-founder of local historical advocacy group, the Connecticut Witch Trial Exoneration Project. "It may be that when people started being ashamed of these trials, some of the powerful families destroyed [them]." Even as a lifelong Connecticut resident, I knew nothing about its role in the colonial witch trials. So, I set out to drive through one of the darkest chapters of my state's past. Dating to 1633, Windsor's historical centre is filled with red 17th- and 18th-Century gabled houses. It's easy to imagine Puritans in bonnets scurrying through the streets. The city was both Connecticut's first English settlement and Young's hometown when her execution ignited the nation's witch trials. As was often the case in witchcraft accusations, the suspected evidence was thin to the point of absurdity: Young and her daughter survived the 1647 influenza epidemic while four children living next door died. It was enough to see Young hanged in the Connecticut Colony's capital, Hartford. "Her case was pretty unjust, and she suffered," says Caruso. "On top of it, nobody even knows her story." I also find a Heritage Brick honouring another Windsor resident, Lydia Gilbert. Gilbert was tried and executed in 1654 after one of her boarders was accidentally killed during a militia training exercise by a fellow soldier, who was acquitted. It's uncertain why blame shifted to Gilbert. "[She] likely would not have been present on the green at the time of the shooting, as only men served in town militias," writes Caruso. "Supernatural speculations such as this would never hold up in any modern court." Nonetheless, Gilbert was condemned and, like Young, hanged in Hartford. Hartford soon became the epicentre of Connecticut's witch trials. The Hartford Witch Panic (1662-1663), a flurry of trials that concluded in four hangings, began when eight-year-old Elizabeth Kelly, delirious from fever, cried out that her neighbour, Judith Ayres, was choking her. Another woman, Ann Cole, was believed to be possessed by the devil. Executions were carried out at the Meeting House Square, located on the site of the current Old State House. Just a little further along the trail is Hartford's Ancient Burying Ground, where I see the graves of 14 of the men responsible. Established in 1640, the 1.3-acre plot is the city's only surviving 17th-Century landmark. As we strolled among the weather-worn headstones, Christine Jewell, Director of the Ancient Burying Ground's Association, told me about the magistrates and jurors buried here who cooperated in zealously sending people to their doom. Their engraved names are tricky to read, but I can't miss the life-sized statue of Reverend Samuel Stone near the cemetery's entrance. Hartford's co-founder, this Puritan minister was part of a tribunal investigating Connecticut's witchcraft charges. Jewell directed me to the monument of Samuel Wyllys. A prominent Connecticut magistrate, Wyllys was directly involved in investigating witchcraft accusations. His preserved collection of court witchcraft depositions was kept in his family for generations. "Part of what we know about the witchcraft trials is because of the Wyllys family," says Jewell. When to go: The Connecticut Haunted History Trail launched on 16 September 2026. The Halloween season sees atmospheric events including Ghosts of New Haven Tours and Downtown Mystic Ghost Tour, but the self-guided trail can be travelled year-round. Where to learn more: The Windsor Historical Society, which displays a photo of town clerk Matthew Grant's diary page citing Alse Young's hanging, or The Webb Deane Stevens Museum in Wethersfield. Spooky stays: The Griswold Inn in Essex, built in 1776, is widely reported to be haunted. The 1754 House in Woodbury is also believed to be home to several 17th- and 18th-Century ghosts. We also visited the tomb of James Richards, a magistrate involved in the 1665 trial of Elizabeth Seager, on trial for the third time. Her conviction was ultimately overturned by the acting Connecticut Governor John Winthrop Jr. A physician and alchemist, Winthrop often reviewed evidence in witch trial cases, intervening on Seager's behalf and saving Katherine Harrison from a death sentence in 1669. He then helped institute the "two-witness" rule and "rejection of spectral evidence" that effectively ended executions in the state. "They would ask him, 'Was this caused by witchcraft?' And he always said it was medical," said Caruso. "He was a voice of moderation at a time when there weren't a lot of voices of moderation." Before embarking on the trail, I knew nothing about Connecticut's role in the witch trials. But driving through the upscale coastal town of Fairfield – home to four spots on the Haunted History Trail – jogged a memory. While working at a Fairfield newspaper years ago, I'd heard the name Goody Knapp. In Puritan society, "Goody" was an abbreviation of "good wife" – a title for married women of lower status. "We know certain women of the town came to Goody Knapp and [asked] her, 'You are a witch and who else is a witch?'," said Walt Matis, programme and volunteer coordinator of the Fairfield Museum and History Center, the town's first stop on the trail. During Knapp's trial, it was intimated that she had "witches' marks" on her body. But she might not have been accused at all if not for another unfortunate Goody – Goody Bassett, a woman from the neighbouring town of Stratford. It is unclear why Bassett herself was being tried, but during her trial (and likely under torture) she intimated that there was another witch in Fairfield that "held her head full high", says Matis. Bassett was hanged in 1651; Knapp was hanged in 1653 in a field located in what is now Bridgeport. Visitors can find her memorial along the trail at Bridgeport's Burroughs Community Centre. In Fairfield, I also linger at Edward's Pond at the Fairfield Museum and History Center's Museum Commons, built on the town's 17th-Century Town Green. Now merely a divot, Edward's Pond was once used for ducking tests – where accused witches were bound and thrown into water. Floating meant guilt, sinking meant innocence. In 1692, accused and tried persons Elizabeth Clawson and Mercy Disbrow volunteered to be ducked. Both women floated but were eventually acquitted. In need of a pick-me-up after all that gloom, I drive to Stratford, with its charming mix of historic Colonial and coastal bungalow architecture, and duck into Goody Bassett's Ice Cream Shop. "If you're from Stratford, you already knew the name Goody Bassett, so it was a fun name for kids growing up, usually around Halloween," says owner Paul Joy. Joy also honours Bassett on his menu – Goody's Cauldron, a nine-scoop sundae ice-cream eating challenge. It is believed that Bassett was hanged in Stratford, though no official records exist. Local legends pinpoint the town's Meeting House, Gallow's Brook or the former Phelps Mansion as possible sites, says Joy. In the absence of concrete proof, a stone plaque on the trail dedicated to Bassett sits under a tree on Stratford's West Broad Green. Connecticut's connection to witchcraft lives on: 35 stops on the Haunted History Trail are witch and occult shops. I visit The Blackbird House in Wethersfield, a colonial inland port where several alleged witches were accused and hanged. I snoop through tarot decks, crystals and minerals before buying a black witches' hat. Justice may finally be near for Connecticut's accused witches. Caruso and Griego's 2017 petition to clear Young and Gilbert's names resulted in the passing of a unanimous resolution. "I think it was an important reckoning for [Windsor] to actually know what happened," said Caruso. Thanks to the project's efforts, First Church in Windsor, where the fervently anti-witchcraft pastor Reverend John Warham presided, also released an apology. The Connecticut Witch Trial Exoneration project also helps locals with genealogical research. "I kept getting emails and notes from so many descendants, saying 'Thank you for humanising my ancestor'," says Caruso. "It just seemed like the right thing to recognise these victims since we know the stories are so absurd in many cases." In 2023, Connecticut legislators passed a joint resolution exonerating all the state's victims. And now, the Connecticut Haunted History Trail is helping visitors – and locals like me – learn about the victims who were wrongly accused and forgotten, one stop at a time. "More and more people are finding out," says Caruso. "It's not that people don't care. It's just that people don't know."

item.title: Commonly asked questions about Southwest's recent Rapid Rewards reboot and Companion Pass changes
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Commonly asked questions about Southwest's recent Rapid Rewards reboot and Companion Pass changes Southwest announced significant changes to its Rapid Rewards loyalty program on Thursday. The airline will roll out new terminology soon while revising the perks and rules of various pieces of the program, all starting on January 1, 2027. Change often creates confusion, and this change is no exception. Southwest has switched up so many things in the last few years. Even Southwest frequent flyers may feel their heads spinning. There are a lot of ways that the airline is marketing the changes as offering "more opportunity" for customers, and there are a few new modest perks of note. But points and miles enthusiasts who have largely been laser-focused on maximizing status perks or earning a Southwest Companion Pass are mostly losers in the new playbook. We've been hearing some common questions from TPG readers about the latest round of Southwest Rapid Rewards changes and what it means for status on the airline. Is your status changing in meaningful ways relative to your travel habits? Is the Companion Pass really dead? Here's what we know about the answers to these and other common questions. Plus, find out what action steps some Southwest travelers should take now to lock in a few perks before it's too late. What Southwest status level will I hold next year? The new Rapid Rewards program goes into effect on January 1, 2027, meaning that program members with elite status will finish out the current year under a familiar program. For travelers who already have earned status on Southwest in 2026 (or who will before year's end), the transition to the new system in 2027 should be seamless. Rapid Rewards members who earn A-List status in 2026 become Silver for all of 2027 as of January 1, 2027. Similarly, those who earn A-List Preferred status in 2026 will become Gold for all of 2027. The transition won't require any action on the part of customers. The only truly new status that Southwest has created is Platinum, which now will include the coveted unlimited Companion Pass, and no one will start 2027 with that status. Instead, it must be earned under the new 2027 Rapid Rewards program rules. If you want to keep the same Silver or Gold status perks beyond 2027 (or earn the new Platinum status), however, slightly modified earning rules go into effect in the new year. Those rules change the pathway to 2028 Gold and Silver status. Will I lose (or gain) any perks or benefits in 2027 with Silver or Gold, as compared to A-List or A-List Preferred? Once A-List members become Silver and A-List Preferred members become Gold, 2027 will look mostly the same for the vast majority of them. Status perks like free checked bags, early boarding groups, and free seat assignments will remain constant at comparable status tiers. Silver (formerly A-List) members will even see improved earning bonuses on qualifying flight purchases in 2027 and beyond—40% extra instead of 25% that A-List received. Gold (formerly A-List Preferred) members, however, will see their earning bonuses on flight purchases reduced, from 100% to just 60%. Thankfully, Southwest will provide a soft landing for A-List Preferred members who earn status this year. The airline's website states, "Members who earn A-List Preferred status for 2027 based on their 2026 activity will retain their 100% flight-point earning bonus through December 31, 2027. The 60% earning bonus applies to Gold status earned under the new program terms." Southwest is also introducing a few intermediate thresholds (before Silver status and between Gold and Platinum) called "Milestone Rewards" that may result in a few extra perks for some members whose earnings fall between status levels. Under the new rules, members who earn 95,000 TQPs or fly 75 qualifying one-way flights can unlock three Companion Pass trips. Each trip can cover a round-trip itinerary. That's a significant distinction for those of you who won't qualify for Platinum. You can still earn limited Companion Pass benefits without reaching the highest tier. But as with most program loyalty changes, Southwest gives with one hand and takes away with the other. Customers who purchase Southwest's two most expensive fare types, Choice Preferred and Choice Extra, will earn fewer Rapid Rewards points on those purchases starting in 2027. Choice Preferred fares will earn 8 points per dollar spent (previously 10x), and Choice Extra fares will earn 10 points per dollar spent (previously 14x). The combination of these changes could make the program substantially less lucrative for some types of status holders. For example, a member with A-List Preferred status currently earns 28 Rapid Rewards points per dollar spent on Choice Extra fares (14x plus a 100% bonus). By 2028, an equivalent Gold member will only earn 16 points per dollar spent on that same fare (10x plus a 60% bonus)—a mere 57% of previous earnings. In contrast, a Silver member who regularly purchases cheaper Basic or Choice fares will end up a bit better off. What types of points count to determine status or earn a Companion Pass? Under Southwest's current program, there are three types of Rapid Rewards points: those redeemable for airfare, those that also count towards A-List and A-List Preferred status, and those that also count towards Companion Pass qualification. The new system essentially merges the final two categories into a single one: Tier Qualifying Points (TQP). Tier Qualifying Points are the primary way to unlock status (in addition to flying a set number of one-way flights), including the Platinum tier, which now awards an unlimited Companion Pass. There are a number of ways that members will continue to earn Rapid Rewards points that can be redeemed for airfare, but that don't award Tier Qualifying Points. Those include: - Points earned from a co-branded credit card welcome bonus - Status bonuses (the multipliers applied to qualifying airfare purchases for status holders) - Points earned from purchases with many partners (hotels, partner airlines, rental car companies, shopping and dining portals) Many of these methods used to count towards Companion Pass qualification. They won't in 2027. Starting in 2027, there will be a very limited number of ways to earn Tier Qualifying Points on Southwest. The most common will be 1) points from spending on a co-branded credit card (1 TQP per dollar spent) or 2) base points earned from spending on qualifying airfare. (Group bookings, booking Getaways by Southwest, and some qualifying debit card purchases also earn TQP.) Members will earn differently on qualifying airfare based on the fare type they purchase: - Choice Preferred: 8 TQP points per $1 spent - Choice Extra: 10 TQP points per $1 spent Southwest may occasionally offer promotions for members to earn bonus Tier Qualifying Points. What's unclear is what those promotions will be and whether they will be sufficiently rewarding to make up even a fraction of the loss caused now that so many kinds of points no longer count towards Companion Pass. What happens to my existing Southwest Companion Pass? Under the new Rapid Rewards program, going into effect on January 1, 2027, the only way to earn an unlimited Companion Pass is by achieving Platinum status. What happens to all the Rapid Rewards members who have already earned a Companion Pass through other methods? If you have earned a Companion Pass that expires in 2026, regardless of the method you used to earn it, nothing changes. You still have the same ability to use it until the end of the year. For travelers who earned a Companion Pass in 2026 with an expiration date of December 31, 2027, nothing changes for you either. You do not have to hit Platinum or worry about Tier Qualifying Points if you simply want to use the pass benefits until year-end 2027. Can I still earn a Companion Pass with credit card bonuses this year? Sometimes when airlines make loyalty program changes, the new rules go into effect immediately. That means there are no opportunities to continue taking advantage of the previous program perks. Mercifully, that's not the case with the upcoming Rapid Rewards changes. In fact, Southwest is giving customers a few more months to earn a Companion Pass the old-fashioned way. Anyone who applies and is approved for a co-branded credit card before December 2, 2026, will still be able to apply card welcome bonus points toward Companion Pass qualification. Additionally, Southwest is giving customers a little more runway when it comes to using this method. Even if the customer completes the spending requirement on that card in early 2027, the welcome bonus points will continue to count towards Companion Pass qualification, as if they had been earned in 2026. The catch is, however, that the Companion Pass awarded for new card signups in the next few weeks will only be valid until the end of 2027. If you had been planning to get one or two new credit cards this fall but were waiting to complete the minimum spend until January 2027 to earn a Companion Pass valid through 2028, that method will no longer work. Of course, in order for any method to work at all, a Rapid Rewards member has to be able to earn the currently required 135,000 Companion Pass Qualifying Points in a very short period of time. Regular Southwest flyers or anyone who spends heavily on a Southwest credit card might be most of the way there. A single credit card welcome bonus might put them over the top. But the road will be hard for many others. There simply isn't a lot of time left in the year to earn under the old system. Additionally, if you've received a bonus on any personal Southwest credit card in the last 24 months, you might not even be eligible for a new personal card. And anyone who plans to earn most of the points through a welcome bonus on two cards—one personal and one business—might have a hard time obtaining both approvals. So consider carefully whether there is a reasonably clear pathway available to you, particularly given that the Companion Pass will only provide one year of use. Will there be any way to earn a Companion Pass with credit cards after January 1, 2027? Welcome bonuses on Southwest co-branded credit cards will no longer count towards earning the Southwest Companion Pass after January 1, 2027 (with the minor exception already discussed). So is all hope lost for points and miles enthusiasts who strategically rely on credit cards after the next few months are up? The answer to that question is still to be decided. The old method of getting the bulk of the points needed for a Companion Pass with welcome bonuses is dead. But there is, of course, still the classic way to earn a Companion Pass by putting a massive amount of spending on a Southwest credit card—$130,000 to be exact. Earning Platinum status requires 140,000 TQPs (you get a 10,000 TQP bonus in 2027 after hitting 130,000 TQPs). The new 1 TQP awarded for each $1 spent will actually make that method a little more straightforward. But that number will be impossibly daunting for many. And with so many other rewards credit cards offering better multipliers on most kinds of credit card spending, the opportunity costs of pursuing this method to earn a Companion Pass might be pretty enormous. In the past, Southwest also offered limited-time promotional Companion Passes. Sometimes these were awarded as a welcome bonus for a new co-branded credit card. Other times, a promotional pass was tied to registering for a promotion and purchasing and flying on Southwest flights within a defined time period. It seems highly likely that Southwest will continue to offer promotions of this nature. So there may be other Companion Pass pathways to come, some of which might involve credit cards. In fact, Southwest has also been sharing bits and pieces about a new premium-level co-branded credit card planned very soon. That card is confirmed to include lounge access and other perks for top spenders willing to pay a presumably hefty annual fee. It's possible that this card might include a perk to help make it easier to earn the Companion Pass, like reduced Tier Qualifying Points or additional bonuses. Let's cross our fingers. Status at Southwest is changing, most significantly with the Companion Pass that has been relatively easy for many points and miles fans to earn for more than a decade. There is a limited-time pathway to getting one more Companion Pass valid through the end of 2027 for some Southwest flyers, but many more are simply out of luck. In 2027 and beyond, everyone except the highest spenders and most frequent flyers will have to look for new ways to fly Southwest for less. Here's to hoping the new year brings some new opportunities. Related reading:

item.title: I just saved $450 on a 2-night hotel stay by changing how I use this Amex Platinum benefit
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
I just saved $450 on a 2-night hotel stay by changing how I use this Amex Platinum benefit I recently saved around $450 on a two-night hotel stay by booking it with the right card. And I did it in a way I honestly hadn't tried before, but absolutely will again. The American Express Platinum Card®, which I have and love, comes with up to $600 in annual hotel statement credits, split into two up-to-$300 credits each calendar year — one from January through June and another from July through December. These can be used on eligible prepaid stays booked through American Express Travel® at either Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection. The Hotel Collection requires a minimum two-night stay. But as I recently discovered, how you use that credit can make a big difference in the value you get from it. Shifting how we use the $300 Amex Platinum hotel credit To be transparent, I've mostly used our Amex Platinum hotel statement credits for stays at Fine Hotels + Resorts rather than The Hotel Collection. That's partly because Fine Hotels + Resorts allows one-night bookings, but also because its properties come with more extensive benefits, including complimentary breakfast for two and guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout. The problem with that strategy is that Fine Hotels + Resorts properties are generally pretty pricey. As in, it's not uncommon for stays to cost $500 to $1,000 per night. TPG Tip: You can use sites such as MaxMyFHR to quickly find some of the lower-cost hotels and dates where you can use these benefits. While a up-to-$300 credit can make a one-night luxury stay more affordable, that isn't always the best fit when I'm traveling with my family. The Hotel Collection includes a range of upscale properties, some of which can be more affordable than Fine Hotels + Resorts options. On a recent long weekend trip to Disney World with my family, we used our $300 credit to book a two-night stay at the Walt Disney World Swan, which is part of The Hotel Collection. For those not familiar with the Walt Disney World Swan, it's actually a Marriott property located on Disney property, within walking distance of both Epcot and Disney's Hollywood Studios. It's basically a perfect combination for someone who loves points, card perks and Disney. The nearby Walt Disney World Dolphin and Walt Disney World Swan Reserve are also Marriott properties available through Amex's The Hotel Collection. How the $300 benefit actually saved us $450 Our two-night stay at the Swan over a busy holiday weekend cost $672 through Amex Travel, plus a resort fee that we paid directly to the hotel. That charge triggered the $300 Amex Platinum statement credit, bringing our pre-resort-fee cost down to just $372 total, or $186 per night. For a nice hotel on Disney property during a holiday weekend, this was already a great deal. But that wasn't the only reason this was such a great way to book the stay. While The Hotel Collection's benefits aren't as extensive as those at Fine Hotels + Resorts, they still made a pretty big difference. In this case, booking through Amex Travel and The Hotel Collection came with a $150 property credit. We used most of that credit on dinner and drinks for the whole family at Rosa Mexicano at the neighboring Dolphin, and the rest on some other incidentals. We charged the meal back to our room at the Swan, allowing us to use the credit on something we would have paid for anyway. The Hotel Collection typically advertises a $100 property credit as part of its benefits, but some hotels offer more, as was the case here. Factoring in the $150 property credit, which we used toward expenses we would have paid for anyway, we received $450 in combined value from the stay. That brought our effective cost to $222 total, or $111 per night, before the resort fee. That's a pretty unbeatable deal for a hotel on Disney property during a busy holiday weekend. We were also able to get a 2 p.m. late checkout, which was pretty generous considering how busy the weekend was. Late checkout is subject to availability with The Hotel Collection, unlike the guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout you'd get through Fine Hotels + Resorts. My Marriott Platinum benefits were also honored on the stay, which tacked on a $20 daily breakfast voucher that we were able to redeem at one of the on-property grab-and-go shops. By combining the Amex Platinum's $300 hotel statement credit with a $150 property credit through The Hotel Collection, we received about $450 in value on a two-night stay we were already planning. That alone doesn't offset the card's $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), but making the most of benefits like this one throughout the year is exactly how you can come out ahead with premium rewards cards. And after years of primarily using my Amex Platinum hotel credits on short Fine Hotels + Resorts properties, I'll absolutely be giving The Hotel Collection a closer look going forward.

item.title: Broiled Salmon Teriyaki
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done. Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Bring â cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, Â¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5â7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes. Step 2Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1Â½â2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.) Step 3Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4â7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes. Step 4Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

item.title: The Diplomat Is Back for Season Four—Where Is the Political Thriller Filmed?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Diplomat filmed? This story contains major spoilers for season four. Watching The Diplomat is like being a fly on the wall in some of the worldâs most powerful rooms and buildings. But the Netflix series, though often immensely dramatic, rarely puts its characters in places that reflect them intimately. Instead, as production designer Curt Beech explains, The Diplomat is about âbringing the characters together physically but never emotionally in spaces the public donât get to see.â âThe places may be historical, but they're almost never personal,â he says. âThat is what's so different about this show from a design standpoint. Usually, we're creating someone's bedroom or their house, and we dig into their family history and who they are and what they like. We don't get any of that here because the spaces that they inhabit are not theirs. They are almost always visitors.â The fourth season of The Diplomat opens with a bangâliterally. In the first episode, US President Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, survives an assassination attempt outside Windsor Castle. She becomes increasingly unpredictable afterwards, confusing her husband Todd (Bradley Whitford), Vice President Hal Wyler (Rufus Sewell), and Kate Wyler, the US ambassador to the UK (Keri Russell). The story brings the characters from Windsor Castle to Washington, DC to Lucca, Italy, where it concludes on a cliffhanger at a meeting of the G7. Beech used some of the same locations and sets from past seasons, but also brought new locations to life in England, New York, and Italy. The interior sets were created at Steiner Studios in New York, while Wrotham House returned as Winfield House, the residence of the United States ambassador in London. Here Beech breaks down the key locations from The Diplomat Season 4. Season 4 opens with an impromptu visit to Windsor Castle. As the envoy leaves the British royal residence to fly back to the US, President Penn gets shot by an unknown assailant. Beech combined nine different locations to create Windsor Castle and its grounds. The exterior and inner courtyard were filmed at Burghley House, while Belvoir Castle, Lancaster House and the British Foreign Office were used for interiors. Back in the US, the team filmed at Woolworth Estate, St. Josaphat Monastery Library and Sleepy Hollow Country Club. The grandiose panic room where Kate and Hal are locked down after the shooting was filmed in the crypt of a church on the Upper West Side. âIt's a lot of different architectural styles, but that is typical of these houses,â Beech says. âWindsor has a bunch of things going on because these houses are very, very old, and they've been built during different centuries with different people in charge of the construction. We embraced that. We also have a mix of things that are accurate to Windsor Castle and things that arenât.â After she is shot, President Penn is airlifted in Marine One to a docked United States aircraft carrier for surgery. Beech used the parking lot at Steiner Studios for the helicopter landing, while a Marine training facility in New York City was transformed into the interiors. âWe did real takeoffs and landings with the helicopter,â Beech says. âWhile it was on the ground, we dressed the interior because Marine One feels like a private jet inside. It's very luxurious and well appointed. But you canât add weight to a helicopter like that without going through a lot of different FAA approvals, so we couldnât keep it dressed while flying.â As in the past, Winfield Houseâs exterior was filmed Wrotham Park, an estate in Hertfordshire. Some of the interiors were built at Steiner, while others were filmed inside Wrotham Park. âThere's a blue room, a library, and a red room in the real building,â Beech says. âThe foyer is also there. The green room, the Wedgewood hallway, and the blue study are on stage in New York. It takes a lot of coordination to keep track. The actors are incredible because they're able to tap back into whatever they were doing at that moment two months ago, and make it feel like they just turned the corner and are walking into a room.â The US Embassy in Londonâs Nine Elms was built on a soundstage in London for earlier seasons. The set was shipped to Steiner for Season 3 and rebuilt there. In Season 4, not much has changed. âWe moved some furniture around to get better lighting, but nothing major has changed in those spaces,â Beech says. The production did shoot one scene, a meeting between CIA station chief Eidra Park (Ali Ahn) and deputy chief Stuart Hayford (Ato Essandoh), in Nine Elms. âThat was right around the corner from the embassy, which was incredible to see,â Beech says. âThat building is in so many different shows now and itâs beautiful.â Eidraâs modern apartment, where Stuart eventually moves in as they begin a relationship, was a real apartment in Tribeca. âThis is another space that's personal, but not,â Beech says. âWe told the story that she moves a lot for the safety of her position. Sheâs never in the same place for very long. So itâs very stark and doesnât have a lot of personality.â For Season 4, Beech made some alterations to the White House set. He decided not to use the Oval Office seen in prior seasons and to shift the action into President Pennâs private study. âThe president typically does have a study, and it's right off the Oval Office, but itâs very small,â Beech says. âYou see lots of pictures of Obama sitting in his. We made a very large study for her that has three separate zonesâa work zone, a meeting zone, and a power zone where her desk is. That does not exist in the real White House, but it does in our White House.â In one scene, Todd is swimming laps in the White House pool. That also doesnât exist in real life. The scene was filmed in the basement of the Woolworth Building in Tribeca. âThere used to be a pool years and years ago in the White House,â Beech says. âThey plastered it over, and it's now the press briefing room. But you see in the old pictures there was a really beautiful room with arched windows and thatâs where the pool was.â Although 10 Downing Street has appeared in previous seasons, the set this year was new. âThat was filmed at a location in the UK that was no longer available, so we built it on our stage,â Beech says. âWe also used the Steinway Mansion in New York for the buildingâs iconic stairs.â When a new prime minister comes into power midway through the season, viewers might notice subtle shifts in the dÃ©cor. âIt got a bit more sparse, indicating that she had just gotten there,â Beech says. âThey had moved him out; she hadn't completely moved in yet. So some pictures are off the walls, and the lamp on his desk changed. It's small stuff.â The exterior of 10 Downing Street was filmed outside the British Foreign Office in London. âWe wound up building the doorway and the lectern in a parking lot in Brooklyn with a green screen, and then we added it together with what we shot in London on that street,â Beech explains. Kate goes to meet with the newly-minted British prime minister in the family home of the prime ministerâs husband, offering a rare glimpse into a characterâs private life. Beech used two different locations to create the vast manor house. The entry and gate were shot at Ingatestone Hall in Essex, and the interior was filmed in a house on Long Island. âIn England with these huge estates, it's very expensive to keep them going, so the family compresses to living in one wing of the house,â Beech says. âWe wanted to tell that story about her house, and thereâs a coldness to it. Her office space is in a room that is gigantic for an office. And there are heaters everywhere.â The season concludes with a tumultuous visit to Lucca, Italy, where the members of the G7 are holding a summit. The production went to Lucca for six weeks to film in eight different locations. These included Villa Viesca, the former summer home of Salvatore and Wanda Ferragamo, and Dimora Ghirlandaio, a resort in Tuscany, both of which comprised the villas where the American envoy stays during the summit. The G7 meetings were held at the recently restored Villa Reale di Marlia, Villa Medici in Poggio a Caiano, and Villa Medicea La Petraia. âWe were going play Florence for Lucca, but we leaned into Lucca as Lucca, and it felt better and more authentic,â Beech says. âWe went to the Pitti Palace in Florence and determined that it wasn't right. Most of the time, the vibe is very modern in these meetings. We decided to make it very classical. We embraced the vibe of this incredible room with floor-to-ceiling frescoes, and we built custom desks that had little fresco elements that matched the walls. These meetings are very bespoke, so everything is always created for them. We did that, but in a slightly different manner.â

item.title: A stay in Pakistan's unspoiled Ishkoman valley
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
A stay in Pakistan's remote Ishkoman Valley, where humans still consult fairies I took a 650km motorcycle ride to this traveller's hostel, where activities include lazing with sheep, enjoying Pakistani hospitality and visiting shamans who can learn your fate. I scramble up a scree-covered slope, trying to keep pace with a flock of woolly white sheep, each wobbly step triggering a mini landslide below us. Unfazed, the sheep charge on, navigating the precarious cliffside as if by memory and leading me like seasoned guides to an overlook. They halt abruptly and begin to graze. I catch my breath and look out across Northern Pakistan's Ishkoman Valley, framed by snow-capped peaks and cut through by pale glacial stream. Pale pink cherry blossom trees line the narrow switchbacks, descending to Coyote Den Ishkoman Hostel – my pastoral mountain retreat for this week, where I'm trekking high peaks and conferring with a female shaman who is said to speak with fairies. To reach the high-altitude Ishkoman Valley in Pakistan's Gilgit-Baltistan region, I had planned a 650km (403 mile) journey from Islamabad, trading the capital's traffic and smog for open skies. Bordering Afghanistan's Wakhan Corridor, Ishkoman is one of Pakistan's least-visited mountain regions. Travellers seeking quick access usually take a short (if notoriously unreliable) flight into Gilgit, followed by a four-to-five hour taxi ride. The overland bus journey can take more than 20 hours. But for savouring Pakistan's wildly diverse scenery, there's nothing like hitting the open road. I rented a 150cc phool patti motorcycle covered in technicoloured truck-art designs for the three-day mountain journey, navigating out of Islamabad's grid-like streets before speeding north on the Karakoram Highway. The Karakoram – the world's highest paved international roadway – follows the trail of the ancient Silk Road, soaring over the turquoise Indus River far below. From Besham City to Chilas and onward to the northern gateway of Gilgit, exposed cliffside highways revealed snow-capped jagged peaks behind each hairpin bend, including the dominating 8,126m (26,660ft) face of Nanga Parbat. After the brimming bazaars of Gahkuch, the road narrowed to a single ribbon of tarmac, following the undulating terrain into the remote reaches of Ishkoman Valley. For three days, I had stopped only to take photos, sleep at roadside guesthouses and share steaming cups of chai with uniformed officers at police checkpoints. Finally in Chatorkhand, I walked wearily through the wooden gates of Coyote Den. Since arriving, I've spent countless hours wandering the grounds, sheep in tow, and picking persimmons with Sana Marwat and Alex Reynolds, co-owners of the sprawling property – conceived as a budget-friendly "traveller's hostel" for wanderers and bikers. "Ishkoman is famous for its masonry," says Reynolds. "The wood used in our construction was all sourced from local pine and poplar trees, and the stones taken from nearby waterways." The result is a collection of stone cottages dispersed throughout a rose-filled garden. Panes of stained glass cap the windows, colourful local rugs adorn the walls and dinner is always served family-style in the mud-walled dining room. Though the key word here is relaxation, visitors can also trek from nearby Nalter back to Ishkoman Valley. "It's a three-to-four day, 45km (28 mile) traverse, including the 4,700m (15,420ft) Pakora Pass and a glacier crossing," Reynolds says. Plan your trip: How to get there: The fastest route is a domestic flight to Gilgit followed by a four-hour private taxi to Chatorkhand. For a more scenic journey, drive up the Karakoram Highway. The drive takes around 20 hours and should be broken into multiple days, with Besham and Chilas good stopping points. What to do: Fish for trout at The Mountain Resort Birgal Valley, hike to the Dain waterfall, trek across the Pakora Pass or take a Jeep or motorcycle to Hayol Meadows. Coyote Den can arrange visits to Rashida and sheep walks with local shepherds. Be safe: Carry your passport at all times for registration at roadside checkpoints. This very isolation is one of Ishkoman's key allures. "We chose to build Coyote Den in Ishkoman because it's one of the most untouched parts of the Northern Mountains," Reynolds explains. "The community here is also, as a whole, quite highly educated and therefore more open-minded and tolerant." Mountain life is also more pragmatic, with both women and men working outside the home on farms. A majority of the valley's population is Ismaili Muslim, a branch of Shia Islam that places particular emphasis on the mystical interpretations and rich inner meanings of the faith. Sipping sweet, homemade red wine, I relax into my floor cushion in the chid, a traditional Pakistani gathering room. The rapid beating of the dadang drum and soulful reverb of the rubab's strings fill the room as a handful of local men swirl in circles performing, not for my benefit, the Dani Hareep dance of the region. Without reliable Wi-Fi or television, I embrace the local way of winding down – an evening of laughter and exuberant traditional dance. Within this particular religious climate a woman known as Rashida, a female shaman who speaks with fortune-telling mountain fairies, is one of the community's most popular residents. Tomorrow, with the help of the Coyote Den crew, I will pay her a visit. The woman who speaks with mountain fairies The next morning, I pile into Marwat's dusty truck bed for the 20-min drive across the river and up the mountain to Rashida's home. Locals have been visiting her family for generations, but Marwat says hostel guests also love dropping by. In local Chitrali folklore, predating the spread of Islam in the region, peris (fairies) are incandescent, winged beings who exist between the human and divine worlds. Shamans were traditionally believed to communicate with them and seek their guidance. Although the tradition has declined sharply over the past century, with few practitioners believed to remain, the two belief systems continue to co-exist – at least the steady flow of devout Muslims filtering in and out of Rashida's home seems to see no contradictions in seeking advice from the mystical realm. Sitting at a small table in her mud-walled home, eyes fixed on a mirror pinned high on the otherwise bare wall, Rashida prepares to relay answers from the peris. By her own telling, she acts as an intermediary between the human and supernatural worlds. With Marwat and Coyote Den guide Hakim Ulluh translating, I pepper Rashida with my burning questions – painstakingly relayed through a telephone game of languages. "Ishkoman Valley alone has 10 spoken languages," Marwat explains. "Khowar or Chitrali is the most common here, and it's entirely different from Urdu, Pakistan's national language." From Khowar (Rashida) to Urdu (Ulluh) and Urdu to English (Marwat) and back again, we examine my future. Where will I end up when I finally stop bouncing from country to country? (New Zealand, apparently.) Should change my career? (No.) Will I divorce my beloved husband one day? (Thankfully, also no.) After four slow days of hammock lounging, riverside strolls with the sheep and sipping milky, mountain-style chai beneath the property's mulberry tree, Reynolds and I set out to explore the valley on foot. As we climb the loose cliffside towards the Dain waterfall, she extolls her love of Pakistan and explains how she has worked within the boundaries of tradition and religion to create a business that empowers women. "Half of the staff at Coyote Den are women, which is quite unusual in a region where women don't have [paid] jobs outside of the home," she explains. "We give them a flexible working schedule so they can go home in the middle of the day to take care of their kids' lunches, and we make sure they don't have to work at all after sunset, unless absolutely necessary." I step across the rushing, glacial-fed Ishkoman River on the narrow wooden plank bridge, the breadth of the valley sprawling out in front of me. I had come to Pakistan seeking adventure and instead found myself craving solitude. Somewhere in this remote valley on the ancient Silk Road, it came to me. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: Want to help Nepal recover from its deadly floods? Here’s what tourists need to know
item.description:
Source: Adventure
Our research following Cyclone Marcia in Queensland similarly found that trust and consistent communication between tourism organizations were critical to effective recovery. The objective is to manage the return of tourism in a way that supports affected communities, without putting visitors or residents at greater risk. People visiting friends and relatives in Nepal, or other tourists who have visited the country before, are the most likely to return earlier once Nepal is ready, due to their stronger personal ties and better knowledge of local conditions. The challenge for Nepal is not simply deciding when the country is âopenâ again. It is being clear about which specific places are ready for visitors to return, and when tourism will support Nepalese communitiesânot complicate their recovery. Travelers should also check their own governmentâs official travel advice, such as Australiaâs Smart Traveller, New Zealandâs Smart Travel and the United Statesâ State Department websites.
