item.title: How Italy's guiltiest food ritual went public
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
'Leaving something delicious on the plate would be a far worse crime': How Italy's guiltiest food ritual went public Once considered improper, a beloved Italian dining ritual reveals a surprising clash between etiquette and the pleasure of eating. Growing up, I spent a lot of time at my Italian grandparents' house in Kent, where bread was never not on the table. I remember my nonna slicing it into thick chunks and presenting it in a plastic basket lined with kitchen roll. We'd eat it throughout lunch or dinner, but its starring role came at the end: mopping up the last of the pasta sauce or soaking up oil and vinegar from the salad. It was, and still is, my favourite part of any meal. Giulia Crouch is a British food journalist specialising in Italian cuisine. She regularly visits family in southern Italy and writes extensively about the country's food, culture and traditions. She is the author of The Happiest Diet in the World and a certified olive oil sommelier. These days I'm baffled when my husband leaves good sauce on the plate. "You’ve missed the best bit," I'll cry, tearing off a piece of bread to mop up what's left. It was only when I got older that I learnt that this ordinary habit has a name in Italy: "fare la scarpetta" – literally "to do the little shoe" – using bread to mop up the last of the sauce or juices from a meal. On a recent trip to Naples, I was surprised to see la scarpetta done at a white-tableclothed restaurant as casually as at my grandparents' table. While my Italian dining companion and I were waiting for our pasta dishes to be cleared away, I noticed his eyes darting towards a bit of pesto left on the plate. He eagerly tore off some bread, wiped up every last bit and popped it into his mouth with gusto. He didn't ask if I minded or look up to register any kind of disapproval on my face – not that he'd have found any. He just did it with an uninhibited enthusiasm I found oddly life-affirming. It communicated: this food is good and should be thoroughly enjoyed. On the second course, I followed his lead. So how did a habit once frowned upon in polite company become something Italians now proudly do in public? There are many theories online as to why the ritual is called "little shoe". Some Italians suggest it's because the piece of bread looks like a small shoe or clog; others suggest it refers to being so hungry you'd eat the sole of a shoe. Italian food historian Luca Cesari says neither explanation has much evidence behind it. "Its origin is uncertain, so I'd leave aside the more fanciful theories you find online," he says. The earliest written example Cesari has found is from 1871, in Roman dialect, when a character in the Roman magazine La Frusta asks to make scarpetta with a little sauce left on the plate. The expression also appears in an 1885 dictionary of the Abruzzo dialect, suggesting its roots lie in central Italy. As for the name itself, Cesari says the most convincing hypothesis comes from the Accademia della Crusca, Italy's leading authority on the Italian language. In central Italian dialect, fare una scarpetta meant "to go for a little walk" – much like the bread taking a stroll around the plate. Francesca Cipolla, a food content creator from Palermo, Sicily, says scarpetta is instinctive, almost a reflex. "It's not something we consciously perform. If there's delicious sauce left on the plate, I tear off a piece of bread and use it to pick up the sauce. I don't really think about doing it; it's how I grew up eating, and everyone in my family is the same." But the custom has not always been considered good table manners, and attitudes have varied by region, generation and setting. Chef Gaia Enria who grew up in Turin, one of Italy's more formal northern cities, remembers being told off by her parents for doing la scarpetta. "It was viewed as improper back then. I think that was specific to Turin. Times have changed now but I remember it clearly." In Puglia, chef Somaia Hammad remembers almost the opposite. "In Puglia especially, it can almost be considered rude to leave anything behind on your plate, so finishing every last bit with a piece of bread is as much about showing appreciation for the food as it is about not wasting anything." Further south in Calabria, the "toe" of Italy's boot, chef Francesco Mazzei of Mezzogiorno restaurant in London, remembers a very different relationship with bread. Bread was a food that commanded deep respect. It wasn't just a vehicle for sauce, it was the integral part of the meal, he explains. In fact, everything else was just a companatico – literally "what you eat with bread". "Our lives centred around bread," he adds "The meal hasn't begun if there's no bread on the table and it can't end without it either." Cesari cautions, however, that the divide has as much to do with class as geography. He explains that traditional bourgeois etiquette frowned upon touching food with the hands. Even the supposed compromise of breaking bread and spearing it with a fork to mop around the plate could be considered boorish – perhaps more so, because it suggested "someone who would like to follow etiquette but just can't resist". Attitudes started to shift more broadly in the second half of the 20th Century, he says, "as Italy rediscovered its cucina povera and began to think of waste as the real bad manners." A symbolic turning point came in 2015, when Gualtiero Marchesi, considered the father of modern Italian fine dining, was defending scarpetta in an interview for Gente magazine. He called it perfectly acceptable – even elegant – as long as it was done with the fingers with nonchalance. It is now becoming increasingly normal to see Italians doing la scarpetta in restaurants – just as they would at home. "It doesn't matter if it's a fancy restaurant, a local trattoria or a bar that does food, they will all serve bread for this purpose and leave it on the table until the end of the meal," says Cipolla. In Naples, one takeaway pasta restaurant has built its whole concept around the ritual: at 'A Scarpetta, every box of pasta has been designed to leave enough sauce for a final mop-up with bread. These days, says Enria, la scarpettais not only accepted but respected. That's because, for a small gesture, it can communicate a lot. "But it's also about pleasure," she adds. "You want to scoop up every last drop because you enjoyed it so much." Mazzei says fare la scarpettahas even become a way of expressing how much you've enjoyed something beyond food. "Someone might ask how your holiday was and you could answer ci farei la scarpetta which means I'd do a scarpetta' or, 'I wish there was more of it'." Perhaps that helps explain how a habit once frowned upon in polite company has become something Italians increasingly love doing in public. As Cesari puts it: "Leaving something delicious on the plate would be a far worse crime than mopping it up with a piece of bread." My nonna taught me well, it seems: good sauce should never go to waste. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: Île Seguin: This tiny island just outside Paris is about to become the city's newest cultural destination
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Paris is hardly short of museums and is a real paradise for art lovers. Not only could you spend weeks hopping between its biggest hittersânamely the Louvre, MusÃ©e d'Orsay, and MusÃ©e de l'Orangerieâbut the city also has an incredible collection of smaller museums and galleries that are less frequented by tourists, yet definitely deserve some love. If, like me, you have a particular soft spot for contemporary art, Gagosian and Perrotin are just two of the many galleries worth visiting in the city, and they're among my favorites to browse on a rainy Parisian day. Although the city center has countless museums to visit, this autumn, one of the French capital's most exciting cultural openings is happening somewhere you might not immediately think to look: on a small island in the Seine just beyond the city limits. Ãle Seguin sits at Boulogne-Billancourt, southwest of central Paris and around a 10-minute walk from the end of MÃ©tro line 9. Once synonymous with industryâRenault operated its enormous factory here for much of the 20th centuryâthe island has been gradually reinventing itself as a cultural district. Now, the next major piece of the puzzle is about to be added. On October 17, 2026, Large, a new contemporary art center dedicated primarily to the French art scene, will open its doors. The 1.25-acre building contains nearly 27,000 square feet of exhibition space spread across several levels, including a vast, pillar-free main gallery rising as high as 46 feet. The building itself is reason enough to visit. Designed by Catalan studio RCR Arquitectesâwinner of the 2017 Pritzker Architecture Prizeâalongside French practice CALQ, it plays with light, scale, and views across the Seine. Visitors enter through a 4,000-square-foot atrium before traveling upwards through the building via corridors, monumental escalators, and galleries overlooking one another. Outside, terraces look towards the river and the hills of Meudon. Large isn't intended to function solely as a museum, either. Around 40% of the building will be accessible without a ticket, with an amphitheater-like atrium designed for talks and performances, a bookshop, a children's art space, and Extra Large, a cafÃ© with a panoramic terrace overlooking the Seine. Entry to exhibitions will also be free for visitors aged 26 and under, among several other groups. Its inaugural exhibition, âMoteur Imaginaire (Imaginary Engine),â couldn't be more closely connected to the island's past. Curated by Cecilia Alemani, the Italian curator behind the 2022 Venice Biennale, it draws on Ãle Seguin's history as the home of Renault's factory and explores our relationship with machines, industry, and the automobile. The exhibition will bring together 120 works by 55 artists from 23 countries, including pieces by Jean Dubuffet, Niki de Saint Phalle, Jean Tinguely, and Victor Vasarely, alongside 17 new commissions. "The exhibition takes its inspiration from the symbolic legacy of the historic Renault factory on the Ãle Seguin, a site that has long been at the forefront of French industry. The selection of artists and works explores the complex relationship between humans (humanity) and the machines (artifacts) we create, with a particular focus on the automobile. The car here appears as a powerful symbol of innovation, progress, and freedom, whilst acting as a catalyst for technological change, environmental transformations, urban development, and new social identities," says Cecilia Alemani, the exhibition's curator. Some of those works make particularly playful use of Renault's history. Bertrand Lavier will display a Renault Formula One car covered in his signature thick, painterly brushstrokes; Bianca Bondi will present a Renault 12 chassis transformed using salt, water, and vegetation; while Ghanaian artist Paa Joe and his son have created a hand-carved coffin inspired by the 1899 Renault Type B. But Large is only part of what is happening here. The wider Pointe des Arts development covers more than 13 acres and is turning this end of Ãle Seguin into something approaching a cultural playground. La Seine Musicale already hosts concerts and performances, while the island is also home to an eight-screen PathÃ© cinema and Parc Gauthier Mougin, which is planned to feature more than 30 sculptures. Restaurants, cafÃ©s, and a forthcoming four-star hotel will complete the picture. It's quite a transformation for an island once dominated by one of France's most famous factories. And with Large opening this October, there is suddenly a very good reason to ride line 9 all the way to the end. âMoteur Imaginaireâ runs at Large from October 17, 2026, to March 7, 2027. Large is open Wednesday to Sunday, 11 a.m.â 7 p.m., with late opening until 9 p.m. on Fridays. Full-price admission is 15 Euros (or around $16.80).

item.title: On this South Pacific island, there are no chains, no high-rises, and no McDonalds. And the locals want to keep it that way
item.description:
Source: Adventure
With no building higher than the tallest coconut tree, the Cook Islands’ ‘Mana Tiaki’ spirit has made its people natural guardians of culture, land and sea. But can it stay true to its values while balancing tourism and hungry developers? Eating ika mata, the national dish of raw fish marinated in citrus and fresh coconut cream, at the Barefoot Bar of the Pacific Resort on Muri beach, I look out over the luminous, jewel-bright lagoon. It’s clear now why my sub-four-hour flight from Auckland to Rarotonga was full of returning New Zealanders. “We come every year,” the woman seated next to me said. “It’s like a second home to us.” With a mix of 15 volcanic islands and reef-fringed atolls, the idyllic South Pacific archipelago is the kind of paradise luxury developers fight to get a slice of—so how have they resisted overdevelopment? “It’s a mix of government policy and people power,” Cook Islands tourism trade manager Rachel Harris-Best tells me. “Nobody wants it.” We’re sitting at Trader Jacks, a popular Rarotongan beachside café in Avarua, the northerly capital of the archipelago. The neutral-colored waterfront Vaka Bar is so low-rise it blends in with the harbor, and its open-terraced restaurant offers panoramic ocean views. My attention shifts to a group of canoeists carrying their outrigger crafts onto the shimmering water. Hopping down onto the warm sand for a closer look, I wonder: How could such a pristine location be the commercial capital of the archipelago? The islands are grouped into low-lying coral atolls in the north and volcanic isles in the south. Roughly 1,864 miles (3,000 kilometers) from Auckland, Aotearoa/New Zealand, ‘Raro’ is just 20 miles (32 kilometers) in circumference, with one ring road circling its agricultural interior. With no traffic lights, and motorcycles the preferred form of transport, I don’t witness a single blaring horn or impatient tailgater—even when newly arrived tourists drive at a snail’s pace. And public transport is even more genteel—a simple roadside wave will halt one of the two buses that loop the island in opposite directions. It’s the notion of hereditary bloodlines, written into the 1965 Constitution, that’s the fundamental bedrock of Cook Island society. It’s the reason no foreigner can own anything outright—which has largely kept chains and franchises at bay. I start to grasp the essence of island life at the Arataki Organic Garden, a short drive from Trader Jacks, where I meet owner Mirella Mairi. It’s rooted in Mana Tiaki. Made up of tiaki (keeper or guardian) and mana (influence or power), this philosophy of sacred guardianship runs through everything, from cultural preservation to taking care of the environment. And that’s exactly what Mirella and her husband Katoa are doing. During the pandemic, the islands were largely cut off, with no tourism and widespread disruption of freight delivery. Islanders leant on their age-old practice of Tapora Kai Enua—sharing produce within the community. “It was then we thought we should make our own food cupboard,” Mirella tells me. From cuttings and planting free seedlings provided by the government, they’ve since created something extraordinary—a garden of Polynesian staples, including taro (root vegetable), ginger and coconut, where visitors can book a botanical walk to learn about biodiversity and regenerative farming. Tours start at the compost section. By breaking down specially grown nutrient-rich plants, Mirella and Katoa have no need for chemical fertilizers. “What’s important is feeding the soil, not the plant,” says Katoa. Bugs are sprayed with chili, fermented overnight in dishwashing liquid, as a homemade natural pesticide. Even mosquitoes aren’t blitzed by DEET. “In the past, we used to light small fires under trees to keep mosquitoes away,” recalls Mirella. I’m reminded of an earlier conversation with a young, island-born woman returning for the first time, whose most vivid childhood memory is the odor of burning leaves: “I knew I was home!” she’d said. It had struck me as strange to think fondly of smoke, but Mairi enlightens me. Burning fires is a wider part of maintaining the land that’s at the beating heart of Mana Tiaki— that you leave a place better than you found it. The Cook Islands have, like many Pacific islands, a complex history. Settled by Polynesians who navigated by sea and stars in vaka, (double-hulled canoes) around 800-1000 AD, the islands became a British protectorate about a century after Captain James Cook’s initial colonialist explorations in 1773. It wasn’t until 1965 that they became a self-governing island nation in free association with New Zealand—meaning islanders have New Zealand citizenship and assistance with education, health and finance. But the House of Ariki, a parliamentary council of hereditary Indigenous High Chiefs, continues to advise on matters surrounding customs, culture and land ownership. And it’s the notion of hereditary bloodlines, written into the 1965 Constitution, that’s the fundamental bedrock of Cook Island society. It’s the reason no foreigner can own anything outright—which has largely kept chains and franchises at bay. Elders insisted that generational succession be written into law—land is inherited by direct descendants—while non-islanders can only buy property on a 60-year lease. By popular demand, Airbnb is one global platform that has broken through. A lucrative way to rent out properties, many say it’s worth the small amount of profit leaked overseas, especially given all accommodation is islander-owned. Even the new five-star Grand Resort Rarotonga, on Arorangi Sunset Coast Beach on the westerly sunset coast, is a local business. I meet its CEO Brett Baudinet at the building site as they prepare to open in March 2027—Baudinet is a Davis Cup tennis player and a doubles record-holder, but that’s another story. Currently a hive of activity, we carefully make our way up the unfinished stairwell to see some of the show suites. There’s little doubt this is going to be the archipelago’s most luxurious offering. On my site tour though, it’s hard not to be skeptical about the ‘no building higher than a coconut tree’ assertion. “Well, let’s have a look, shall we?” says a smiling Baudinet. “You can see for yourself.” We head up to the fifth-floor rooftop. He’s right. Even here, we’re surrounded by taller palms, with the tree-clad hillside behind us and ‘Golden Mile beach’ out front. It’s impressive. Back down on the sand, looking up at the new structure, it strangely seems to fit into the environment. The government acknowledges that this includes balancing “economic growth interests, such as tourism, fishing and deep-sea mining, with conserving core biodiversity and natural assets.” And there are tensions. Baudinet explains that there are building height restrictions, but the tree measurement, for him, is more of a guiding philosophy “than a hard and fast rule”. Measuring trees is never going to be an exact science, of course. Similarly, the ‘no chain’ maxim isn’t strictly true either—luxury hotel brands have been wooing him with partnership and investment offers, but he made the decision to decline them and retain control. I also hear later of an infamous 1980s derelict government-sanctioned Sheraton resort in Vaimaanga, that despite being almost complete, never managed to open. Beset by political and financial obstacles, people whisper of mafia involvement and the archipelago’s near bankruptcy over the debt. Island Elder and knowledge holder, the renowned artist and master carver Mike Tavioni, adds to what I’ve heard elsewhere, with talk of “the curse”. Dating back to last century, it’s said that a long-held dispute over land rights had culminated in the murder of an islander by a European settler in 1911. A powerful hex, or makutu, was put on the land by the dead man’s daughter—and reignited by her descendant on the day the Sheraton developers broke ground. With 70 percent of the islands’ GDP tied up in tourism, it’s clear there’s a fine line to tread between the economy and conservation. In 2017, the Cook Islands announced the world’s largest marine park—Marae Moana—spread over 734,000 square miles (1.9 million square kilometers) and designed to protect and conserve biodiversity and the ocean environment. But the government acknowledges that this includes balancing “economic growth interests, such as tourism, fishing and deep-sea mining, with conserving core biodiversity and natural assets.” And there are tensions. Like elsewhere in the the world, deals with US corporations to begin explorations into deep-sea-mining for fossil fuels and rare earth minerals have been met with local condemnation. Environmentalist and upcycle artist Sabine Janneck is one of those voices. Originally from Germany, she moved to the Cook Islands with her tourism dive business, but it was concerns about ethical practices on the reef that drew her into conservation. Now making items from plastic waste (think burst inflatables and car tyres), her CIRCLE Cook Islands luxury handbags are highly prized, with prices to match. As the Vice President of the Te Ipukarea Society, which translates as ‘our heritage’ and is the only non-government environmental group on the archipelago, she’s the very embodiment of Mana Tiaki, upholding island values as a papa’a, or foreigner. It’s clear that marine conservation is key to this South Pacific island nation—marae moana means sacred ocean, and it’s a fundamental principle of life on the archipelago. During the trip, I’d flown to the nearby island of Aitutaki to observe and swim with humpback whales where ‘Bubbles Below’ dive company owner and skipper Onu Hewett unpicks the dichotomy around the pressure to increase visitor numbers. “We have to be careful what we wish for.” As he watches his clients following whale-swim guide Chanaya Aukaha-Larsen in her Olympic-level pursuit of another humpback, he says he’d prefer year-round tourism, rather than even bigger numbers during the Australasian winter, from June to August. Back at the Grand Resort site, I ask Baudinet one last question before leaving. “Do you think there’ll ever be a McDonalds here?” He hesitates before replying. “Probably.” It’s not the answer I was expecting, especially when the thick-cut, purple taro and cassava ‘island fries’ here are the best chips I’ve ever eaten. Maybe he’s just being pragmatic—it’s a worldwide battle to hold back the tide of capitalism, after all. But this is one Eden nobody’s going to give up without a fight. The writer’s travels were supported by The Cook Islands Tourism Corporation—Te Mato Manava Turoto (CIT) Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. We are powered by, but editorially independent of, Intrepid Travel, the world’s largest travel B Corp, who help ensure Adventure.com maintains high standards of sustainability in our work and activities. You can visit our sustainability page or read our Contributor Impact Guidelines for more information. Award-winning photographer and travel writer Nori Jemil lives between London and Perth, Australia. She writes for numerous publications including Rough Guides and National Geographic Traveller UK, teaches travel photography courses, and is the author of 'The Travel Photographer's Way', published by Bradt in 2021. item.title: Listen to BA Bake Club’s Podcast on Glazed Apple Pie Fritters
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
âI've always wanted to go to a state fair,â Shilpa tells cohost and fellow Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk. âI only know that there's a lot of fried food, and there's sometimes butter sculpturesâ¦. Oh my God, what a magical place this sounds like!â In her latest BA Bake Club drop, Shilpa makes at least a part of this dream a reality in the form of her Glazed Apple Pie Fritters. Theyâre studded with tender chunks of apple, and spiced with nutmeg and cinnamon, and yes, deep fried. Food journalist and podcaster Mark Bittman and his cohost and daughter Kate Bittman from the podcast Food with Mark Bittman stopped by to help coach Kate in the fine art of frying. âFrying dough is kind of benign, right?â assures Mark. âAnd once it's browned, it's doneâ¦so start with that [cue for beginners].â Itâs as easy as appleâ¦fritters. Weâd love to hear from you! Send your questions to BA Bake Club on Substack or send a voice memo or email to [email protected]. Jesse Szewczyk: I'm Jesse Szewczyk. Shilpa Uskokovic: And I'm Shilpa Uskokovic. JS: We're both senior test kitchen editors at Bon AppÃ©tit. SU: And this is BA Bake Club. JS: Bake Club is Bon AppÃ©tit's community of confident, curious bakers. SU: We're creating the nerdiest and most wholesome corner of the baking internet. JS: Every month we'll publish a recipe on bonappetit.com that introduces a baking concept that we think you should know. SU: Then you'll bake, send us any questions that you have or pictures of your finished creations. JS: And then we'll get together here on the podcast to talk about the recipe. SU: Our October Bake Club recipe is for salt bread, and it's now live on bonappetit.com. We'll tell you more about it at the end of the episode. JS: But today it is time for Shilpa's state fair fantasy, her glazed apple pie fritters. SU: Which a week ago we found out may not even be a state fair thing, but we'll go with the premise. JS: I just indulge this all the time. I'm like, yes, yes. SU: For those of you who are listening and who may not know this fact, but I think you do, I wasn't born here. And when I moved to America, I think the most American thing was the idea of a state fair. And it has been my longtime dream to go to one. I haven't yet been to one. Inez, our colleague, teases me with all of the wonderful descriptions of the Wisconsin State Fair. JS: That's a big one. Yep. SU: And I've always wanted to go, and it's just... I only know that there's a lot of fried food at the state fair. And there's sometimes butter sculptures. Oh, my God, what a magical place this sounds like. JS: I think we could very easily make your dream happen. Okay, next year we're going to New York. SU: Oh, okay. JS: Also, everything looked beautiful on the substack. All of the fritters looked beautiful. SU: Oh, yes. Fritters were amazing. Yeah, everybody just knocked it out of the park with this one. JS: Maybe they've all been to the state fair. SU: I mean, we have been running Bake Club for almost two years, or more than two years now. JS: Yeah, they're professionals now. SU: Almost two years. Yeah, all of our Bake Clubs are pros now, Jesse. We got to step up our game. JS: Okay, okay. So, the fritters. And before we get too far, can you walk us through the recipe? And for that we'll need what else but our jaunty Bake Club music. Yes, there it is. Shilpa, where do we start? SU: I think Jesse, that this might be one of our easiest Bake Club recipes. It's certainly one of our quickest. To make the fritters, you cook a bunch of apples down with sugar and spice, and everything nice, I guess. And then separately you make a batter with ricotta, eggs, flour, and leavener. And then you combine both of these mixtures.
