JS: We are so excited. SU: Mark is a former New York Times columnist and author of 30 cookbooks. And Kate is running the editorial direction for The Bittman Project. And she is a part of the extended BA family because her husband, Nick, is one of our colleagues who we adore. Hi, Mark and Kate. Mark Bittman: Greetings, you two. Kate Bittman: Hi, friends. SU: Yes, we haven't ever spoken to each other before. JS: This is our first time ever speaking. MB: That's a lie. SU: Mark, I have a story for you, saving for the segment. MB: Great. SU: When I first started teaching myself to cook, I actually found a chocolate pudding from your book, and that was one of the first things I cooked in my family. SU: With cornstarch. MB: Yeah. SU: Because that was the first recipe that I saw for a pudding that didn't use eggs. And I said, "Wow, okay, I love this." And I made it and I loved it so much, and it's still in my notebook. I need to find my recipe notebook from when I was a kid. I have it at home, actually. I'm going to take a screenshot and send it to you. I'm going to do that bit. MB: I'd love to see that. Isn't it? When I started cooking and I discovered that you could make custards with cornstarch instead of eggs, I just though, God, this is the most amazing thing. But it's not terrible, cornstarch custard. It's actually good stuff. JS: Don't get Shilpa started on starch. SU: Oh, my God, yes. JS: She's number one fan. SU: This is true. This is true. No, I loved it. It became a part of our family's repertoire for dessert a lot when I was a kid. So, thank you. Know that you were a part of my life many, many years before this conversation. MB: Now I want to make some this weekend. Yeah. SU: Okay. Let's talk about baking. Mark, where did your love of baking come from? Do you like baking? Can you say you love baking more than cooking? Where do you stand? MB: Well, the thing is that cooking is like water to me. It's just there all the time. I cook constantly. And there's no way that I would say that I bake constantly. I've spent many years baking bread. And there have been many, many years when I was obsessed with baking bread. But my grandmother's a really good baker. I'm sure you guys know this, but to me it was always very exotic. She made this cream cheese butter dough that she would wrap around rugula, and these things she called chocolates wee back. Which were you'd roll out this cream cheese butter dough and spread it with a mixture of Hershey's cocoa powder, milk and sugar, just both chocolate paste and then roll that up like a jelly roll and bake that. It's really good. It's the only recipe I've never published. It's just kind of funny. JS: And Kate, do you have any favorite memories of baking with your dad? KB: Oh, my gosh. I'm just going to call you out. MB: Yeah, call me out. KB: He doesn't like to bake that much. He really doesn't. He's such a cook. And I think he's such a flexible cook that I do think that the exacting nature of baking is not as appealing to him. That being said, he did make the cookies that my great-grandmother made a lot, or a fair amount, and they're amazing. And we call them Mama's Cookies. And they're so good. Sometimes he'll make a cake, and it's always very good, but he's very critical of it in a way that he's not critical of his cooking. So, I cooked with him growing up, but not baking as much. I love to bake, but I have a stupid rental apartment stove and it really freaks me out because I think I need to get one of those chef alarms, or something like that, so that I can know what temperature of my oven. How do you guys handle that? SU: Okay. My dirty secret is that I don't give a damn about the oven temperature. In the sense- MB: That's so great. I love that. KB: Tell me more. Yeah. JS: I actually have some thoughts too. SU: Okay. JS: Great. SU: I just turned the oven on and I trust it to do its job. I have never put an oven thermometer in any oven that I've ever owned in my whole life. And I'm just like, yeah, la-la, it'll be fine. JS: I think oven thermometers also are a trap because people are like, why is it 280? I'm like, because it's cycling. JS: And then people freak out and they actually make it worse. KB: What's cycling, Jesse? What does that mean? JS: Cycling is like, so if your oven's at 350, it's not actually supposed to be at 350 the whole time. It goes through these waves, the average of the waves. MB: Just like your air conditioner, your heater or anything else. JS: Exactly. MB: It's called swing. JS: So people freak out and they're like, okay, crank it up 30 degrees higher. I'm like, no. KB: Oh, yeah. KB: Okay. SU: Yeah, you just got to wing it. JS: Live life. SU: Yeah, live life. Bake a cake, and if it burns, turn your oven down the next time. And if it doesn't bake- KB: I will never let it burn. Never. If anything, [inaudible 00:37:37] I want a nice underdone cake. I'm not going to- JS: She wants that pale. KB: I do. MB: It doesn't count for them unless they make it five times, so they want to burn it the first time. SU: Yeah, kind of. JS: [foreign language 00:37:49]. SU: [foreign language 00:37:50]. Our favorite word here. And I think I want to move on to asking you guys about podcasts. What has it been like working on the project together? KB: Ooh, dad, you go. MB: It's been what, five years? KB: Yes. That's crazy. 2021. MB: These guys came to us 10 years ago and said we should do a podcast. It was many years in the making, but we finally started doing it. For me, it's been really interesting because Kate's taken charge and I've gotten to watch her grow in a whole different way. And, I don't know, it also feels like an extension of... I was a journalist for a long time and I don't really do that anymore. Because for years I just traveled around and talked to people about cooking, and then I wrote stories about that, and I don't do that anymore. And it's obviously much more relaxed, I get to talk to people about what they do and I don't have to write anything down, which is really like a vacation. JS: And Kate, how is it working with your dad? KB: He's one of my best friends. Yeah, he's the best. We've been working together full-time now for six years, because we started before the podcast started. And I was working in corporate PR for a long time and I got tired of it, but we ended up working together. MB: And told me that I needed to hire her. KB: Your agent called me and said, "Can you help me wrangle Mark a little bit?" And I was like, "Yeah, I can do that. I've been doing it my whole life." What I think about often is that I tend to soften his edges a little bit. Not that he's anything but the sweetest person alive. And I, because he's older and wiser, learn a lot from him. It's interesting. It's an interesting dynamic. Sometimes I feel like we're like Howard Stern and Robin. SU: I know we just taped an episode with you. KB: You did? Shocker. SU: What has it been like talking to developers like us? But I know you guys have also had a varied cast of guests from journalists to politicians to celebrities, all of these different personalities for the show. How does that feel? Are there some common threads that you've found? KB: You know what the common thread I find is that everyone is embarrassed to tell you what they had for dinner night before. MB: Or pretends to be, but it's true. JS: It's such a hard question. KB: Everyone is like, "Oh, no." MB: Are we sure that everybody... Either no one listens to our podcast ever, or they turn it off before it ends, or they're all pretending that they don't know they're going to get asked what they had for dinner last night. Because we do ask everyone. And everybody goes like, "Oh, wow, I hadn't thought about it." Well, not everybody. Some people you can tell have been prompted by their PR agent, or whatever. They're like- KB: Well, and some people are like, "Okay, I listened to the podcast. I was waiting for this. I came prepared." And you're like, "Okay, great." So you planned your dinner around? SU: Oh, yeah, sure. KB: Yeah. We've had a couple people plan their dinner around it so that they could have a good answer. SU: Wow. KB: The best answers are the ones from people who don't know what's happening. So, actually, I'm sorry, Jesse's answer is the best answer. MB: Yeah, Jesse's answer was really good. JS: I thought it was just like dog food premium. SU: It's a good answer. MB: You're going to have to listen to our podcast to find out what it was. SU: That's true. It's a good one though. Well, Mark, I lack your conversational skills, unfortunately, so I'm going to have to make a very, very brief and abrupt jump. JS: Time for fritters. KB: I totally disagree. And we have to do it every week when we do what's for dinner last night. It's always an awkward jump. SU: Okay. On that note, it's time to talk about fritters, the reason for the show. So, this month on Bake Club we are talking about glazed apple pie fritters. And we are curious, we want to know from both of you, do you have a preference when it comes to members of the donut family? Are you a fritter person or a yeasted donut person, or a cake donut person? MB: I like plain cake donuts from Dunkin' Donuts circa 1973. I mean [inaudible 00:42:15]- SU: They were probably good then. MB: I was just thinking about donuts as I never ever eat donuts, but I do occasionally make beignets. So, I guess then it's beignets, fried hot, served, like you burn your tongue kind of thing. I really like that. KB: I love donuts so much. There have been many birthdays of mine where I have donuts instead of cake. JS: I like that. I like it. KB: I would like to make these fritters, but I have never deep-fried anything. And I'm [inaudible 00:42:50]- JS: Really? SU: What? KB: Yep. KB: Dark, dirty secret. SU: Wait, why? Tell us why. KB: The mess. I know we all know Nick. He would be like, "Oh, God. Oh, God," if I deep-fried something. SU: Got it, got it. KB: The air purifier is really loud and it goes on when I cook, and he would just... It would be hilarious. I would have to record it for you. But, no, I don't know. I think at this point it's just a mental block. SU: Mark, actually what I do want to ask, if you didn't know Kate, and Kate came onto your podcast and she said, "I've never fried anything before in my whole entire life," what tips would you give her? MB: When she said that I was kind of surprised, I have to say. Because I really like frying, and it was a very... To go back to the 1970, the next year I lived alone and I cooked obsessively. That's when I started teaching myself how to cook. Don't ask me why, but I just started doing it. And one of the first things I made was French fries, but for real, from scratch. And- JS: That's impressive. SU: That is such an impressive thing. MB: Because my mother, who didn't cook anything well, made incredibly good French fries, for some reason. Impossible to understand. So many things are impossible to understand. But I think if you're going to fry, if you're afraid of frying, then beignets or fritters are the first thing you should fry because they don't spatter much. It's really hard to get them wrong because they cook through pretty quickly, and you're not worried about... It's not like fried chicken where it's like, "Oh, my God, I took it out and the bone is still bloody," or whatever. Or like fried squid where you know you're going to get burned because it's going to spatter into your face no matter what you do. But frying dough is kind of benign, right? And once it's browned, it's done. That's almost infallible unless you're making a giant fritter. It's kind of that works. So, that's what I would say, start with that. Make beignets, make Zeppole. SU: Oh. KB: I'm going to make this apple fritter recipe. MB: There you go. SU: Wow. Thanks for selling everyone on the recipe, Mark. JS: Benign was a beautiful word choice. That was lovely. SU: The way you described that was... I never thought about frying something batter-based as being one of the best things to start with. JS: It tells you a story. MB: It's spattering that people are afraid of, and setting things on fire, grease all over the place, all of that stuff. Really, frying's not hard, but I get why it's intimidating. SU: We're going to move on to the part of the podcast that, Mark, may not be your favorite, because it is a rapid fire question round. MB: Oh, man. I'm just warning you, I'm really bad at this. [inaudible 00:45:47]- KB: He's really bad. SU: I would be terrible too, to be honest. JS: Me too. What is the best baking smell? KB: Melting chocolate. MB: Browning butter. JS: Both good. Both good. SU: Both very good. MB: Or bread. JS: Bread is my answer. MB: [inaudible 00:46:05] bread is kind of great. Yeah. SU: This is a little philosophical. Do you have a motto or words that you live by in the kitchen? MB: I don't know. Fuck it. I don't know. SU: I love it. JS: Great. That's it. SU: Yep. Put it on the cover. MB: Good enough. Sometimes I used to think we could do a cookbook called Good Enough, which is sort of the opposite of obsessive test kitchen cooking, right? JS: Mark, I'll write it with you. I've been pitching The Indifference of Cooking. MB: Yeah, there you go. KB: I love that. That's such a good title. MB: You know how MP3s are good enough? It's like the MP3 of cooking. It's like you can- KB: MP3. MB: You can listen to it. It sounds like the music you know it is. There's just some things missing because it's not really all there. JS: I love that. Okay, last question. What is the best compliment you've ever received on something you've cooked or baked? KB: I have these friends who, for the past three years, have come to stay with me and Nick on Cape Cod for a few days. This summer it was a week. And their daughter, who's seven, soon to be eight, says that I'm her favorite cook. And she says it regularly. MB: But I will say this, people do like it when you cook for them. Even if it's not great, they like it when you cook for them. JS: I agree. MB: So I often sit there telling people what's wrong with the food that they're eating while they're telling me how good it is. JS: It's like a human intrinsic trait we all have. I kind of messed up, but... SU: Yeah. Guys, on that note, I want to say thank you so, so much for being here. We had the best time with both of you. MB: Us too. SU: Thank you. And before we sign off, I want to ask you guys, tell our listeners where they can find you on the internet. MB: We'll leave that to Kate. KB: You can look up Food with Mark Bittman wherever you get your podcast. JS: Beautiful. SU: Amazing. JS: Thank you so much. MB: Great spending the afternoon with you. KB: Same here. JS: That's it for this month's edition of BA Bake Club, and now is the part of the podcast where we tell you about the October Bake Club recipe. SU: It's salt bread, and the recipe was developed by Hana Asbrink, our amazing deputy food editor. We've spoken about Hana so many times, I think. For pizza. JS: For pizza, yes. JS: She was our biggest fan. SU: Yes, she was our unofficial tester of the recipe. So we're very happy to have Hana back this time with her own recipe, where she blessed us with these brilliant, beautiful, gorgeous Buxen salt rolls. JS: They looked like little emojis. SU: Oh, they're so cute. [inaudible 00:48:49] They really did look like emojis. SU: And I'm sure Hana will explain a little bit more, but salt bread essentially originated in Japan, which is called Shio pan, and then it moved on to Korea where it really blew up. And they're essentially enriched dough rolled up. Think of it as a cross between a Parker House roll and a croissant. JS: Yeah. And it has so much butter that it fries on the bottom, so you get a really crispy bottom. SU: Yes. It's glassy almost at the bottom. JS: And I don't think there's anything special you need to stock up on really. SU: No. JS: No. SU: Nothing special. Your stand mixer, obviously, but that's it. Nothing really special. JS: That's it. Yeah. Well, great. SU: It was spectacular. JS: Yeah. Once you bake through it, you can send us your pictures and questions, and there are so many different ways to get in touch. SU: You can comment on the recipe on the Epicurious app, or on the Bon AppÃ©tit website. You can comment on our Substack, or you can email us at [email protected]. And if you've made it and loved it, please rate and review the recipe on our sites. JS: Or you can tell a friend, because the more, the merrier. SU: True. We're your hosts, Shilpa Uskokovic. JS: And Jesse Szewczyk. SU: This month's episode was produced by Emily Elias. JS: James Yost is our studio engineer, and we had editing by Michele O'Brien. SU: Research editing by Ryan Harrington and Sangita Vasikaran. JS: This episode was mixed by Amar Lal and Macro Sound. SU: If you like this show, leave us a rating and review, and hit that follow button so you never miss an episode. JS: And if you're not already part of the Bake Club, you can head to bonapetit.com/bakeclub to find out all the information you need to join. SU: Thank you for listening to BA Bake Club, we'll see you next month.

item.title: “Beauty, Breadth, and Epicness”: Colorado’s New, 2,000-Mile Thru-Hike Is Gorgeous and Hard as Heck
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
An idea struck Donovan “Iceman” Rice in 2024 at the Colorado-Wyoming border. He had just finished the 700-mile Colorado section of the Continental Divide Trail and couldn’t get over how much he’d enjoyed it. Rice had hiked the Pacific Crest Trail in 2020 and fell in love with thru-hiking. But no part of that trail, or any part of the New Mexico section of the CDT, resonated with his soul like the mountains of his home state. The scrambling, the alpine ridgelines, fourteeners, and endless side quests had been an absolute thrill for the 29-year-old from Golden. He reflected at the border, “If there were a 2,000-plus-mile hike that was a longer version of what I just did, that would be my dream hike.” That moment planted the seed for Colorado’s newest thru-hike, the Great Colorado Route (GCR). Over the next several years, it would grow within Rice’s mind until life presented the perfect opportunity to sit down and build it. He was between jobs and put all of his energy for several months into mapping and planning the route. The result was an epic, 2,000-mile backpacking loop that traversed the breadth of Colorado’s Rocky Mountains. “[The GCR] goes as far west as Rattlesnake Arches, as far south as Alamosa, as far east as Colorado Springs and as far north as one mile shy of the Wyoming border,” he explained to Backpacker. When he was finished mapping (or as close as he was going to get), there was only one thing left to do: hike it. On May 14, 2026, Rice embarked on his journey, starting in Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park. He wouldn’t return for five months. In that time, he’d gain thousands of online followers who tracked his journey and cheered him on. He’d grow a beard, meet hundreds of new friends, and eventually become the first person to complete Colorado’s newest long trail. Because it’s a loop, you can start the Great Colorado Route from pretty much anywhere along it. Rice began in the far west and hiked counterclockwise. The trek touches some of the most beautiful national parks and other public lands in the state. Highlights include national parks like Black Canyon of the Gunnison and Rocky Mountain; wilderness areas like the Indian Peaks, Eagles Nest, Flat Tops and Lost Creek; fourteeners like Pikes Peak and the Maroon Bells, and more. “I really, really liked Indian Peaks Wilderness and the Wild Basin inside of Rocky Mountain National Park,” he said, recalling some of his favorite segments. “And then, I was also a big fan of the Sangre de Cristos and walking directly across Great Sand Dunes National Park—across the dunes themselves.” In total, the GCR passes through three national parks, two national monuments, all 11 of Colorado’s national forests, 29 wilderness areas, eight wilderness study areas, and accesses 13 Fourteeners, and 47 Thirteeners. Officially, Colorado has two long trails. There is the famous Colorado Trail, which extends from Denver to Durango and covers 567 miles of the state’s mountain region. There is also the previously mentioned CDT, which starts at the US-Mexico border and follows the continental divide up through New Mexico, Colorado, Wyoming, and Montana to the border with Canada. A third route exists, though it’s not technically “official.” The Northern Colorado Route was mapped and designed by another thru-hiker like Rice, named Kevin Silvernale, who established it in 2024. That thru-hike starts in Estes Park and traverses the northern Rockies before terminating in Glenwood Springs. When Rice was designing the GCR, he reached out to Silvernale. He wanted advice on whether he should make the route as accessible as possible for as many people as possible, or if he should design it more selfishly, to his hiking tastes and mountain preferences. Silvernale didn’t hesitate. “He was like, ‘Dude, make something that resonates with you. Hike your favorite hike,’” Rice recalls. “And it was really cool to give myself permission to do something a little more extreme.” Rice warns that the GCR isn’t for first-time thru-hikers or beginners. He tracked 364,000 feet of vertical elevation gain, and “that’s probably an undercount.” He loves scrambling, doing off-trail navigation, and connecting routes that don’t have an official connector. Rice said he didn’t design it to be difficult for difficulty’s sake, but rather because he wanted to experience as much of Colorado’s diverse landscape as possible, without backtracking, doing too many out-and-backs, or road walks. In fact, from the outset, Rice set design rules he wanted to follow. “The three core design philosophies were beauty, breadth, and epicness,” he said. Beyond pursuing those, the route had to avoid crossover with the CT and the CDT. It also couldn’t have technical rock climbing or require special equipment like packrafts or climbing ropes, and it had to be doable, but challenging for an experienced hiker like him. Staying honest to those rules kept things very interesting on the trail, he said. “This whole hike was kind of a scouting mission,” Rice said. He’d find closed trails, or obstacles no other hikers had reported online, and have to problem-solve his way around them. “It was a lot of building the plane while flying it.” During his four-and-a-half-month journey on the GCR, Rice started an Instagram page and used Corsa Live Tracking for people to follow his progress. And boy, did they. Rice’s Instagram for the GCR has 7,482 followers (as of this writing). If you scroll back to the very beginning, it’s clear how interest in his adventure built over time. “It was kind of a funny evolution as the trip progressed, where more and more people would start recognizing me,” he said. “It started off as, ‘Wait, are you That Guy?’” As the hike went on, he graduated from being ‘That Guy’ to ‘Great Colorado Route,’ to, finally, ‘Iceman.’ Being recognized, he said, was “a really surreal experience.” While the hike itself was the reward he sought from the beginning, he said that the heroes of his trip were the small towns dotted along the route. Just about everyone Rice met was stoked about the hike, and many offered support along the way. “The vast, vast majority of responses I’ve been getting are overwhelmingly positive,” he said. When he finally arrived back at Black Canyon of the Gunnison on October 1, Rice said he felt a sense of accomplishment that was totally unique compared to his other thru-hikes. “Not only did I complete this trek, but I created this trek … It definitely made it more awe-inspiring,” he said. “I would say that was probably my primary emotion for the entire trip: this experience of awe and being completely struck with wonder.”

item.title: The Enchantments Hike Guide (For First-Timers)
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com
The Enchantments Traverse is 19 miles of jaw-dropping beauty that feels like you are hiking through a postcard. But between climbing Aasgard Pass, the focus needed to navigate, and over 7,000 feet of knee-crushing descent, it’s much tougher than the stats let on. I’ve done the Enchantments 10 times over the years, both as a day hike and as an overnight trip with a nearly impossible-to-get permit. If it’s your first time doing the hike, here’s everything you need to know, including what I wish I’d known before my first trip. Here’s a video I made showing you exactly what the hike looks like and what to expect along the way. While you can technically just show up and do this as a day hike, you’re going to want to do some planning beforehand to not only get the most out of the hike, but also to stay safe. Which Direction? There are a few ways you can do the Enchantments, but the most popular route for first-timers is from the Stuart Lake Trailhead to the Snow Lakes Trailhead (West to East). Here’s why: - There is about 2,000 feet less climbing when going in this direction. - Going up Aasgard Pass is tough, but going downhill on the loose slippery dirt there is worse. - It’s easy to get a hiker shuttle in this direction. - Even though it’s long, it’s doable as an all-day hike. So for this guide, we’ll be assuming West to East. Day Hike or Overnight? This is a popular hike. Permits limit the number of campers, but the trail can have hundreds of day hikers. Weekends, as you’d expect, are the worst times if you want solitude. On my last mid-September hike on a Tuesday, I counted 35 other people on the whole route. For 19 miles I don’t think that’s a big deal. When you cross paths with other hikers, remember that these are public lands. Every visitor has an equal right to be there, regardless of their experience level or whether they were inspired by social media. If you meet someone with less trail knowledge, choose to treat them with kindness and respect. Is It Worth It? If you research the route online or browse Reddit, you’ll inevitably stumble into debates about whether the Enchantments has been “ruined” by crowds, whether social media is destroying the outdoors, or if there are nicer, quieter alternatives. Tune that crap out. You can find these exact same arguments about any beautiful, popular natural space. If you haven’t done the Enchantments and it looks fun to you, do it. I think it’s worth the expense and hassle of doing at least once, especially if you can land an overnight permit. I have a non-hiker buddy who I drag around on various backpacking trips, the Olympics, Sierras, Mojave, all over the place. I took him here to do the day hike and he still refers to it as his favorite trip we’ve ever done. An AllTrails review I read perfectly sums up why: This hike is the most beautiful, incredible thing I have ever done. This hike is also the hardest thing I have ever done. AllTrails Reviewer The heart of this hike is exposed above 7,000 feet, through an alpine basin in the Cascades. It’s cold and holds the snow longer than the surrounding area. That makes the ideal season for doing your first hike here snow-free relatively short. Even if you have winter hiking experience, this is not the place to show up without local knowledge. Do it first without the snow, then find someone local to take you on the winter/snow routes. There have been multiple deaths here in icy shoulder seasons. A permit zone is an area where you camp. All permit zones have many dispersed backcountry camping sites and usually a toilet nearby. - Core Enchantment is the most beautiful area. It’s full of alpine lakes that feel like you’re camping in a postcard. - Colchuck is just below Aasgard Pass, offering beautiful lakeside camping. - Snow offers camping along lower altitude lakes and is still picturesque. - Stuart has camping along the first 2 miles of trail, alongside Mountaineer Creek. - Eightmile/Caroline isn’t on the Enchantments Traverse hike route. My favorite Core Zone areas to camp at are around Inspiration and Perfection Lakes. Later in the guide you’ll see what camping and the different areas look like, but here are my ideal itineraries based on how much time you can/want to spend in the Enchantments. - Figure out how much time you have to spend in the Enchantments. - Apply for the overnight permit lottery with your ideal timing. For me that’s 2-5 days in late August / early September. - If you get your overnight permit, you’re all set. - If you don’t get a permit, train for the day hike and do that. Try for an overnight next year. Overnight permits are some of the hardest to get in the USA, but day hike permits are free and just a formality. - You need a permit for overnights between May 15 and October 31. - Unlike the day hike permit, “demand for overnight permits far exceeds the number available” according to Recreation.gov. Based on public lottery data from the Forest Service, your chances of landing an overnight permit range between 1% and 12%. - You are only allowed one permit per season. - A Core Zone permit allows you to camp in any zone, but other zones only allow for camping in the respective zone. Obviously there are many factors, including luck, in deciding who wins or not, but based on an analysis of recent official Forest Service permit data, here are some tips on nabbing a spot, ranked from best odds to worst: For me the months are non-negotiable because it’s not a route you want to be slipping and sliding on, so I always go for late August and early September. But I’ll often try the days with better odds. I’ve only scored an overnight permit 3 times in 15 years of trying. Once you have your dates, figure out lodging and trailhead logistics. Leavenworth, WA is a cute Bavarian-styled tourist town. It’s got the basics like grocery stores, restaurants, and smaller shops. There are two small sporting goods stores in town if you need to pick up a last-minute piece of gear. It’s popular with tourists and can get busy during times like Oktoberfest. I’ve stayed in a different hotel every time I’ve visited, and they’ve all been decent. You can also find campsites and dispersed camping in the area. Have a dog? Dogs aren’t allowed on the Enchantments Traverse because they disturb the native ptarmigan. Let your dog live it up while you’re away at the pet lodge. The easiest way to do the point-to-point is to park at Snow Lakes Trailhead, hop on the regularly scheduled shuttles to Stuart Lake Trailhead, and then finish your hike back at your car. The shuttles can book out in advance, so I recommend booking the shuttle once you lock your permit and lodging in. Make sure you use the “Snow Lakes Trailhead” in Leavenworth, WA. There’s another “Snow Lake Trailhead” about 2 hours away. - If you can hike 15 miles with 4,000 feet of climbing, you should be ready for the Enchantments. - If you’re not at the level yet, start where you are and gradually build your climbing and mileage up every week until you get there. - Over the years I’ve found that my knees hurt way less on the descent when I do leg strength training. Work in squats and lunges to build up your leg muscles and descents aren’t so bad. If your fitness and preparedness levels do not meet the trail conditions, seek an alternate trail to recreate on. Chelan County Sheriff’s Office So what are appropriate “fitness and preparedness levels” in ideal conditions? A common sentiment I hear from day hikers is “the Enchantments is tougher than Mt. Whitney, but without the altitude,” and I agree. Plan on the Enchantments Traverse requiring more focus and energy than a standard hike or backpacking trip. - Even with a well-groomed and graded trail that you can cruise on, 19 miles and 5,000 feet of climbing is a tough day. - The Enchantments generally doesn’t have well-groomed and graded trails, stacking 10+ hours of intense focus onto those already daunting stats. - Much of the surface is covered in rocks, roots, and uneven ground, requiring care for every step. - About 15% of the trail is extremely steep climbing or descending, requiring a much slower pace, and sometimes butt sliding or hands on the ground. The steep downhills often take a toll on people’s knees. - There are many social trails, and finding the official trail requires a slower pace, checking for upcoming cairns (rock piles used for navigation), and sometimes cross-referencing with a GPS. - Some people with a fear of heights can find sections of the descent from Lake Viviane to Snow Lakes scary and emotionally draining, especially when slick. When you add up all the effort, it’s easy to be tired and make a mistake. For example, a misstep on the steep descent to Snow Lakes at mile 10 could mean a sprained ankle, and now the remaining 9 miles will take longer. Having an overnight permit means you can do shorter days and get more rest, but you also have to carry a heavier pack. I’ve canceled trips to Leavenworth when the conditions weren’t ideal. For me, if there is a solid chance of rain forecasted, I give this a skip. Temperate rain in Leavenworth usually means cold rain, sleet, or snow at higher altitudes, adding another challenge onto an already challenging day. And descending wet granite slabs isn’t a fun time for me. Aside from gauging the effort correctly, there are some other things to watch out for. - If you are going early in the season, expect snow. I strongly recommend waiting until August to do this as a first-timer. Snow on Aasgard and the Core Zone can hide weak snow bridges and avalanche zones that can result in death. - Don’t assume people ahead of you are in the right place on the trail. Rely on your GPS and the cairns before cross-referencing where the other group is. - Thunderstorms happen, and in the Core Zone there isn’t really any shelter. Luckily the basin is surrounded by high peaks, which are more probable targets for lightning. But it can really hit anywhere, so it’s just part of the deal. - September and October can bring big swings in temperature and early winter conditions. - This isn’t a high-altitude hike, but if you’re coming from sea level you may find yourself short of breath, especially on the Aasgard climb which gets close to 8,000 feet. Hard to say if it’s the altitude or effort though. - Be careful swimming in the (cold) lakes. In 2025 a hiker died in Colchuck Lake. For a day hike, give swimming a skip and focus on finishing. - Nearby fires can affect the air quality. Check conditions on WatchDuty.org and Firesmoke before heading out. If you’re in the area and can’t or don’t want to do the full Enchantments Traverse, use this guide to do the out-and-back hike to Colchuck Lake. That section of the trail is your standard PNW rocky and rooty trail under tree cover, but Colchuck Lake gives you a magical alpine experience. At Colchuck hang out for a bit, enjoy the amazing views, and then simply hike back down to the Stuart Lake Trailhead. Having the right gear can help keep you safe, but it’s not a substitute for good judgement. Here’s what I bring and why. - Headlamp - You’ll likely start before sunrise, and you may finish after sunset, so a headlamp with a battery backup is a must. Don’t rely on the flashlight on your phone. - Extra Layers - It’s often much cooler in the Core Zone than at the trailhead. I bring a long-sleeve top, convertible pants where I can hike in shorts and put the bottoms on as needed, a rain jacket and pants, gloves, and a beanie. If conditions change, you need to be prepared. - Water Filter - I use a 1L bottle and a 2L bag and filter that I can scoop water up with and filter right into the bottle. When I stop to filter I’ll usually drink 0.5 liters right away (camel up), then just carry 1L with me. There are lots of water refill spots along the route. - Food & Gels - I usually have trouble eating when I’m doing longer days at altitude, and gels and bars are easier to get down. I’ll try to eat breakfast before the start, then fuel up at Colchuck, the top of Aasgard, and again at Lake Viviane before the descent. Gels give me the extra boost in places like Aasgard. - Long Pants - It’s easy to scrape your legs on the granite scrambles, and pants give you some protection. - Multiple Navigation Tools - I find the best system is to have your track loaded onto a GPS watch that you can glance at as you go. If you don’t have a watch, make sure you have the route on a phone (with a battery backup). I carry both just in case. I also have a paper map from National Geographic that has trail segment distances on it. - Trekking Poles - Because there’s lots of loose dirt when climbing and descending, poles are crucial on this hike. If you don’t have poles, plan on more butt sliding and crawling with your hands. - Trail Runners - I use trail runners with good grip for the granite. Trail runners are the most comfortable option for this long day. - Satellite Communicator - Don’t rely on cell phone coverage. I bring a dedicated satellite communicator (Garmin inReach), which has a battery that lasts days and can be used for SOS and non-emergency messages. The last time I did this hike I was running late and simply messaged my family so they didn’t have to worry about me. - Gallon Ziploc Bag - This is key for carrying out my trash like sticky energy gel and food wrappers, and maybe picking up trash you may see along the way. - Full Hiking Essentials - I carry the things needed to not only stay comfortable but also light emergency gear to stay overnight if things don’t go as planned. Overall it may seem like a lot, but it should be under 10 lbs if you pack light. The less weight you carry the happier you will be. If I’m hiking earlier than August, there’s generally more moisture on the lower slopes and lingering snow in the Core Zone. - Bug Spray & Headnet - Mosquitoes and flies can be intense on the lower-altitude portions of the hike. - Microspikes - Snow can linger late into the season, but I’m usually safe leaving these home in August. Earlier in the season I carry them just in case. You may also need to scoop and melt snow to filter and drink, but there’s usually water flowing somewhere, even if the lakes are frozen. You can see all the overnight gear that I recommend here, but these are some specifics for the Enchantments. - Bathroom Kit - Bring toilet paper and hand sanitizer, and pack it out in the Ziploc bag that I mentioned earlier. - Camping Stove - There are no campfires in the Enchantments, so bring a stove and canister. If you are flying and can’t bring fuel, you can get canisters in town. - Bear Canister - While it’s not required to use a bear canister, I use one anyway because it does the job. Rodents are probably the biggest hassle with food. Seeing bears is rare on this hike, but they are here, and I’ve seen a tent site pillaged by a black bear at Nada Lake. If you have an Ursack and want to save weight, I think that works well too. - Warm Sleeping Bag - Check the conditions for your trip (see below) but usually a 20°F to 30°F sleeping bag does the trick for an in-season overnight. - Tent Stakes - It can get very windy in the Core Zone, so make sure your tent is sturdy and staked out properly. 18, 19, or 20+ Miles? I’ve seen reported distances from 18 miles to well over 20. After looking at all my tracks over the years, the actual route clocks out to approximately 19 miles. But doing things like visiting a viewpoint or lake, or maybe taking the wrong trail and then backtracking, etc. will nudge the mileage up toward 20. It’s important to get an idea of where you should be, and when, for this long hike. This table takes your pace and builds a timetable with gut-check points and directions along the way. If you’re running late, there aren’t bailout points, so it just means you’ll likely finish later than planned, maybe in the dark. - Pace - Pick your average total pace for hilly hikes, complete with ascent, descent, and the normal breaks you take. The chart will adjust your average pace based on the terrain. - Aasgard Pass - Can be a wildcard because it’s steep and challenging to navigate. Most people take 1.5-2.5 hours to climb it, but it can take longer, especially with a full backpacking kit. - Aasgard Break - It’s fairly normal to stop at the top, have a snack, refill your water, and regroup. Don’t linger too long or you could start getting stiff. - Turnaround Check - If you get to Colchuck Lake way behind schedule, the full Enchantments Traverse is probably not a smart move this time. Since going down Aasgard can be sketchy, make Colchuck Lake your gut check turnaround point. If you shuttled up to Stuart Lake, it shouldn’t be hard to hitch a ride from the trailhead back to Snow Lakes. - Daylight - Check the sunrise and sunset times against your timetable. You’ll want to see as much as possible during the day, but doing the first stretch to Colchuck Lake in the dark isn’t a big deal, you won’t miss much. Summer days are plenty long at this higher latitude. Colchuck means “Cold Lake” in a language called Chinook Jargon, a mashup dating back to 1790 of several Indigenous PNW languages, English, and French, used by Indigenous peoples and Europeans to communicate. The Chinook didn’t actually live here; the local tribe was the Wenatchi. Fuel up at the viewpoint for the next couple of miles over the boulders and up Aasgard. Here is the navigation workflow I find easiest. - Know your general direction of travel from the map above. - Look ahead to the next cairn. - Look down to find the most trodden path to the next cairn. - If you can’t see the path or next cairn, consult your GPS and see where the track goes. You’ll use that same method of navigation for the next several miles, until you reach the lower slopes closer to Snow Lakes. For Aasgard specifically: - Expect this to take between 1.5-2.5 hours for most people. - The dirt can be loose on the steep slopes; anchor your foot into solid rocks lodged in the ground. - Trekking poles are very helpful here. - It’s a north-facing gully, so it can be shaded when hot but also hold snow and ice longer than usual. - If you knock a rock loose and it starts to tumble down, yell “rock!” to warn anyone below. - After going left of the larch grove, there are a few false summits. I have a waypoint in my GPX called “climb over” letting you know when the pass is truly done. - I wouldn’t call the climb scary, but it is steep. If you have a problem with heights, stay focused forward until you reach a spot with a flat rock where you can rest and enjoy the views. Aasgard or Colchuck Pass? The official name here is the Colchuck Pass, and you’ll see that on USGS maps. Aasgard is a term from Norse mythology loosely meaning “the place where the gods live,” and was given this name (unofficially) by local climbers Bill and Peggy Stark in the 1950s. At the top of Aasgard Pass you’re not halfway, but rather about a third of the way through the entire hike. This is a good place to fuel up for the rest of the Core Zone. If there’s still snow in this section, be extra careful when crossing snow patches, which could be snow bridges across lake outlets. Are There Fish in the Lakes? Yes! The lakes have been stocked for roughly the last 100 years with trout. I’ve seen golden and cutthroat trout in the clear waters many times. If you want to fish, you’ll need to pick up a license. Now we start a stretch which has some of the sketchiest sections of trail. Please be advised: the trail between the Core Enchantments and Upper Snow Lake is a primitive route marked with rock cairns. It’s hard to navigate, challenging, and is recommended only for experienced hikers. Wenatchee River Ranger District What's the Deal With the Water? In the 1930s the Bureau of Reclamation dammed Nada and Snow Lakes to supply water to the fish hatchery in Leavenworth. As part of that they built a tunnel from Upper Snow Lake to the cliffs above Nada Lake to release the water. Every summer they turn the valve on creating the plume you see today. The Bureau of Reclamation also built the trail that you’ll use to get back to the start. Make sure you have enough water for the descent by filling here. There are some spots to fill from Snow Creek on the descent, but this is the easiest option. The last 5.5 miles or so aren’t tricky, but really for most people just a formality to wrap up. It’s a long 3,600 feet of descending on numerous switchbacks and straight trails. There are two small talus fields to cross, but other than that you should be able to just grind out the miles here. Was this helpful? If so, please do me a solid and send this guide to anyone you know who’s planning the Enchantments. And if you see someone asking about the hike on Reddit or social media, share it there too. I appreciate it and I’m sure it will help keep others safe.

item.title: The New Sense and Sensibility Film Takes Us to Bucolic Devon and Dorset
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Sense and Sensibility filmed? Jane Austenâs Sense and Sensibility is a tale of contrasts. Sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood have wildly different approaches to love, family and happiness, with reserved and practical Elinor falling for the understatedly charming Edward Ferrars, while the more impulsive Marianne becomes swept up in her feelings for the charismatic but impish John Willoughby. As romance gives way to heartbreak, misunderstandings and difficult choices, the sisters may not always see eye to eye. But if differing opinions are a theme throughout the film, things were more aligned behind the scenes: one thing the cast and crew could all agree on was thatâDartmoor is always a good idea.â âWe just fell in love with the West Country, Devon and Dorset,â says location manager Ian Hutchinson, of his time working on set. âIt was a lovely time making a beautiful movie.â Itâs a fitting sentiment for a film in which landscape plays such an important role. Austenâs story follows the Dashwood sisters after they are forced to leave their family home in Sussex when their fatherâs death leaves them and their mother in a precarious financial position. After moving to a more modest home in Devon, the sisters find themselves navigating the very different expectations of love and marriage in Regency society â with the grand country houses, windswept moors and historic landscapes around them providing a sumptuous backdrop to their changing fortunes. The result is predictably lush. Viewers are swept through the country estates of Dorset to the wilds of Dartmoor, before heading into Regency London and out to the palaces of Buckinghamshire. Englandâs winding lanes, rain-soaked woodlands, imposing stately homes and windswept landscapes almost become characters in their own right. Below, Ian talks about the places that made it onto the screen, his painstaking search for the perfect properties, and the surprising challenges of filming Austenâs world in our own. Kingston Maurward House and Parnham Park, Dorset The Dashwoodsâ vast and beloved Norland Park, which they lose following their fatherâs death, is set in Sussex in the book. For the film, however, the team used two separate sites in Dorset to recreate the romantic magic. The interior and exterior architecture of Kingston Maurward House provided the main backdrop for the grand home; its characterful 16th-century interiors and expansive grounds fit so well with the brief that it was an obvious starting point. But it didnât have everything the production was looking forânamely, that all-important lake at the back of the garden where the sisters often gathered. Nearby Parnham Park provided that missing piece, with its quaint wooden bridge and glassy lake completing the Dashwoodsâ idyllic estate. Ian wasnât especially sentimental about this park but, after they started filming, he was pleased when he quickly realised: âThis is not just a body of water, this is a sea of wildlife!â It allowed them to really exaggerate the scenes filmed there, enhancing them considerably from what was originally conceived. âWe were always hungry for more,â he says. The fun really began when the team moved to Dartmoor to film the Barton Cottage scenes, the considerably more modest home the Dashwood women are forced to relocate to after their bereavement. It wasnât easy to find the right place. The production team searched through around 50 remote properties across the region to find one that felt suitably isolated, in a process that started three months before production even began. âA lot of properties in the area have had a lot of money spent on them to modernise them,â says Ian. âWe were like, âHow do we bring that look down?â" They eventually settled on a completely derelict stone shell, devoid even of doors and windows, deep within the national park near Plymouth. Its insides were full of rubble so, to make it work, the crew built a custom two-storey stage set inside the ruined walls; a decision that allowed director Georgia Oakley to film characters seamlessly as they moved between the homeâs tight interiors and out to Devonâs wilds without need to cut the scene. âWe built a false floor to create an upper ground, created the stairs, and built a box within a box,â says Ian. âIt created that massive contrast between Barton and Norland.â It wasnât without its challenges. For one, there was the batsâ nest to contend with, which required a bat specialist who had to spend three nights in the property to gauge how many bats flew in and out. If any were near the filming area, they wouldn't have been able to shoot. âBats are very protected!â says Ian. âWe had to do a whole ecological survey of the area. A lot of conservationists said, "No, you shouldn't be filming there," but we put measures into place â which takes time and is quite costlyâand once we convinced everyone we wouldn't disturb anything, we were given a permit.â The remote location presented some logistical hurdles, too. âOne moment weâd have glorious blue sunshine, and the next we could have driving rain with thunder and lightning,â says Ian. âThen we had mud to deal with, and we were 40 to 50 minutes away from any civilisation in Plymouth. Getting the lunches, even, was a challenge.â Dartmoorâs famous tourist spot Haytor, with its sea of unusual jagged, rustic rock faces, also served as the backdrop for one of the filmâs key travelling montages. The team brought a horse and carriage to rumble along its steep granite tracks at dawn. "Not many people get to film there, and not many get to go there at dawn,â says Ian. âStanding there at four in the morning with the first light in the sky... I did stand there and think, 'This is why I love my job.'" Knebworth House and Broughton Castle, Hertfordshire and Oxfordshire In one of the filmâs pivotal points, Marianne famously takes a walk in the rain in the surrounds of Cleveland HouseÂ â after which she falls gravely ill. The mood of the film darkens, and the interiors follow suit. The team paired the iconic Gothic exterior of Knebworth House in Hertfordshire with the interiors of Broughton Castle, near Banbury, to represent this sad twist in the tale, ensuring the ominous feel was retained both inside and out. âIn that time period there were lots of different architectural styles. Knebworth has a very Gothic exterior, but feels different insideâthereâs lots of wood panelling, which makes it feel like a different era,â says Ian. âWhereas inside Broughton, the interiors very much feel like a Gothic castle.â To evoke the tight, claustrophobic atmosphere of Georgian London without relying on modern set builds, the team looked for period locations in and around the capital that have been altered minimally since they were built. National Trust property Rainham Hall in Havering doubled for the interiors of Mrs Jenningsâ house at Portman Squareâan especially good fit as its historic rooms are literally now preserved as a museum. âWe wanted real locations with genuine age,â says Ian. âWe didnât want people to question on screen whether itâs a build or not. We wanted it to feel real.â For the street scenes and exteriors, the crew filmed at Lincolnâs Inn in Holborn. This part of London retains a great variety of period features without many additional modern elements. It meant they didnât need to build anything artificial in a studio. âThere was the odd electrical line going from building to building, a satellite dish, and road markings that we had to paint out, but it was nice to use a part of London that was still real old London,â says Ian. âAll the way through the film, in terms of locations, we strived not to recreate anything, but to try and take what was already there and make it fit our world.â The decadent, Italianate architecture of West Wycombe Park provided the right visual shorthand for the immense wealth and rigid social standing of the Ferrars family. Again, the historic Palladian house required virtually no set dressing from the art department. âWe knew that was the look we wanted to go for because itâs a contrast to everything else in the film,â says Ian. âVisually, it raises the class with beautiful Italian curtains and wallpaper; it sets a clear contrast. We were very much about contrast throughout the film â using locations to tell the story of the charactersâ different levels of wealth and lifestyle through the properties they lived in.â Sometimes, the simplest shot can prove the hardest to pull off, proven here by the search for a specific hero image requested by the director: a carriage reflected perfectly in a body of water as it travels across the grounds. âBelieve it or not, that was hard to find," says Ian. "If the bridge is too high and the water is too low, you never get the full reflection.â The team finally found it after a five-month search in the estate grounds of Blenheim Palace in Woodstock. It took the entire duration of the film to locate. The result was worth the effortâthe scene is one of the loveliest in the film. âIt was probably only about three hours of waiting for the right light to shoot when we eventually found the right bridge,â says Ian. âI kept looking while carrying on with all the other important stuff. We found it right at the end, and it was one of the last things we shot.â A version of this story originally appeared on CondÃ© Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: Megan Thee Stallion Revealed Her Favorite Glute Exercise—Donkey Kicks. A Personal Trainer Says Hikers Can Do Them As a Warm-Up.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
The donkey kick exercise isn’t new: this move is a longtime staple in Pilates, barre, and bodyweight workouts. But it is newly trendy, thanks to Megan Thee Stallion shouting out the donkey kick as one of her go-to exercises in a recent interview with The Cut. “I’m going to call them stallion kicks,” the Grammy Award-winning rapper joked in the interview. What’s much less funny, though, is how much this exercise can fire up, and burn out, your glutes. As a certified personal trainer, I’ve programmed this move into my own workouts and into group fitness classes, too, because it’s a really effective way to isolate your butt muscles. Here’s why the donkey kick is so good for your glutes. And doing them regularly can keep your lower body ready so you can take on the trails with ease. The starting position for the donkey kick is really simple. First, get on all fours with your wrists under your shoulders and knees under your hips. From there, lift one leg straight up, keeping the knee on that same lifted leg bent to 90 degrees. Then, with control, lower your leg back down to complete one rep. Do a set number of reps; you can do the standard ten reps if you’d like, but if you want to bang out more, then that’s totally OK. Then switch legs and do ten on that leg. That’s one set. Repeat for three sets. This move looks pretty easy, and in a sense, it is. Many other lower-body exercises that work the glutes—like squats, lunges, step-ups, and deadlifts—also engage other muscle groups. But because the donkey kick keeps your knees bent, which largely takes your hamstrings out of the equation, you’re really just isolating your glutes here. That means it hits those muscles—hard. The gluteus maximus (your biggest butt muscle) does the heavy lifting to raise your elevated leg, while your gluteus medius and minimus (two smaller muscles that form your side butt) help stabilize your hips. Your core also stabilizes the move, and an engaged core keeps your torso still while you move one leg at a time. You’ll know you’re doing the move correctly when you feel lots of tension in your butt. Though it’s a great way to isolate your glutes, donkey kicks do have their limitations. For one, they’re not the most functional—meaning the exercise doesn’t closely resemble how we typically move in sports or day-to-day life. Contrast that with a step-up, squat, or lunge, which also work the glutes but in more typical movement patterns similar to how you’d hike up or downhill. Second, it’s hard to add a bunch of external load to the donkey kick. Sure, you could place a dumbbell under the knee of your lifted leg, or loop a resistance band above your knees (or even wear ankle weights), but you can’t easily pile on a ton of external load. The end result? You eventually reach a ceiling with your glute-strengthening gains. If you’re a hiker, runner, or backpacker, the donkey kick can have a time and place in your workout routine. As the International Sports Sciences Association points out, incorporating this exercise into a warm-up can help you activate your glutes more effectively during the rest of your workout. That’s exactly how I’d program them for outdoor athletes: do them before your next hike, run, or backpacking adventure to switch on your glutes so your butt is ready to work as soon as you hit the trail. When your glutes are fired up and ready before your favorite outdoor activity, you’ll be better able to push forward with each step and may reduce your risk of knee pain and injury. Plus, the donkey kicks give you a little stretch in your hip flexors—muscles that are chronically tight in many people—so loosening them up can help you more comfortably navigate terrain. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: Hike of the Week: Colorful Mushrooms, Not Leaves, Are the Main Attraction on This Fall Overnight
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Washington State hikers have made headlines this month for clogging up highways, parking areas, and trails in pursuit of Larch Madness—the fleeting time of year when deciduous conifers bedeck the alpine with their brilliant aureate needles. The fall colors are indeed stunning, but if you prefer not to hike nose-to-tail with hundreds of others, there are plenty of solitudinous trails worth visiting in October. Last weekend, I experienced the best of autumn in the PNW on this seldom-visited overnight route in the Mt. Baker Wilderness. The trail was alive with mushrooms, moss, and clear skies to backdrop glacier views from a subalpine camp—and my hiking partner and I had it all to ourselves. A washout on the dirt forest service road to the Elbow Lake and Ridley Creek trailheads means you’ll have to work a little harder to reach the trails, but it’s worth it for the solitude. A gently climbing 4-mile bike ride or walk on the dirt road from the closure to the trailhead follows leaf-lined gravel alongside the Middle Fork Nooksack River, making for as pleasant a roadwalk as you could ask for. The loop itself wends through a forest that’s exploding with fall activity: Moss lining the forest floor and dripping from the trees is turning a deep emerald with the beginning of the wet season. Massive fungi of all shapes and pigments are reaching their peak: chanterelle, bear’s head tooth, violet webcap, rusulla, king boletes, and more paint the forest with fall colors of their own, from deep violet and rust red to sunshine yellow and snowy white. The loop’s highpoint is Mazama Camp, which offers wide-open mountain views. The Park Butte fire lookout perches on the prominence above; we heard laughter from the lookout as we cooked dinner, but never saw another camper (Park Butte is a popular destination for dayhikers and campers, but most hikers reach it from the Park Butte trailhead on the other side of the ridge.) We watched the Easton and Squak glaciers on Mt. Baker’s looming slopes turn blush pink at sunset. To the west, the apricot-colored dunite crags of the Twin Sisters lent their own unique hues to the landscape. On the hike out, we craned our necks to take in enormous Alaska yellow cedar and western hemlock, then stopped for lunch on the peaceful and sun-drenched shores of Elbow Lake. Park at a pullout beside the road closure at milepost 7 on Middle Fork Nooksack Rd (FSR 38)—a Discover Pass is required for parking here. Bike or walk 3.7 miles up the dirt road to the Elbow Lake trailhead. Here, stash your bikes in the woods and continue walking the last 1.4-mile stretch up the road to the Ridley Creek trailhead. From the rocky shore of the Middle Fork Nocksack River, look for a newly-installed log crossing with a rope handrail, which offers solid footing. [Note: Two sturdy log crossings exist as of October 2026, but these tend to wash out seasonally.] Across the river, climb a series of steep switchbacks through mature forest. Once you’ve worked up a pleasant burn in your calves, bust out of the trees into subalpine meadows where water sources are abundant in fall. After just 3 miles of hiking from the trailhead (about 8 from your car), set up for the night at Mazama Camp, where you can choose between a log shelter or one of a few scenic tent sites. Optionally, take a 3-mile roundtrip, 950-foot detour up to the Park Butte lookout for views over Mt. Baker, the Twin Sisters, and into the North Cascades. Spend the night at Mazama Camp, then the next day complete the loop by following the Bell Pass Trail for 4.4 miles until it dumps into the Elbow Lake trail. At mile 13.5, enjoy a break on the slice of land between Elbow Lake and Lake Doreen (there are also campsites in the area) before busting out the final 3 miles to the Elbow Lake trailhead. Just before reconnecting with the road, look for another log crossing over the Middle Fork Nooksack: This one also features a handline, but the log hasn’t been leveled on top like the other—step carefully, especially in wet conditions. After crossing, rejoin the forest road and ride or walk back to the car. It’s clear this loop gets less traffic than others in the area; the path is overgrown in spots, and several blowdowns cross the upper section of the Elbow Lake Trail, but the way is mostly clear thanks to hard work by local crews and volunteers. The rugged nature of the trail makes it feel all the more remote and special.

item.title: Lake Mead’s Man in a Can Has Been Identified. But Questions Still Remain.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
One of the most grisly mysteries in the recent history of America’s national parks has finally been solved. Well, for the most part. On October 15, police in Las Vegas, Nevada, revealed the identity of human remains that were found inside of a rusting barrel on the shores of Lake Mead in 2022. The grisly discovery by boaters led to a lengthy Outside investigation into the identity of the corpse. Law enforcement now believes the body is that of Edward Lelburian Jackson, an Arkansas man who vanished in the 1980s. In a press conference held in Las Vegas, officials said they used DNA from bone samples to determine the man’s identity. “We were able to confirm that the remains were in fact Edward Jackson,” Clark County coroner Melanie Rouse said. But there’s still a lingering question at the heart of the story, authorities admitted. Nobody knows how Jackson ended up murdered and sealed in a metal drum. The mystery of the man in the can dates back to May 1, 20022. That spring, Lake Mead was in the midst of a record drought, and water levels dropped to the lowest point on record—a depressing statistic sadly surpassed in 2026. Rapidly receding waters exposed parts of the lakebed that had been submerged for decades. And that afternoon, beachgoers near the Hemenway Harbor saw a rusted steel drum emerge from the water. When they looked into the barrel, they saw human bones and the remains of clothes. Photos of the grisly discovery were uploaded to Instagram and quickly circulated on social media. On May 3, authorities held a press conference to reveal what they found inside the can: a body, believed to be male, who died by a gunshot wound to the head. Authorities hypothesized that the murder had occurred in the seventies or eighties, based off of the style of clothing found in the can—garments they traced back to Kmart. The discovery kicked off a frenzy of speculation in Las Vegas, and one podcast even invited divers to try and discover more bodies from the receding waters. That prompted the National Park Service (NPS), which manages Lake Mead, to post a terse statement. “Visitors are not permitted to come to the park in efforts to independently search for artifacts or other theoretical cold case evidence,” the NPS said. It also prompted longtime Outside columnist Mark Sundeen to travel to Las Vegas to try and solve the mystery. Over the course of a week, Sundeen spoke to a wide array of sources, from retired police officers to local lake divers to the family members of people who died in Lake Mead. But after speaking with his sources, Sundeen was still left wondering who, exactly, was in the can. In a press conference, Lieutenant Robert Price of the Las Vegas Metro Police Department shared additional details of the investigation. The case had gone dry after authorities released the basic information of the discovery back in 2022. It wasn’t until DNA from the remains was sent to an FBI laboratory in 2024 that investigators had a break, Rouse said. Authorities then worked with the Forensic Science Department at Oklahoma State University to complete a genealogy trace. The work helped narrow down the origin of the body to Arkansas. Additional detective work narrowed the scope to Jackson, who was believed to be in his early fifties at the time of his death. Finally, law enforcement officers tracked down family members of Jackson and were able to secure a DNA sample that was sent to Oklahoma State University for testing. “The OSU report back to us said it was a compelling match,” Rouse said. Family members told investigators what few details about Jackson they knew. He traveled widely in the seventies and eighties. He was married in California in the seventies and lived in Los Angeles and did not have children. He had a brief criminal history in Utah in the early eighties, and was arrested in Salt Lake City on suspicion of arson. “He was last seen visiting family in the early eighties,” Lieutenant Robert Price of the Las Vegas Metro Police Department said in the news conference. “Which aligns with the homicide that occurred in the early eighties.” Price said that the latest revelations, however, did not point to who killed Jackson, or the events that led to his death. The body’s placement in a barrel created speculation that it was the work of the mafia. “I know there’s been speculation that the homicide had ties to organized criminal groups,” Price said. “However, at this point in our investigation, we don’t have any information to support those theories.” Whether or not authorities will ever determine how Jackson ended up at the bottom of Lake Mead is unknown. But the lake is likely to offer up more mysteries to authorities in the coming years. In October 2026, the lake fell to 1,037 feet, the lowest mark in history, surpassing the 2022 record by three feet. The reservoir is operating at just 26 percent of its full capacity. Shortly after the 2022 discovery of the man in the can, divers found a human skull on the bottom of Lake Mead, kicking off new speculation about who the remains belonged to. On August 16, a visitor at the lake’s Boulder Beach was walking along sections of dry lakebed when she picked up a jawbone with teeth attached. The woman found additional bones nearby. Authorities later determined that the bones were, indeed, human.

item.title: These 28 credit cards can get you free checked bags on your next flight
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Checked bag fees can add up quickly, especially if you travel frequently or with companions. Fortunately, many airline credit cards offer a free checked bag for the primary cardholder and, in some cases, several travelers on the same reservation. Here's a look at the cards that can help you avoid checked bag fees, how their benefits work and what to know before booking your next flight. *The information for the Frontier Airlines World Mastercard, the Hawaiian Airlines World Elite Mastercard, the JetBlue Plus Card, the JetBlue Premier Card, the JetBlue Business Card, the Southwest Rapid Rewards Premier Credit Card and the United Club Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuers. Alaska Airlines' first checked bag fee starts at $45. A second checked bag costs $55. But if you have the Atmos Rewards Summit Visa Infinite credit card ($395 annual fee), Atmos Rewards Ascent Visa Signature credit card ($95 annual fee) or the Atmos Rewards Visa Signature Business Card ($70 for the company and $25 per card in annual fees), you're in luck. You can check the first bag for free for yourself and up to six additional passengers (seven people total) on the same reservation on flights marketed by Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. Note, however, that you must purchase your Alaska or Hawaiian flight with your Atmos card in order to receive this benefit. American Airlines charges $45 for a first checked bag when purchased online ($50 at the airport) on domestic itineraries and flights to neighboring countries like Canada and Mexico. The second checked bag is $55 if purchased online ($60 at the airport). There are four cobranded options that offer a first free checked bag on domestic American Airlines itineraries: - Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select ($99 annual fee; $0 introductory annual fee) - Citi / AAdvantage Business ($99 annual fee; $0 introductory annual fee) The Platinum Select and Business cards extend this free checked baggage benefit to you and up to four traveling companions on your reservation. Meanwhile, the Globe and Executive World Legend cards offer the same free checked bag benefit, but it extends to up to eight traveling companions on the same reservation. Keep in mind that there are route restrictions on these baggage benefits. Delta charges $45 each way for a first checked bag on flights within the U.S. A second checked bag costs $55. However, most of the carrier's consumer and business credit cards offer two free checked bags on eligible flights. Eligible Delta cardholders receive a free first checked bag for themselves and up to eight companions on the same reservation. On domestic U.S. flights, primary cardholders also receive a free second checked bag. However, companions only receive this benefit if they hold their own eligible Delta credit card as a primary cardholder. To receive these benefits, make sure your Delta SkyMiles number is included in your reservation. Here are the six Delta cards that offer this perk: - Delta Gold ($0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150; see ) - Delta Gold Business ($0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150; see ) - Delta Platinum ($350 annual fee; see ) - Delta Platinum Business ($350 annual fee; see ) - Delta Reserve ($650 annual fee; see ) - Delta Reserve Business ($650 annual fee; see ) Frontier Airlines charges varying prices for checked bags depending on how and when you buy them. It is generally cheapest to prepay for checked baggage at the time of booking. Here is an example of Frontier checked bag fees on a flight from Denver International Airport (DEN) to Washington National Airport (DCA) in mid-January, starting at $69 each: Luckily, if you hold the Frontier Airlines World Mastercard ($99 annual fee), you'll receive two free checked bags on all Frontier Airlines-operated flights when you pay with your card. Checking a bag on just one round-trip itinerary can cover the card's annual fee. Hawaiian charges $45 for the first checked bag and $55 for the second checked bag on flights between the U.S. mainland and Hawaii. For interisland travel, the first checked bag is $30 and the second checked bag is $40. Hawaiian Airlines World Elite Mastercard holders receive two free checked bags (when they use the card to purchase tickets directly from Hawaiian Airlines or Alaska Airlines); however, travel companions aren't included in this benefit. The card comes with a $99 annual fee. Note that the business version of this card does not come with free checked bags. Eligible Atmos Rewards cardholders may also receive a free first checked bag on Hawaiian Airlines flights, as outlined above. First checked bags on JetBlue start at $39 for the first bag and $59 for the second bag on domestic flights. For transatlantic flights, first checked bags start at $64 and second checked bags start at $109. These prices can vary depending on whether the flight is during off-peak or peak season. Thankfully, you get a free first checked bag with the JetBlue Plus or JetBlue Business (both with a $99 annual fee) when flying on JetBlue-operated flights. You can also receive this benefit with the JetBlue Premier, which charges an annual fee of $499. The free first-checked-bag benefit extends to you and up to three travel companions on your reservation. Keep in mind, the flight must be booked on your eligible JetBlue card to receive this benefit. Southwest, once famously known for its "bags fly free" policy, now charges $35 for the first checked bag. A second bag will cost $45. A-List elite status members receive one complimentary checked bag, and A-List Preferred members, Business Select passengers and those traveling on Choice Extra fares receive two complimentary checked bags. If you hold any of the following five cards, you and up to eight traveling companions on the same reservation will receive one free checked bag each: United charges at least $50 for the first checked bag on all domestic flights and $60 ($55 if prepaid) for the second checked bag. However, you can apply for one of five Chase cards to avoid checked bag fees: - United Explorer ($0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150) and United Business ($150 annual fee): One bag for you and a companion on your reservation - United Quest ($350 annual fee), United Club and United Club Business (both with a $695 annual fee): Two bags for you and a companion on your reservation However, there's a big caveat here: For the perk to apply, you must have your MileagePlus number on your reservation and purchase your ticket with the applicable card. So, if you use a different card with a better earning rate on airfare, you may miss out on the free checked bags. While opening any of the airline credit cards above is a great way to save on checked bag fees, what happens if you fly with multiple carriers throughout the year? If you prioritize price or convenience over sticking with one particular airline, it may not be worth applying for a cobranded credit card that offers perks solely on that one carrier. An alternative is to apply for a credit card that comes with more general travel benefits and can offset your checked bag charges: - Chase Sapphire Reserve® ($795 annual fee; see ): Receive up to $300 in statement credits for travel purchases charged to your card each account anniversary year. - American Express Platinum Card® and The Business Platinum Card® from American Express ($895 annual fee for each; see rates and fees for the and the ): Receive up to $200 in statement credits for incidental charges on one selected qualifying airline (enrollment is required; terms apply). A common misconception is that your credit card will offer an additional free checked bag because of elite status, your ticket class or an international itinerary. Unfortunately, these cards' fee waivers don't usually apply if you already get a free checked bag due to your elite status, class of service or travel to an overseas destination. Therefore, you will not receive an additional free checked bag beyond your existing allowance just for holding a credit card that offers this benefit. Some airlines make exceptions, but check your airline's policy before assuming an additional bag will be covered. Some credit cards offer free checked bags for multiple companions. This sounds great, but there’s a potential downside. When you search for flights, airlines usually show one fare class for the entire reservation, not a mix of cheaper and more expensive seats. That means if only three seats are available at $300 and the next fare is $400, booking four people on one reservation will price all four tickets at $400. In that scenario, paying an extra $100 per person just to save $70 per round-trip checked bag clearly isn’t worth it. Before booking group travel, compare prices by searching individually or in smaller groups and weigh the savings against any baggage benefits. Flights can be costly on their own, not to mention when checked bag fees are added. Thankfully, there are several ways to avoid these costs. In fact, some of the cards on this list that offer a free checked bag carry annual fees under $100. Even if you fly with a specific airline just a few times a year, it can be easy to justify paying the ongoing annual fee, and that's not even factoring in any welcome bonuses or other perks the cards offer.
