item.title: The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses Trevor Warmedahl has spent years documenting rare and traditional cheesemaking methods, and believes that "cheese is an edible manifestation of a place". Trevor Warmedahl was working as a commercial cheesemaker in Seattle when he realised he was using milk that came from animals he never saw. So, he quit his job and set off on what has become a global odyssey to discover places that still make cheese the old-fashioned way. In 2019 he arrived in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, and lived alone in a yurt with a dog as his companion. He soon discovered that dairy was sacred there: the women flicked milk into the air before cheesemaking, a gesture of respect called a milk libation. He visited homes where whey bubbled over central hearths and fresh, unripened byaslag cheese covered tables. After hiking to shrines, he noticed people offered dairy products as a symbol of purity. As summer unfolded and city-dwellers migrated to the Mongolian steppe to farm, Warmedahl itched to join. He jumped on a Soviet-era coal-powered sleeper train for a rickety overnight ride across the Gobi Desert. On the journey back to Ulaanbaatar, he met a local who invited him to stay with her herder family on the Zavkhan grassland. Warmedahl spent that summer waking before dawn to milk yaks, chasing livestock up the valley on horses, listening to shepherds' folk songs at sunset and cooking milk into dehydrated, sweet-and-sour curds called aaruul. The experience inspired him to seek out other places preserving rare cheesemaking traditions before they disappeared. During the past six years, Warmedahl has hitched, hiked and driven through more than 20 countries, documenting traditional cheesemaking and pastoral lifestyles, and offering workshops on natural dairy processing. After recently completing a 193km (120-mile) cheese trek across the Peaks of the Balkans Trail, he shared with the BBC what cheesemaking reveals about a place. Ancestral cheeses in Georgia have no analogues – I call them "fossil cheeses" because they were almost lost but are making a comeback as part of a broader post-Soviet cultural revival. My pinnacle moment happened in Tusheti, a mountain region bordering Russia near the tourist village of Omalo. I showed up with vague directions to the shepherds' summer camp, which was deep in the valley. That's a theme: the cheeses I find are always far out, made by hermit types sticking to the old ways out of sheer stubbornness. It was drop-dead gorgeous, just me and my backpack. The valley ends on an abrupt cliff, with deteriorating medieval stone towers. Shepherds build their camps from the decay. I saw how these guys milked sheep by hand with wooden pails, rustic-style. It's a feta-like cheese called Tushuri guda, aged in inside-out sheepskins. At the end of the season, I walked about 130km (81 miles) back down the valley with them and 300 sheep. The herd has done this for generations – they know where to go. The shepherds just coordinated, and it created this crazy lawless feeling with dogs barking and me, chasing stray sheep down ravines. At night we'd build a campfire and drink, and even with the language barrier, we'd relate through food. Sometimes language isn't needed. In cheesemaking, if two hearts want to connect, they'll find a way. How is cheese and cheesemaking a reflection of a community's history and culture? Cheese is a sensory experience and embodies larger ideas about how we live. It represents how meaningful human cultures can be. At its best, cheese reflects this complex relationship between humans, landscapes, microbial life and livestock at a time [when] we've become so separate from how food is made. And the cultural element holds the constellation together. The cheeses I highlight represent an older mentality, with a sense of stewardship over the places we live and farm. So, a little bit more of the wildness of nature slips into the product. [Cheese is] an edible manifestation of place, of cultural history transformed into delicious food. Why is cheesemaking especially important today? The diversity and range of cheese is infinite. When animals eat, they transform grass and entire landscapes into milk that becomes cheese, and animals can graze [almost] anywhere. So, it's a lifestyle that can move in response to climate uncertainty and desertification – real challenges today. The cheeses I focus on – natural farmstead cheeses [made exclusively with milk from a farmer's own animals] – reflect deep, ethical relationships between people and livestock and highlight the incredible diversity of heritage livestock. With industrialisation, that diversity is vanishing at an alarming rate. So pastoral cheesemaking strikes me as profoundly sustainable. What can so-called "exotic cheeses" that challenge us reveal about a place? There's this greyish-brown cheese from Norway, gammelost, [covered in] moulds like fruit rot. It tastes like a musty cellar with bold, mouth-numbing spiciness. It wasn't for me. But deliciousness is cultural. It's taught. So, I always say: don't try something once, try it 10 times. Uncomfortable foods open doors. But be sure to eat them because you're interested in the culture, not because they're freaky to you. One of the easiest ways to express interest in a culture is to say: feed me what you eat. When people realise you're genuine, the relationship deepens and you begin to understand their history through food. Funky cheeses become cultural emblems because of how obscure and special they are. You set out on your global cheese journey without a real plan. What did this approach add to your experience? Back then [in 2019], I was hopping on a whim from one volunteer gig to the next, drawn to remote places where people worked to protect and revitalise traditional cheeses. Workaway on farms, or staying for a while at guesthouses where cheese is made, are still amazing ways to go beyond tourism to see how people really live. Cheese gives you access to a global community, like at [the Slow Food Cheese Festival in] Bra, Italy. But anything you can do to find that deeper experience – food, handicrafts – is worth it, even if you can't always plan in advance. If your heart is in the right place and you jump fully into adventure when it calls, the details will almost always work themselves out. What advice would you give fellow travellers about how to best experience unique cheeses abroad? Find the cheese shop or cheesemonger that has the most local tilt and ask them which cheesemakers you can and should visit. Organising it yourself is cheaper. But there are also paid tours where you can experience a range of cheeses in a short period and really get to know a place. Just make sure that the cost actually supports local producers – that's what I call responsible "lacto-culinary" tourism. How can other travellers seek out responsible agrotourism experiences? Look for local cheesemakers and guides. It's also important to not expect farmers to sanitise things. It's normal to go to a farm and see broken-down equipment and mud. When we romanticise tradition, it encourages locals to put themselves in a museum. But tools [and] tradition have always evolved. More like this: We need to be open to the fact that it's not all grandmas spinning wool on wheels outside stone cottages. Then it becomes kind of a show, and we're pushing farmers to become something they're not for tourists. What places have exciting, overlooked, or under-the-radar cheeses? Where are you keen to travel next? Hands down, Turkey. It's a universe of cheese that doesn't get enough attention. Tulum peyniri is emblematic of pastoral lifestyles and the extreme sacrifice at the root of dairying and – I'd argue – life. That's because it's aged mainly in furry goatskins, so it looks insane because it can take on animal shapes. Somehow, I didn't think it would be delicious. How good can goatskin-aged cheese be, right? It was phenomenal. I was blown away by deep flavours and textures I'd never seen in cheese before. Turkish cheese needs to be talked about alongside Western Europe. More remote places have just as many fascinating cheeses to preserve and celebrate. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. If you liked this story, – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: Wisconsin’s Longest Trail Might Be the Midwest’s Best Fall Thru-Hike
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Out-of-state visitors travel to Wisconsin for many things—the cheese, beer, football, fishing—but rarely for hiking. And yet, winding through the Badger State is one of the Midwest’s longest hiking routes: a nearly 1,200-mile National Scenic Trail that crawls along glacial terrain, skirts peaceful lakes, and showcases some of the state’s most spectacular landscapes. It’s not the kind of trail that’s going to destroy your legs with vertical climbs or challenge you to cross inhospitable areas, but for hikers who want to cruise, crush miles, and get lost in the flow state of forest hiking, the Ice Age Trail (IAT) should be at the top of your list. In September, Backpacker’s editorial team traveled to Wisconsin to see for ourselves what all the IAT was about. We’d covered this trail previously.:Earlier this year, we interviewed Jamieson Hatt, who set the record for the longest unsupported hike ever on the IAT, covering 1,160 miles in 30 days. In 2025, writer Grayson Haver Currin wrote about everything he wished he’d known before thru-hiking it (tip: prepare for roadwalks), and fellow Triple Crowner Barney “Scout” Mann reported on how it stands out from the Big Three. However, none of our editors had ever set foot on the IAT. So we decided to change that. Backpacker couldn’t have hiked it at a better time. Not just because the deciduous forests were exploding with gold and vermillion fall colors, but because the temperatures were perfect, there were almost no bugs to contend with, and we saw very few other hikers along the way. The trail was all ours, and it had a lot to show us about Wisconsin. The IAT’s eastern terminus is in Potawatomi State Park in Sturgeon Bay. From there, it squiggles down the eastern side of the state into southern Wisconsin before turning north, skirting around Madison, and finally hooking west to the other terminus on the Minnesota border. While Wisconsin is just about 260 miles wide, the IAT covers nearly 1,200 miles. Twelve thousand years ago, this area looked very different. In fact, you wouldn’t have seen much of it because it was buried under massive sheets of glacial ice. Mammoths roamed the area, and the climate was more like Alaska’s is today. As the Earth warmed over the next several thousand years, the glaciers retreated, revealing the sculpted landscape that exists today. Those glaciogenic features are a hallmark of the IAT. We hiked along multiple eskers—long ridges that elevated us above the forest floor. We camped beside ancient glacial lakes, walked along moraines, explored dells (narrow river gorges with steep rock walls), and more. If you’re into glaciology, this trail is a kick. As Backpacker cruised along, it was fun to identify the features and talk about them as we went. Unfortunately, the Backpacker team only had time for a taste (for a full, detailed trip report, check out the story Mann wrote in 2025). Instead, we backpacked about 25 miles between Jerry Lake and Mondeaux Flowage. The forests were thick, and tree roots crisscrossed the loamy trail beneath our feet. Boardwalks traversed muddy areas and small creeks, and occasionally we’d pop out of the trees onto a dirt county road, offering a brief glimpse of uncanopied sky, before plunging back into the woods on the other side. We put down about 10 miles of hiking a day, with plenty of time for casual mornings and nights around a campfire. With its frequent road crossings, this trail is very accessible for day and section hikers, making it easy to plan sections based on how much time you have or the distance you want to cover. Some of the most popular sections are the Baraboo Segment (which is actually an urban path through the quaint town of Baraboo, WI), Mondeaux Esker Segment (which we hiked), Eagle Segment (which passes through prairies, over limestone outcroppings, and through thick oak forests), and the St. Croix Falls Segment (the western terminus of the trail, which offers views of the St. Croix River). Explore each individual section with the IAT Alliance’s Segment by Segment Tour page. Thru-hikers should expect the trail to take between seven and 12 weeks to complete. There are nearly 30 official “IAT communities” (recognized trail towns) along the way, which make resupplies and hotel breaks relatively easy to line up. Those communities are also opportunities to experience Wisconsin’s culture, taste its flavors, and meet its people. The IAT Alliance even has a story map detailing itineraries, local highlights, and places to explore for each community along the route. If you’re thru-hiking the IAT, be warned: The trail is still unfinished, and many sections follow roads for significant distances. Currently, about 700 miles are marked with the distinctive IAT yellow blazes. The remaining 500 miles linking those segments are unmarked, although IAT Alliance volunteers blaze 10 to 15 miles of new trail every year. It’s a good idea to download your maps or bring a hard copy. As we learned while hiking the IAT, it is easy to branch off in the wrong direction if you aren’t paying close attention. Check the IAT Trail Reports page for up-to-date information on closures, reroutes, and more. The IAT is open year-round. In the winter, it’s popular for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. For hiking, the optimal months are May to October. However, the best time for hiking is in the fall (September and October). The colors we witnessed as the maples, oaks, birches, and hardwoods settled into their fall palettes were mesmerizing. We caught the color change early, so the bright greens of summer were still mixed with the vibrant yellows, oranges, and reds of fall. There are also very few bugs on the trail this time of year. Everyone in our group exercised tick caution, but we didn’t have to worry about mosquitoes, horse flies, or wasps. September and October temperatures are also ideal. In the winter, Wisconsin gets cold, and unless you’re prepared for winter camping, overnight hiking trips are off the table. In the summer, temperatures rise into the 80s, and sometimes 90s, and the humidity can be brutal. The easy answer is Midwesterners who want to experience the region on foot, get closer to the landscape they live in and around, and dive deep into Wisconsin’s trail town culture. If you love the Midwest, this is one of the best trails to experience its natural beauty. The IAT is also a great long trail for beginner backpackers. The terrain is manageable, following clear, mostly level singletrack. Rolling hills and features like the eskers provide some elevation change. The access to IAT Communities along the way also makes this a good trail for beginner backpackers. Resupplies are easy; you can access wifi and download maps, get a hotel room, meet other humans, and generally break up the hike. Logistically, that makes planning a backpacking trip simple. By that same token, I think experienced thru-hikers and even FKT seekers could find that the IAT has a lot to offer. If you really want to crush miles and cruise through days, this is a great trail for that, assuming that the idea of a few hundred miles on roads isn’t enough to scare you off. The IAT might not be for everyone, but it has something for every type of hiker. I’m really glad I got to experience even a piece of it, and I know there’s much more to explore. Next time I travel to the Badger State, I’ll be bringing my backpack again.

item.title: Chicago’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Is Cooking From 900-Year-Old Recipes
item.description:
Source: Eater
Chicago’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Is Cooking From 900-Year-Old Recipes An interview with the chef behind Muhājir This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings. Zubair Mohajir is one of Chicago’s most prolific new chefs and restaurateurs, behind such openings as Lilac Tiger, Mariela, Mirra, Sarima, and most recently, Muhājir, a restaurant that traces historical spice routes to tell the story of global migration. I talked to Mohajir about how the opening is going, how he thinks about collaboration across his different projects, and why Muhājir is finally the restaurant that feels like home. Pre Shift: What did you want to explore with Muhājir that you hadn’t been able to do yet with your previous restaurants? Zubair Mohajir: Muhājir is such a personal story for me, because my last name is Mohajir, and the meaning of “muhājir” in Arabic and Urdu is “one who migrates.” When the partition [of India and Pakistan] happened, the Muslims that were moved from India to Pakistan were named Muhājirs because they were migrated. In my family, we always wondered why that was our last name. When I started cooking [after working in finance], it really started to settle in. Our late maternal grandfather was obsessed with mapping where this family name came from. It comes from Southern Basra, Iraq, and that was so mind-blowing for me because it’s one of the biggest spice roads. At Coach House for the past five years, I’ve been exploring ancient recipes in southern Spain and southern Portugal. [They] bring in pre-Crusade Muslim, Christian, Jewish [influences] that are also affected by the Southeast Asian traders coming on the spice road that shoots through the Mediterranean and hits North Africa and the Iberian Peninsula. I’m just obsessed with history and it started to become very evident for me that I really wanted to feed people, but with the context of where the food came from. At Muhājir, it’s all about riding the spice road that runs from Portugal through the Mediterranean, through the Levantine [region], and then hits out of Basra, Iraq, into the Persian Gulf, and the first landmass it comes across is southern India, where I’m from. We’re all muhājirs — you know, all of our families came from somewhere, and that really has been the driving force for me. Why did you decide to build the restaurant around live fire? I’d never cooked on live fire, but we’re cooks, and it was going back to core things. I remember growing up in my grandmother’s house back home in India, and it’s not like there were gas stoves everywhere. When I decided that I was going to do Muhājir, it became so obvious to me that it couldn’t just be a sauté pan on a stove. The story that we wanted to tell had to be told through wood fire. Is there a dish that feels especially representative of Muhājir? We do a duck that is inspired by a 927-year-old recipe we found from southern Spain that is influenced by Roman garums, Muslim origins, and Jewish origins. We do this duck “experience,” where we take a whole duck, butcher it, and have the crown dry-aging for seven days. We take the wings and make a jus [and] take the legs and make a confit. We blast that duck crown over the fire when we start service every day, and then it gets finished in the brasa. If you’re sitting in the restaurant, you can see the ducks hanging over the fire. When we present it, we have this beautiful ornate Turkish platter. There’s black raspberry achaar, the duck jus in a saucier, the duck rice next to it, the duck skin cut in these beautiful medallions on top almost like duck chicharrón, and then we’re also presenting the duck breast itself that has a very crispy skin. The top of that duck breast is the spice mix from that exact recipe that’s more than 900 years old, with cumin, coriander, cardamom, toasted pine nuts, red wine vinegar, and fish sauce. It’s a story of cross-cultural collaboration. You have a bar called Bobo behind the restaurant. How do the two spaces complement each other? Bobo’s really inspired by Jacob Dela Cruz, who’s my partner here. We built Sarima together, and it became very important to me to highlight his upbringing and his background as well. He was one who said, “You should name the restaurant Muhājir.” His point was that we’re all immigrants. I was like, “That’s such a simple statement, but such a profound statement.” It was kind of vice versa when we were talking about the bar: Jacob’s father is an amazing person and his name is Bho, and “bobo” in Tagalog means “silly” or “stupid,” as a term of endearment. We always say that as Spice Road-driven and transformative the food experience at Muhājir is, we still like to have fun. If people are early for their reservation, we take them back to Bobo, or they stop by after dinner. You can’t get to Bobo without walking through the restaurant, so the spaces contribute to each other. If you came to Bobo, you might be like, “I want to eat there.” And if you come straight to Muhājir and see people walking back constantly, you might be like, “What’s happening back there?” I wouldn’t say it’s easier [than my other restaurants], but now I don’t freak out. I’ve created a methodical way of approaching issues or problems head-on and figuring it out as a group or with the people that support us. We don’t have investors who are private equity firms; our investors are our guests. When it comes to managing expectations and navigating obstacles, you get better with repetition. I’m living a dream. Sometimes, when you’re building restaurants with others, you’re not necessarily in the kitchen. [At Mirra, I] was like, “I’m helping create and build this concept, but that’s [chef Rishi Kumar’s] kitchen to run.” Here, it’s the home that I’ve been yearning for and working toward my whole career. I plan to be old in this place. Things have been so crazy and wild and amazing, but slowly, every day, I sit more and more in that moment where I’m like, “This is home.” This interview has been edited and condensed. See More:

item.title: What to pack in your travel first-aid kit
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
What to pack in your travel first-aid kit One way to ensure your vacation goes smoothly is to be prepared for anything — including illnesses, weather and hotel evacuations. Minor injuries and ailments are another risk. That's why we recommend taking a portable first-aid everywhere you go. If you get sick or hurt while abroad, having the right remedies on hand can save you the hassle of searching for a drugstore in a foreign place — and, in some cases, even save your life. Here are some basic items to pack in your travel first-aid kit so you'll never be caught off-guard. Travelers with severe allergies are probably accustomed to packing prescription antihistamines or an Epi-Pen wherever they go. But even if this isn't you, you never know when you may encounter a new type of pollen or get a bad reaction to an insect bite while traveling. Or, like me, you might learn the hard way that you're allergic to a new brand of sunscreen on the first day of your beach vacation (yikes). Ever since that experience, I always bring a supply of over-the-counter allergy pills and antihistamine eye drops, plus anti-itch cream for heat rashes, bug bites and the like. Band-Aids, Steri-Strips, butterfly bandages and hydrocolloid plasters can come in handy for minor cuts and scrapes. I keep an emergency supply in my carry-on, and rarely a trip goes by that I don't break into it, whether for a passport paper cut or hiking-induced blisters. Not only will the right bandage make you a lot more comfortable (so you can actually enjoy your trip), it can also help prevent infection (so you won't end up spending your vacation in an emergency room). Before applying any bandage, be sure to clean the wound first. Liquids like rubbing alcohol antiseptic sprays could be tricky to get through airport security, so go for antiseptic wipes instead. Hemostatic gauze or emergency trauma dressing If you or a traveling companion suffer a more severe injury and are bleeding significantly — especially if you're out in the wilderness — one of these could buy you time while help arrives. Hemostatic gauze is treated with chemicals that encourage blood coagulation, or clotting. Instead of placing it over a wound, pack it tightly inside the wound and apply firm pressure. Meanwhile, an emergency trauma dressing, also known as an Israeli bandage, has a locking bar to apply 40 pounds of pressure. Just make sure you read the instructions and understand how to use it properly before adding it to your first-aid kit. Dehydration can strike anywhere, whether you're sightseeing during a heat wave or suffering through a long-distance flight in economy. Many TPGers swear by electrolyte powders to combat dehydration. Simply pour one into a water bottle and shake thoroughly, and it will go a long way in keeping you feeling your best. Tweezers are essential if you get a splinter. In more serious scenarios, a pair of trauma shears or a multitool can come in clutch when you need to remove clothing fast. And it's never a bad idea to carry an emergency glass-breaking tool. These shears have a built-in strap cutter, glass breaker and oxygen tank wrench, and this multi-tool offers everything from tweezers to scissors to a magnifying glass. Not only can a good flashlight help you assess and treat after-dark injuries, it can also light your path to help you avoid tripping and hurting yourself in the first place. Plus, a bright, long-distance light will make you easier to locate when you're calling for help, and you can even use it to signal SOS in Morse code. This pocket-sized option is under four inches long with a beam that can reach over 200 feet, and it's USB rechargeable. Sunscreen isn't just for long beach days and high-altitude hikes. Sometimes, the worst burns happen to travelers who didn't apply sunscreen because they thought they weren't at risk while, say, casually strolling around a city. It's always a good idea to pack some aloe vera gel to soothe any burns — but your best bet is to stop the burns before they start, so pack sun protection wherever you go. I keep a small Cadence capsule of sunscreen in my travel purse so I can easily reapply it to my face and shoulders while I'm out sightseeing. Ice packs are handy for everyday aches and pains, sports injuries and burns. The single-use chemical variety is activated by pressing or squeezing, which sets off an endothermic reaction to provide you with instant cooling relief — no freezer required. Many instant ice packs contain TSA-regulated ammonium nitrate. You can still pack them in your carry-on or checked bag, as long as the capacity of each container and overall quantity you're bringing do not exceed TSA limits. Some everyday ailments are even more common when we travel — like viruses caught on airplanes, motion sickness from boat rides or upset stomachs caused by overindulging in a new destination. Plus, some countries regulate common remedies, making it impossible to get your hands on them without a prescription. I always pack a travel-sized quantity of over-the-counter painkillers, stomach settlers and sleep aids in case the need arises. I use a pill container to keep them all in one place and avoid the chaos of half a dozen bottles or plastic baggies rattling around in my suitcase. Before zipping up your first-aid kit, check out our guide to traveling with medicine to make sure you aren't packing something that isn't allowed in your destination. If you or a travel companion has heart issues, it could be worth investing in St. John Ambulance's Pocket AED, which is roughly the size and weight of a can of soda. This device doesn't come cheap at around $1,400, but considering the 90% mortality rate for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest victims, it could be a true lifesaver. Ready to pack your own travel first-aid kit? You can purchase travel-size portions of common remedies, or get a pill container and refill it from your larger bottles at home (this one comes with pre-printed labels). Alternatively, you can purchase a pre-packed first-aid kit designed for travel; consider a waterproof option if you'll be spending lots of time at the beach.

item.title: The 'deadly' drink that symbolises New Orleans
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
The Obituary Cocktail: The 'deadly' drink that symbolises New Orleans Combining a martini's wallop with one of the world's most notorious spirits, this recently revived cocktail embodies the city's distinctive approach to life and death. Like a rake's progress, it starts with gin. Then vermouth. Then absinthe, delivered by atomiser, eye-dropper or spoon. A lemon twist, with its burst of essential oils, anoints it. My first Obituary Cocktail was in New Orleans, the city that invented it, forgot it and then revived it. In the eight years I lived there, it never appeared on a menu, but savvy local bartenders could make one on request. That evening's details are as hazy as the Wednesday after Fat Tuesday. I could not tell you the year, nor the season. I only remember it was good and that it was sometime after absinthe became legal again in the United States in 2007. I drank it at Cure. Neal Bodenheimer's legendary bar is graced by an enormous scientific print of a palmetto bug, the flying cockroach residents know as the city's native bird. Uplighting shines through the liquor bottles, turning them into bejewelled reliquaries. In a city that uses "costume" as a verb and shimmies into one at the drop of a hat, visuals are important. Poured into a vintage Nick and Nora coupe glass, the Obituary Cocktail is a head-turning drink. It also captures something of New Orleans' carefree approach to life and nonchalance in the face of death, where a clinking glass and party is often a response to worldly travails. "[The Obituary Cocktail] sums up the allure and the appeal of the city," says Clayton Rosenthal, manager and head of the drinks programme at Fives, a cocktail and oyster bar located in a historic 19th-Century building on Jackson Square. Rosenthal uses Old Tom gin, Drapo Dry vermouth and Mata Hari absinthe in his Obituary, warning first-time drinkers: "The first sip can be a bit of a punch in the mouth." It's an appropriate warning for a cocktail that combines a martini's wallop with one of the world's most notorious spirits and then names the result after a death notice. The Obituary Cocktail is a remnant of the louche and bohemian world of the French Quarter in the years following the end of Prohibition in 1933, when artists, writers and creatives like Tennessee Williams and Truman Capote gathered in cafes and bars. According to Sue Strachan, a New Orleans historian and author of The Obituary Cocktail, the drink was likely invented in Café Lafitte on Bourbon Street. She notes that the first known reference to the cocktail was in a 1942 guide to the city called "The Bachelor in New Orleans", which promised to introduce "unattached gentlemen and ladies of spirit" to "the Paris of North America". But while the drink subsequently surfaced in newspaper columns, nobody seems to have recorded who invented it or who gave it its morbid moniker. "There's no definitive documentation on how the cocktail got its name," says Strachan. "No doubt its powerful punch led to some rough mornings, much like the phrase 'death warmed over'." Absinthe supplied its mystique and maybe a throb in the head. "The Obituary is about intrigue," Strachan adds. "You bring absinthe into the picture and suddenly you have a drink with a little mystery, a little bohemian spirit and a whiff of the forbidden." During the Belle Époque (1871-1914), New Orleans was one of the US's greatest absinthe-drinking cities. Ted Breaux, a New Orleans-born historian and distiller who helped return genuine absinthe to the US market after its 95-year absence, says the finest French brands flowed into the city. By the 1890s, absinthe was showing up in New Orleans drinks ranging from the Sazerac to the Absinthe Frappé and Absinthe Suissesse. Then it became notorious, Breaux says. The spirit was blamed for everything from nervous disorders to hallucinations before the US banned it in 1912. The blame, he argues, was its popularity, which encouraged cheap imitations and disreputable ingredients. "You [could urinate] in a bottle and call it absinthe, much to my dismay," he says. Breaux compares absinthe's role in a cocktail with something else New Orleanians understand instinctively. "If you have a bowl of gumbo, what happens when you put in a big dash of Crystal Hot Sauce? It amplifies the flavour and gives it a pop," he says. "That is what absinthe does to [the Obituary Cocktail]. Absinthe is cocktail hot sauce." There was a problem, however: when the Obituary Cocktail was invented, its defining ingredient, absinthe, had already been illegal in the US for decades. Strachan believes Café Lafitte stashed bottles of absinthe smuggled into the country by well-travelled patrons, while other bartenders reached for substitutes. The liqueur Herbsaint, developed in New Orleans after Prohibition ended, replicated absinthe's distinct anise flavours without its prohibited ingredients. Ojen, an Andalusian anise-based liqueur, was also used. But after Café Lafitte moved down the street from its original location (now occupied by Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop) following a property dispute in 1953 to become Café Lafitte in Exile, the Obituary gradually slipped from view. When Strachan began researching her book in 2023, she found only one bar – Jewel of the South in the French Quarter – that listed it on its menu. Since then, however, interest in the Obituary has begun to climb with a renewed focus on artisanal cocktails. Now, Strachan says, Fives, and Mildred's, a new martini bar located in the boutique Warbler hotel on St Charles Avenue, feature the drink. In a way, the Obituary Cocktail embodies its birth city. Death and pleasure often occupy the same space in New Orleans. This is a city that holds an annual Vampire Ball in honour of the late hometown horror writer Anne Rice and where the corpse of local socialite Mikey Easterling even presided over her own 2014 wake, Champagne glass in hand. "New Orleans is a very complex place," says Eric Seiferth, a senior curator at the Historic New Orleans Collection, the French Quarter's history museum. "The willingness to accept that two things can be in the same room at the same time is part of life here." Unlike in other US cities, Seiferth says mourning in New Orleans has historically remained public, communal and intertwined with faith, music and life. At funerals in New Orleans' African American community, it is not uncommon to see musicians parading through the streets in a celebratory "second line" procession. On Mardi Gras Day, the North Side Skull & Bone Gang, a historic Afro-Creole secret society, honours their ancestors by waking the spirits while dressed in skeleton costumes to remind the living of their own mortality. And on All Saints Day, 1 November, families gather in cemeteries to clean, repair and decorate ancestral gravestones and tombs. For Helena Heavey, a bartender at Avegno, a stylish bar and lounge in Uptown New Orleans, the Obituary Cocktail's very name encourages a quiet inventory of one's own mortality. "An Obituary can act as a memorium for the day, and however it's unfolding – if it's celebration or atonement," she says. "It's a very New Orleans way of drinking: with reflection. And the name encourages it." New Orleans never needs reminding that death is nearby. An Obituary Cocktail blends pleasure, danger and beauty in a glass, daring drinkers to gulp it all down. "It could be too much for most folks elsewhere," Rosenthal says, "but we see it as perfectly balanced." – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: ‘A winning combination of culture and nature’: exploring Germany’s green heart by bus
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
Itâs early morning in Erfurt, the capital of Germanyâs Thuringia region, and Domplatz is abuzz with local growers setting out crates of vegetables and flowers beneath the soaring medieval cathedral towers. This 14th- and 15th-century engineering wonder holds the Gloriosa, the worldâs largest medieval free-swinging bell, cast in 1497 and weighing 12 tonnes. Though the city and surrounding landscape are notably flat, its skyline is pierced by soaring church towers and steeples, the atmospheric old town hardly changed over the centuries. Thuringia â often called the âgreen heart of Germanyâ â lies in the centre of the country, between Hesse, Saxony and Bavaria. Itâs famous for its dense forests, intellectual heritage and hearty cuisine, and Iâm here for four days to explore using public transport. Leaving Frankfurt behind, my three-hour coach journey rolls through rising forested highlands before descending into the wide, agricultural basin that cradles Erfurt. After checking out Domplatzâs morning market, itâs just a short walk to one of the townâs other famous sights, the 120-metre-long KrÃ¤merbrÃ¼cke â a 14th-century bridge lined with colourful half-timbered houses. Erfurt was once at the crossroads of two major trade routes, and the wealth that built its impressive churches and merchantsâ houses came partly from waid, or woad, a plant cultivated in the surrounding fields and processed for its blue dye. I stroll past the craft shops (some still sell the dye) to Petersberg Citadel, one of the largest and best-preserved fortresses in Europe, with a maze of underground tunnels. This is also the city where the Protestant Reformation took root â Martin Luther studied here and was a monk in the Augustinian monastery (you can join a guided tour or even stay overnight). Dinner is in a suitably historic setting; Wirtshaus Christoffel, in the Haus zur weiÃen Lilie (House of the White Lily), dates back to the 12th century (the house-brewed beer and beef roulade with Thuringian dumplings are delicious). Next morning, I head to Egapark (a seven-minute bus ride or a 30-minute walk from town). Spread across 36 hectares (89 acres), it was created for the 1961 international horticultural exhibition. The old Cyriaksburg fortress houses the German Horticultural Museum, which traces the history of gardening, while displays range from landscapes of cacti and succulents to tropical planting. The city of Weimar, a 30-minute bus journey away, is next on my list. The birthplace of the artistic Bauhaus movement, and where Germanyâs first democratic constitution was adopted, itâs full of interesting historic sites and design gems. I visit the Bauhaus museum, with its ceramics, textiles, metalwork and painting, and wander around town, passing the former art school buildings that now house the Bauhaus-UniversitÃ¤t. The next morning, I swap culture for chilling and take another bus to Bad Langensalza, a spa town of 10 parks and themed gardens, 40 miles (64km) away. My guide, Markus Fromm, explains that people come here to âcure, to relax, to refreshâ. Sulphur springs were discovered here in 1811, and today, the Friederiken Therme is the townâs main thermal spa, offering natural sulphur, brine and drinking mineral waters, alongside indoor and outdoor pools, saunas and treatments. Traces of the older spa history remain around the town: at FriederikenschlÃ¶sschen, an 18th-century summer residence, a fountain still runs with sulphur water that has been used for healing since 1812. But itâs the townâs gardens that really win me over. I wander FriederikenschlÃ¶sschenâs restored baroque garden and visit the Klagetor, a gate tower dating from about 1365, where the old town gives way to the Japanese garden, Kofuku no Niwa (Garden of Happiness), with its koi ponds, clipped azaleas and sculpted pines. For nature on an even grander scale, I take a bus to Hainich national park, 10 minutes away (you can easily rent a bike/e-bike and follow cycling paths to get there too). Spanning 7,500 hectares, Hainich offers more than 75 miles of signposted walking trails through its beech forests, part of a Unesco world heritage site. The wider Hainich is Germanyâs largest unbroken deciduous woodland area. âParts of this landscape have been left entirely untouched for decades, abandoned to their own devices without a shred of human meddling,â says park director RÃ¼diger Biehl. Before hitting the trail, I stop at the parkâs restaurant, Forsthaus Thiemsburg, for a regional lunch â roast pork in black beer and Thuringian dumplings, washed down with a cold KÃ¶stritzer pilsner. Then, into the trees. Deep in the beeches, the sun sporadically breaks through the branches and the leaves crunch loudly under my boots. Up in the canopy, itâs mostly just the birds making noise â chaffinches and wood warblers chatter, interrupted by the occasional sharp rattle of a middle spotted woodpecker drilling into a trunk. The Baumkronenpfad, a wooden walkway through the treetops, rises to a 44-metre observation tower. Here, the canopy of an oak that is estimated to be 350 years old is almost at eye level. Itâs a spectacular view, but the forestâs real engine is down below. Deadwood is left to decay where it falls, providing habitat for rare wood-boring insects and endangered Bechsteinâs bats. Back in Erfurt that evening, I catch the final symphony concert of the season at Theaterplatz. Itâs a reminder of the winning combination of culture and nature that Iâve enjoyed over my four days in Thuringia. I had come looking for a less familiar corner of Germany and found a region that offers plenty of variety â and all accessible with a few short bus rides. The trip was provided by the German National Tourist Board. Dorint Hotel am Dom in Erfurt has doubles from Â£85. For journey planning, VMT has information on buses, trains and trams across central Thuringia, as well as a free app with live departure updates

item.title: These Resorts Offer a Real Taste of American Regional Cuisine
item.description:
Source: Eater
American resorts are once again having a moment — and it’s not pickleball partisans driving the trend. A new generation of travelers, beset with decision fatigue in their daily lives, are embracing the all-inclusive stay where activities, amenities, and dining are all on the menu and usually just a short walk from their rooms. These Resorts Offer a Real Taste of American Regional Cuisine No more generic resort food. These culinary-savvy properties bring a distinct sense of place to the all-inclusive experience. Fortunately, stress-free no longer needs to mean bland or generic when it comes to cuisine and culture. Resorts have begun forging deep culinary connections to their surroundings, far beyond merely offering a few regionally specific cocktails or themed burger toppings. Onsite farms, creameries, and distilleries provide fresh ingredients with true terroir, as well as a new category of resort activity: food-and-drink-focused tours and workshops to fill the time between morning yoga and an afternoon poolside nap. Some resort restaurants, like Clay at Wildflower Farms in New York’s Hudson Valley and Sierra Mar at the Post Ranch Inn in Big Sur, California, have become destinations in themselves, where star chefs take diners deep into a region’s foodways. These resorts leave visitors not just relaxed but also satisfied, having truly experienced — and tasted — a particular place. Acura has always done things its own way. We believe the best experiences are created through intentional choices, thoughtful craftsmanship, and the confidence to pursue a different approach. This spirit is reflected in our philosophy of Precision Crafted Performance. Learn more. By the time you get to Hawks Cay Resort in the middle of the Florida Keys, the blue vistas of the Overseas Highway will have made mainland worries seem very far away. The 60-acre resort on Duck Key offers a spa, five pools (including a saltwater lagoon), and soon a full water park. Also making a splash is Salt + Ash, the resort’s flagship live-fire restaurant from Florida native, Top Chef winner, and former Eater Miami Chef of the Year Jeremy Ford. Of course, fish and seafood from the surrounding waters feature prominently. But Florida flavors shine through in other ways too: Much of the produce on the menu comes from Ford’s Farm, strategically located between Miami Beach and the Keys. That might mean homegrown lychees in a uniquely local take on conch salad, or heirloom tomatoes just hours off the vine accompanying crisp-fried spear-caught fish. Many resorts lay claim to a signature dish or cocktail. But the Tides Inn, situated on a quiet tributary of the Chesapeake Bay about 3 hours’ drive from Washington, D.C., has something few resorts, if any, can boast: its own oyster. Cultivated near the property by resident ecologist Will Smiley and served exclusively at the resort’s Salt & Meadow restaurant, the Widgeon oyster provides guests with an intimate connection to the estuary it calls home. To taste it is to taste the tides and the weather. “Our oyster changes salinity as the season changes, and as the weather changes,” says executive chef Kyle Perkins. He further notes that the freshwater influx with a heavy rainfall can quickly, if temporarily, change how much of a salty punch a Widgeon possesses. Beyond bivalves, Perkins sources everything from beef to blackberries from the region. Along with activities from lawn games and pickleball to kayaking, guests can even help themselves to the harvest: Those blackberries, a thornless variety, grow in abundance on the property, giving many children a first foraging experience. Though it’s only about a 90-minute drive from the concrete canyons of Manhattan, Auberge Collection’s Wildflower Farms feels a world away. The Hudson Valley property’s 65 cabins, cottages, and suites feature floor-to-ceiling windows framing arcadian views. Thistle, an Auberge Spa, makes use of local botanicals and blooms in its treatments, while the on-site farm provides more than 14,000 pounds of produce annually for the restaurant, Clay. “The Hudson Valley is unique in the array of locally grown ingredients available,” says farm director Will Conway, noting that the resort’s culinary reach extends beyond its 140 acres. The menu is resolutely seasonal; even a dish like ricotta meatballs provides a changing taste of what is coming from nearby producers, with the protein shifting from pork to lamb depending on the time of year. The Kohler name is, for most people, synonymous with kitchen and bath fixtures. But the company is also a serious player in hospitality, most notably with Kohler, Wisconsin, its sprawling resort in the town where the company is headquartered, two and a half hours from Chicago. Along with golf, a legendary spa, and outdoor activities like canoeing, hiking, hunting, and fishing, Kohler, Wisconsin, puts a strong emphasis on dining with Midwestern ingredients and hospitality. Among the on-site options is River Wildlife, a log cabin restaurant offering regional specialties like walleye, pheasant, and duck. The Wisconsin Room, meanwhile, combines steakhouse fare with Wisconsin supper club favorites like a “Not So Lazy” Susan, which includes deviled eggs, chicken liver mousse, and pickled vegetables in a nod to the classic relish tray. Regional cocktails like a brandy Old Fashioned and a grasshopper (de rigeur after dinner) leave no doubt where you are. This resort three and a half hours northwest of Denver is big — about twice the size of Manhattan big. That leaves plenty of room for culinary operations that include a distillery, a bakery, and a greenhouse. Brush Creek Ranch’s herd of American wagyu cattle is raised using Japanese methods, which minimize stress in the name of producing superior marbling for added tenderness. You may not run into a steer getting a facial in one of the resort’s two spas, but rest assured, these animals are living their best lives. The ranch’s goats, meanwhile, don’t just assist with yoga classes: Some provide milk for the property’s Medicine Bow Creamery and its range of excellent cheeses. It all comes together at the Cheyenne Club restaurant, where meals and most beverages — like many of the resort’s activities, ranging from horseback riding and hiking to fly-fishing and standup paddleboard yoga — are included in the room rate. At Castle Hot Springs, everything comes back to the water. The 130-year-old resort in the Bradshaw Mountains, about an hour north of Phoenix, was Arizona’s first spa retreat; families like the Rockefellers and Astors would come to soak in the spring-fed pools first discovered by Native American people thousands of years before. Along with a full roster of wellness and outdoor activities, the resort grows 35 types of citrus and features a 3-acre farm, irrigated by the same mineral-rich water that fills the pools. “Everything tastes a little bit better because it’s already pre-seasoned for me,” said executive chef Chris Knouse. To get a taste of “the farm on a plate,” Knouse recommends the lunchtime “farmer’s hummus,” which comes with that day’s harvest as a crudités assortment. At dinner, Harvest restaurant offers a tasting menu where dishes like cavatelli with corn, zucchini, tatsoi, and cherry tomatoes offer a deeper dive into what the Sonoran Desert can produce. Arguably the only thing more beautiful than Post Ranch Inn is the drive there. It is, after all, located along what might be the most picturesque stretch of road in the entire country: Highway 1 in Big Sur. On a cliff overlooking the Pacific Ocean, the resort offers guests access to a spa and three pools, as well as activities like forest meditation and stargazing. Of Post Ranch Inn’s 100 acres, 90 are kept wild, and just over one is dedicated to a chef’s garden, which supplies the resort’s restaurant Sierra Mar. On this patch of land, chef Reylon Agustin and his team grow everything from apples and tomatoes to herbs and specialty ingredients like celtuce. From the surrounding forests come wild mushrooms, while nearby waters provide treasured ingredients like abalone for Sierra Mar, which is housed in a glass and wood pavilion that feels like it’s hovering over the cliff’s edge. Augustin knows well enough not to try to compete with the view. Instead, dishes like abalone congee and Grimaud Farms guinea hen with sunchokes and stone fruit highlight local ingredients to “complement the experience” of being in such a singular place.

item.title: Where Chef Eric Sze Eats on His Day Off in NYC
item.description:
Source: Eater
Chef Eric Sze, the owner of NYC’s Wenwen, shows us the bakeries, pizzerias, and restaurants he visits weekly for everything from simple baguette sandwiches to oversized wontons. Where Chef Eric Sze Eats on His Day Off in NYC Award-winning Taiwanese chef Eric Sze takes Eater on a food tour of NYC Sze starts his day off with a sandwich at Bakeri; his go-to order is honey, apple, and brie layered on a crunchy baguette. Then he heads to The Meat Hook, Wenwen’s meat supplier, to get a specialty cut of steak and dry-aged short ribs for dinner. Next, he grabs a whole, crispy, NY-style pie at Chrissy’s Pizza (chef Chris Hansell has been perfecting this pie for years). The jalapeño and garlic pie has perfect proportions of each ingredient, all on a doughy, yeasted crust. For his final stop, Sze goes to Maxi’s Noodle 2 in Flushing for the nostalgic Chinese food he’s craved since leaving Taiwan. Owner Maxi Lau-O’Keefe teaches him how to make her iconic wontons, filled with shrimp and pork before being expertly folded. After being humbled by the complex folding process, Sze settles in for a soup full of thin noodles made with duck eggs and those classic wontons, alongside beef soup. Watch the most recent episode of Chef’s Day Off to see how chef Eric Sze spends his day off at his favorite restaurants, bakeries, and butcher shops around New York City.

item.title: Enjoy Fishing, Foraging, and Focaccia-Making at These U.S. Resorts
item.description:
Source: Eater
Plenty of resorts across the country have excellent restaurants, but travelers seeking more should explore the hands-on side of culinary resort experiences. From New York’s Hudson Valley to the South Texas Coast, adventurous food lovers can partake in workshops and experiences that get them out of the dining room and into the kitchen, garden, farm, or ocean. Whether you’re looking to forage or fish, these excursions will introduce you to local people, ingredients, and techniques, and ultimately offer a true taste of the destination. Enjoy Fishing, Foraging, and Focaccia-Making at These U.S. Resorts Guests today expect more than a Michelin-starred restaurant. They want to get into the kitchen and out in the field. At these properties, it’s less about what’s on your plate and more about how it got there. Big Sur is the perfect place to forage for edible botanicals and aromatics, and on Chesapeake Bay, harvesting and shucking oysters is woven into the community’s cultural fabric. Those wanting to escape the hustle and bustle of New York City can head up to the Hudson Valley for focaccia-making, while a desert oasis on the outskirts of Scottsdale, Arizona, teaches you how to craft pasta like a pro. No matter your level of expertise, these resort experiences are designed to connect curious travelers with an impressive network of chefs, farmers, ecologists, mixologists, and bakers. For a vacation that will also quench your thirst for knowledge, head to these exciting culinary resorts. Acura has always done things its own way. We believe the best experiences are created through intentional choices, thoughtful craftsmanship, and the confidence to pursue a different approach. This spirit is reflected in our philosophy of Precision Crafted Performance. Learn more. Head down to the South Texas Coast for a true catch-to-table culinary experience. Local guides at La Pesca Lodge take guests to prime spots throughout Baffin Bay, offering everything from fly-fishing and wading to drifting and sight casting. Though you’re welcome to bring your own gear, the lodge provides spinning rods, lures, and live bait if needed. Expect to reel in an array of speckled trout, redfish, flounder, and black drum. Your catch will be cleaned and bagged for you to take back to the lodge, where chefs transform your bounty into ceviche, grilled fillets, and more. Just remember that you’ll need to purchase your own Texas fishing license in advance. Those more interested in old-fashioned hunting can partake in dove, duck, or nilgai shoots. The Andaz Scottsdale Resort & Bungalows is a retro, palm-tree-lined oasis with a premier spa, unique art collection, and the on-site restaurant Weft & Warp. Every Thursday, guests can beat the desert heat with a hands-on pasta class in the restaurant for $65. You’ll learn a variety of techniques while crafting a few different pasta shapes. You might make agnolotti filled with a chive and shrimp paste; and you will also learn simpler pastas, like classic linguine or fettuccine. Once you’re done, enjoy your finished product with an optional wine pairing on the patio. If you’ve got dessert on the brain, book the Sweet Escape truffle-making workshop (hosted every Friday) and elevate your pastry skills by learning the basics of chocolate tempering. Virginia’s Tides Inn gives travelers the chance to live like a Chesapeake waterman for the day. This signature activity pairs guests with a resident ecologist who takes you out to oyster cages via boat for an educational experience that’s all about shellfish. You’ll haul up your own oyster cages and sort through the very best bivalves, all while learning about the region’s longstanding history with oystering and the positive impact it has on the local ecosystem. Oysters harvested during the excursion need to be refrigerated for at least 24 hours, so when you return to the inn, enjoy a shucking how-to with the previous day’s haul while sipping on local wine and beer. The Chesapeake Gold experience is a similar outing, but includes a visit to one of the inn’s very own oyster farms, meaning you get to consume the same ones you collect. Once back at the inn, enjoy them both raw, grilled, and topped with your favorite seasonings. Located in the foothills of Tennessee’s Great Smoky Mountains, Blackberry Farm is a working estate that maintains a strong connection to Appalachian agriculture. A twice-daily farmstead tour is available all year long, giving guests an in-depth look at the heirloom gardens, heritage livestock pasture, and dairy barn. These manicured, bright green gardens create a scenic backdrop to your itinerary, which includes sampling of farmstead cheeses, cured meats, preserves, and a rotating seasonal beverage. Those wanting a more formal culinary experience can book a three-hour artisan cooking demo with a three-course educational lunch and a glass of wine to pair. Located about an hour and 20 minutes away from Phoenix, Castle Hot Springs is a picturesque desert resort with a thriving agricultural operation. The 3-acre garden yields more than 150 seasonal fruits, veggies, herbs, and flowers, supporting a dynamic farm-to-table ethos across the resort’s Relais & Châteaux-approved restaurant, Harvest. Start your day with a one-hour farm tour, tasting your way through a variety of crops as you learn about the fertile soils supported by the area’s natural geothermal hot springs. In the afternoon, test your skills with a hands-on mixology class using produce and botanicals straight from the property grounds. The Osthoff Resort & Spa is about 150 miles north of Chicago, right along the shores of Wisconsin’s Elkhart Lake. It doubles as a professional cooking school, hosting a plethora of gourmet classes fit for any season or holiday. The culinary curriculum is overseen by chef Rodney Schulz, with courses changing week to week. October’s schedule features everything from paella- and pasta-making to creepy themed cocktails for Halloween. November sees hearty soup demos and holiday pies, while December embraces a festive spirit with Christmas libations and cookies. There is plenty of hands-on instruction, and you’ll be returning home with a new set of skills that are far more useful than any souvenir. Ready to hard-launch your sourdough baking era? Learn the basics with Ashley Napoli, also known as the Focaccia Flourist, at the Hudson Valley’s Wildflower Farms. This Auberge Collection property is about 90 miles away from New York City, which makes it an easy escape for city dwellers needing to touch some grass. The focaccia workshop costs $168 per person and starts by teaching you how to care for and maintain a living sourdough starter. You then knead, arrange, and shape your loaf, topping it with herbs, onions, florals, olives, and anything you’d like before baking. This particular workshop is being offered every Sunday and Tuesday through the end of October, but the resort typically hosts some version of a focaccia class throughout the year. In Big Sur, towering redwood forest meets dramatic, bluff-lined coast, creating a diverse ecosystem brimming with unique plant life. The serene 54-room Alila Ventana Big Sur is a wellness-focused resort that spans 160 acres of lush, open meadows, tree-lined trails, and shaded ravines, creating the ideal conditions for a plethora of fungi and botanicals. Every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, the hotel hosts a complimentary foragers hike for guests, who will learn all about wild-food harvesting and spotting secret ingredients hidden within the local terrain. There’s also a year-round Foragers Cocktail class ($99), a more in-depth experience that begins with an outdoor search for various herbs and aromatics, and culminates in a mixology lesson where you craft small-batch bitters for a custom cocktail.

item.title: A lakeside idyll: laid-back cycling and autumn hikes on Italy’s Lake Iseo
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
Rust red and burnt sienna speckle the green mountain rising from Lake Iseo. Golden autumn sunlight shimmers on the water. Monte Isola, Italyâs largest lake island, is a peak of sheer cliffs and dense forest, dotted with old fishing hamlets and hillside villages, each as pretty as the terraced villas of Lake Como and Garda, but with far fewer visitors. I arrive at the small port town of Peschiera Maraglio â where striped wooden boats jut from the water like the gondolas of Venice â on a ferry from Sulzano, a five-minute hop across the water. âOnly three people on the island are allowed to own a car: the priest, the doctor and the mayor,â says Chiara, my tour guide from Brescia. Residents can zip up and down the steep island roads on mopeds, and a small fleet of van-sized buses trundle around throughout the day, but nearly all cars are forbidden and visitors have to explore on foot or bike. Even bikes are banned from boats at the weekend. Not that it matters: the harbour front is lined with bike rentals (from â¬4 an hour for a standard bike). Iâm normally a nervous cyclist, but car-free roads raise my confidence. Plus, most other visitors have the telltale front-wheel wobble of novice riders. This isnât the place for Lycra and personal bests; the smooth-as-silk, quiet roads are for slow pedalling, and neck swivelling to take in another gorgeous view of Lake Iseo. The circular lakeside route winds past olive groves tumbling to the shore. I thought Iâd need base layers and gloves this far into autumn, but Iâm in shorts and a T-shirt and already working up a sweat in 24C sunshine. I pedal through the lakeside hamlet of Sensole in the islandâs south-west and stop in Menzino, just along the shore. Thereâs a cafe-bar catering to cyclists, so I fuel up with an espresso con lake view. The view from the western side of the island is somewhat marred by a huge concrete factory on the mainland, so I keep my head down on the pedal to Siviano, the islandâs capital. The shambling streets are sleepy; the stacked skyline of orange, lemon and magnolia villas is punctuated by the looming facade of Santi Faustino e Giovita church and a medieval stone tower. Monte Isola has been inhabited since the Roman era. Venetian rule in the 15th and 16th centuries left the main towns resembling those on Garda and Como: hillside terraces of wooden-shuttered pastel villas. In the late 18th century, Monte Isola found its main industry: net making. At Retificio La Rete Srl, a small shop and net factory at Sivianoâs port, fishing nets have been handwoven for centuries, along with nets for basketball hoops, football goals, shopping bags and hammocks. At the northern tip of the island, I get the best views of Lake Iseoâs craggiest mountains. The south of the lake is chalk-white bell towers against gently undulating hills, draped in franciacorta vineyards. The north is where jagged peaks scrape the sky, plummeting to the emerald-green lake water. Just off the shore, a speck of an island (Isola di Loreto) is topped with a grand, castle-like building, which Chiara says is privately owned. A flotilla of kayakers from Marone make their way towards the private dock, slipping across the glass-still water. In Carzano, I pause to admire thepink-and-white facade of San Giovanni Battista church, before cycling along the more functional stretch of road along the eastern shore. The traffic-free spell is broken by an old Fiat Punto, apologetically crawling along the road. Maybe the driver is the doctor or priest. I complete my circle back in Peschiera Maraglio, where a late lunch of lake fish awaits at La Foresta restaurant. To begin, pickled tench so vinegary it makes my mouth water and a chub carpaccio that tastes like fresh lake water; followed by the island staple of dried, salted sardinas on grilled polenta. âSardina is not a sardine; itâs actually a type of shad fish,â Chiara explains. âIn the middle ages, when Monte Isola had to pay tax to Venice, they didnât understand how money worked, so they paid in salted sardinas instead.â As the last ferries leave for the evening, it feels as if I have Peschiera Maraglio to myself. Accommodation is private holiday apartments or restaurants with rooms. At Decio, a modern bistro dominates the ground floor, with a handful of sleek bedrooms above. The glass front shows off an uninterrupted lake view and the room is bathed in orange light at sunset. I spend the evening perched on a stool outside LâIsola dei Sapori, a no-frills alfresco spot where sparkling franciacorta wine is perfectly chilled, and snacks of local salami, olives and fish dishes combine for a light dinner. The next day, I forgo my bike and lace up my hiking boots. The steep trail to the top of the island begins with the enclosed cobbled streets of Peschiera Maraglio and wends into thick chestnut forest. I pocket a particularly beefy conker, unable to resist the childhood urge for a blinder. My legs start to burn against the gradient â the trail is 450 metres of climbing. Rocks and twisting roots burst through the forest path and thereâs a sheer drop to one side, but the glimpses of Lake Iseo between the trees are worth every wheeze. After an hour, the trees thin out and I emerge at Santuario della Madonna della Ceriola. The striking white sanctuary was built in the 13th century, on the remains of a pagan temple and early Christian chapels. A vast golden altar and detailed frescoes adorn the interior, but itâs the panoramic view outside that really makes the hike worthwhile. The ferry to Sulzano is a toy boat, leaving a white tail of wake. From up high, I see that autumn colours are already creeping into the forest. I wipe the sweat from my eyes. This view is only going to get prettier as the season evolves, and the prize conkers are yet to fall. The trip was arranged by Visit Brescia. Bike rental starts at â¬4 an hour. The ferry from Sulzano to Monte Isola is â¬2.60 each way. Trains run from Brescia to Sulzano from â¬4.10. Rooms at Decio start at â¬90 B&B

item.title: A Frequent Flier’s Guide to Every Single United Lounge at Newark Airport
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
The only problem with indulging in the chocolate chip cookie skillet at United Polaris Lounge dining room at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) is that you know the best part of your trip is already behind you before you even take off. Topped with vanilla ice cream and chocolate drizzle, the dessert is served warm out of the oven in a cookie-sized skillet, a perfect portion for one while relaxing pre-flight with a front-row seat to the taxing planes backdropped by the New York City skyline. Having lived in Hoboken, New Jersey, for more than two decades, Iâve become a diehard loyalist to my neighborhood airport EWR, as well as its largest carrier, United Airlines, which accounts for nearly 70% of the hubâs flights. While the skillet cookie is top of mind, Iâve spent collective hours enjoying all of its lounges, most of which have been refreshed in the last four years. All told, they hit that perfect mix of the comfort of your local coffee shop, the suaveness of boutique hotel design, and delectable fresh-made food options that fuel you instead of weighing you down. Each is conveniently open from 5 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily, with the exception of the location near Gate C123, which is open until 10:30 p.m. If youâre trying to decide which lounge to spend time in before boarding, hereâs what to expect at each United Club and lounge at Newark. United Club Near Gate C123 (Terminal C) United first started its transformation of its Newark lounges when it opened the doors to this 30,000 square-foot space with 480 seats in May 2022. And with it, it made a statement. These were no longer just utilitarian lounges for a quick refresh and refuel before flights. These are design-forward spaces that meld that pre-flight care and comfort with boutique hotel-style decor rooted in its New York City and New Jersey culture. This particular club remains my longtime favorite. Whenever I pass the self-scan entrance into the welcome lounge, Iâve made a habit of stopping for a glass of fruit-infused water in and admiring the eclectic decor of the wooden shelves. If United sold United Club workspace membership, Iâd be in this lounge every day. One of the first things travelers will notice is the wall art: United collaborated with the The Newark Museum of Art and Newark-based Gallery Aferro on murals by local artists including Gilbert Hsiao and Dahlia Elsayed, capturing the areaâs musical and historical pasts. Each part of the lounge, which features a full-service coffee bar, premium bar, wellness room, and spa-like shower suites, has a distinct feel. With chefs and servers stationed behind the buffet, the foodâwhich includes a salad bar and entrees served in cast-iron skilletsâtastes fresher than standard lounge offerings. Business travelers will relish in the sleek recessed workstation booths and plush couchesâand the firm sense of place delivered by New York subway-style wall tiles and signage. As you take a breather from the chaos of the airport, be sure to peek out of the vast windows for views of Manhattan's skyline rising in the distance. United Club Near Gate C74 (Terminal C) The second United Club in Terminal C debuted in October 2023 near Gate C74, elevated above the busyness of the terminal below. Its circular design attempts to give an infinite loop, but thereâs no hiding from the fact that at 18,000-square-feet for more than 400 seats, itâs a bit more cramped. Overall, the style reads more utilitarian, which makes sense since the look was inspired by midtown Manhattan, and even includes ceiling art thatâs an ode to Grand Central Station. The buffet is broken up into a few sections (the gummy bears lured me straight to the snack bar), and I love catching the breakfast-to-lunch switchover when fresh chocolate chip cookies are brought out (I may have stashed away a few for the flight). While it also has a self-scan entrance, bar, and wellness room, my favorite part is sitting at the counter along the windows, looking down at the humming terminal below. A few times, Iâve been lucky enough to be staring down right at my gate, so I could milk every lounge moment. United Club Near Gate A27 (Terminal A) Newark officially transformed its reputation when its Terminal A, which opened in January 2023, won Skytrakâs Worldâs Best New Terminal the following year. It exudes high-tech vibes, offers some quality local food (I still can't believe my Jersey City favorite Bang Cookies has a shop here!), and there's the bonus perk of two calming sensory rooms. And the United Club near Gate A27 is more immersive than the others, as itâs an open-air space hovering above the terminal. At 15,000 square feet, itâs technically the smallest of the lounges, with about 300 seatsâyet, without walls, has an airy loft-like feel. It comes with a buffet, bar, and wellness room, and the art is all locally sourced, including a striking mixed media mural by Newark-artist Antoinnette Ellis-Williams. During a visit in August, I was charmed to find that the fresh Jersey peaches infused into the water were cut in the shape of hearts. United Polaris Lounge (Terminal C) Originally making its debut in May 2018, the United Polaris Lounge already got a major refresh in June 2025, growing the space to 30,000 square feet. Undoubtedly the most luxurious of the airlinesâ Newark lounges, itâs now the largest in the Polaris network, and is reserved for those flying on the same day in the Polaris class on long-haul international flights, as well as first and business passengers on Star Alliance international flights. The highlight is the lounge's full-service restaurant, included with entry. A reservation is required during busy periods, which can only be made in person by checking in with the host. Despite being quoted longer times, I usually end up getting a text that my table is ready about 15 to 30 minutes later. My favorite seats are the solo tables facing the tarmac, although I will say the space is tight if I need to use my laptop. Among the meals Iâve enjoyed there are the small plates of lump crab cake and fish tacos, as well as the wild mushroom bisque. For mains, Iâve been tempted by the Polaris signature burger, but I tend to go for the seared scallops. Cocktail options include a classic Bloody Mary, as well as the airlineâs own Polaris Star with gin, ginger honey, and lemon, but I canât help but go into vacation mode with an Aperol spritz. And of course, the skillet cookie is always a requirement. Utilizing the space that was formerly used by the speakeasy Classified, the Polaris Lounge expansion allows for broader views of the New York City skyline. The seating area features a mix of table sizes, ranging from those designed for solo travelers up to two-tops that can be pushed together for groups of eight (the former dining area is now part of the buffet seating). The rest of the lounge also received some light refreshes, most notably extra seating near the front entry under two United Airlines NYC Half Marathon art pieces. Other amenities on offer include private phone booths, showers, nap rooms, and a dedicated United help desk. Simply put, if you can get in, this is the place to be. This story has been updated with new information since its original publication date.

item.title: 'Changed My Life' Lentil Soup and More Recipes We Made This Week
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Itâs no secret that Bon AppÃ©tit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes weâre whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here. A fried fish sandwich has no season. Also, Iâm currently in Tennessee, where itâs hit 90Â° this week, so itâs basically still summer. I used my colleague Shilpa Uskokovicâs excellent Fritto Misto batter to coat some flounder. After frying, I slid a couple small fillets into top-split hot dog buns with juicy slices of tomato and a quick tartar sauce. It was pure summer satisfaction, even this deep into October. âJoe Sevier, senior editor, SEO and cooking We are squarely back in school and with that comes snack requests. The Gourmet stalwart, Chocolate Chip Cookies, remains a reliable favorite in our household. I know this is a hit because itâs the one requested by not just my own child, but her hungry friends. The 2026 update has me sprinkling just a touch of flaky salt on top of each one. âHana Asbrink, deputy food editor The days when my husband and I both commute are, to put it lightly, b-a-n-a-n-a-s. Thatâs when my deep freezer fulfills its destiny. Case in point: this superlative basil pesto, thawed overnight, tossed with hot rigatoni, plus frozen peas thrown in with the pasta for the last few minutes of boiling. It is nourishing and feels purposeful, even if it took less than 10 minutes of effort. âEmma Laperruque, cooking director Andy Baraghaniâs Honey-Chipotle Shrimp Tacos are one of my most-made recipes of all time. Last week I decided to change things up and eat the shrimp over some homemade Mexican rice and beans instead of wrapping them in a tortilla. The shrimp are so easy to make (just toss in a two-ingredient marinade and pan-fry) that I ended up cooking fresh batches for lunch on the following days to pair with the leftover rice and beans. The canned chipotles in adobo lend a smoky complexity, and I love how the honey helps the shrimp take on just enough char. A luxurious WFH lunch if there ever was one! âAlaina Chou, commerce writer Soup on a weeknight? Itâs a foreign concept to me. If Iâm making soup, Iâm committing hours to the cause. But this week I couldnât quell my craving for a sippable bowl, so I scoured the archive for a quick hit and landed on this Curried Lentil, Tomato, and Coconut Soup. Red lentils break down and create a substantial body, while golden Japanese S&B curry powder adds a mellow earthy kick. After mixing in crushed tomatoes and coconut milk, I went rogue and followed up with a couple dashes of fish sauce for extra umami. âNina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking The ever adaptable rotisserie chicken is one of my favorite emergency dinners. When crunched for time, Iâll grab one on my way home and transform the bird into something unrecognizable. Most recently, I used it to make Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkserâs Nuoc Cham Chicken Salad. The pulled meat is tossed with the quickest mayo-lime dressing, then stuffed into lettuce leaves. I like to finish the cups with sliced cucumber, fried shallots, and a flurry of fresh herbs. Donât bother bringing out plates. I eat this with my hands straight from the platter like nachos. âCarly Westerfield, manager, audience strategy Whenever I want something more for breakfast, but I donât want to work for it, itâs a Dutch baby all the way. Heat a skillet with butter, dump a couple of always-on-hand ingredientsâeggs, flour, milk, sugarâinto a blender, and 20 minutes later, it isnât breakfast: Itâs brunch. Last weekend I tossed the reserved browned butter from Epiâs Take It Easy Dutch Baby into a bowl of sliced Italian plums. I added a glug of maple syrup and a pinch of salt, then let the fruit soak in the flavors while I fiddled over my coffee. Puffed bÃ©bÃ© out of the oven, the plums and all their juices went on top, and I sat down to enjoy my morning. âJoe Sevier, senior editor, cooking and SEO I make lentil soup pretty frequently once the âfeels likeâ temperature dips below 50 degrees. And I was just about to mince up my mirepoix when I stumbled upon senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovicâs Soy-Braised Black Lentils. The promise of salty, tender-but-toothsome legumes on a bed of rice was good enough to shake up my routine. I hauled out my rice cooker, set it to steam, and started a dead-simple simmer of a pack of shiny black Beluga lentils with glugs of soy sauce and thin slices of garlic. Once the liquid was mostly gone, I stirred in glossy agave nectar plus added sugar until they formed a loose, syrupy glaze. We ate half the pot tucked into sheets of toasted seaweed snack along with generous spoonfuls of rice. The next morning, the rest was eaten with crusty bread and fried eggs. âKelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor Ever since I started working at BA, Iâve seen this single recipe for Bolognese top the charts time and time again. An oldie but a baddie, itâs received over 500 comments that would taunt me on a daily basis, with one overall glaring thesis: Make this! Now! So I decided to hunker down, put on a killer album (Once in a Lifetime), and get comfortable in the kitchen. Yes, this Bolognese takes timeâcough cough, three hoursâbut so do all good things. For those who need immediate gratification, your kitchen will be awash in the savory, primal smells of browned beef and pancetta in just 10 minutes.
