After adding a good amount of liquid from wine, stock, and milk (in stages), then stirring, dancing, and stirring, it was finally time to serve my meaty sauce tangled with fat pappardelle and a charitable shower of Parmesan. âNina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking When I saw a bunch of bright-eyed leeks at the farmers market from my favorite vendor, I knew just what to do with them: my colleague Rebecca Firkserâs cheesy baked pasta. It was one of those love-at-first-sight recipes for me in the Test Kitchenâsomehow minimalist and dramatic at the same time. Save this one for a chilly night when youâre having friends over. The sauce uses a cup of white wine, so thereâs most of a bottle left to enjoy with dinner. âEmma Laperruque, cooking director Iâve been making a lot of solo dinners lately, and nine times out of ten that means Iâm cooking an omelet. My version with fried shallot, apple, and Fontina cheese is a go-toâI wrote all about it for our series, Me, Myself, and Dinnerâbut if I havenât gone grocery shopping, Iâll just cobble together fun stuff from my fridge. Some recent wins: chopped kimchi and yellow cheddar; spinach, feta, and dill; black beans, avocado, and salsa macha. âRebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor This week I did something I havenât done in years. I roasted a chicken. And it was revelatory. Not fussy. Easy! Rewarding. Inspired by the method in Kitty Cowlesâs cookbook, I sprinkled the bird with salt and let it hang out in the fridge for a few hours. Then I rubbed it with olive oil, threw some lemon and garlic in the cavity, and roasted it as high as my oven would go, convection on. While the chicken was resting, its skin a golden crackle, I deglazed the pan juices with white wine, and let those simmer into a tangy gravy. Served with a salad, it was the coziest supper, even romantic if you ignore my toddler cooing. The next day, the carcass simmered in a pot of water with onion and ginger for a broth Iâll sip for days. The surplus meat has morphed into a rice bowl, towering sandwich, day care lunch box, 3 p.m. snack. And the joy from it all? Incalculable. âE.L. Iâm always on the hunt for a protein-rich, not-too-finicky dinner that I can pull together in a blip. Itâs gotta taste good because Iâll probably cook it for five consecutive days, at which point I will tire of it and resume my hunt anew. Like sands through the hourglass, these are the recipes of our lives. This week I settled on customizable Soy-Glazed Salmon Bowls. Cook the salmon in that salty-sweet soy and honey sauce, throw it atop rice, and add whatever vegetables you have. This time, I went with shreddy carrots and cukes, plus some of those crispy sheets of nori that I used to scoop up bite after bite. âSam Stone, senior editor My very talented colleague Shilpa Uskokovic forever changed the way I cook ground chicken. She mixes the chicken with baking sodaâyes, baking sodaâfor clusters of bouncy nubbins. Now, anytime a recipe calls for ground meat, I use this hack. This weekâs victim: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps. It has a sweet, fiery sauce made from sriracha, brown sugar, soy, and fish sauce that deliberately clings to the juicy meat. I piled the chicken into butter lettuce with a squeeze of lime, and a handful of torn mint for freshness. âNina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

item.title: ‘We hang on to summer a little longer here’: five of the best places for autumn sun in Europe and Turkey
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
A Kalkan sunset is always a beautiful thing â the horseshoe-shaped bay deepening to azure blue against an apricot-rose sky â but, in October, when the light is low and the sun drops early, itâs almost transcendentally lovely. In some Turkish resorts, youâd be sitting watching it surrounded by quiet streets, half-empty bars and that melancholic sense that another season is over. In Kalkan, it still feels like summer; the harbourfront restaurants throng with visitors, the day gulets (wooden boats) still putter in and out of the bay and you donât have to wait an hour to get a taxi back to your villa. For me, the best thing about an autumn break â besides the sunsets â is that I can visit some of my favourite places that just get overrun in summer. The glittering beach at Kaputas, sandwiched into a triangular gap on the mountainous Kalkan-Kas road, has become a victim of Instagram; from May to September, itâs impossible to get near. In October, the waters are still warm and the beach â although still busy â has plenty of space for a dip and a laze. About 20 minutesâ drive inland, the mountain village of Bezirgan, which used to serve as a summer retreat for wealthier Kalkan residents, settles back into complete peace in autumn, save for the woodpeckers battering away at the bark of the almond trees and the squirrels skittering through the leaves. The Lycian Way weaves through the village, past Ottoman-era grain stores, with the lush gardens of the Pirha KÃ¶y SofrasÄ± restaurant a great bet for a plate of traditional manti (dumplings in yoghurt) or kofte (meatballs), before setting off for a hike (they do fantastic breakfasts too). Back in Kalkan, itâs always cocktail hour somewhere; often on a roof terrace, with a jazz soundtrack floating out above the streets of the Old Town. This year, the Fountain Terrace Cocktail Bar has been popular, but I still love sitting in the Merkez Cafe, a Kalkan institution since the early 1990s, smack-bang in the heart of the village and a prime spot for people-watching when the evening begins. And because the seasonâs end is in sight, all the restaurant owners and waiters are cheerfully giddy, and the whole place swings with an end-of-term vibe. Sitting at the Blue Marlin (tucked away beneath the Pirat hotel) with a cold Efes beer and a selection of the townâs best meze, the only thing that makes me rueful is that it will be several months before Iâll be back here again.
Along Spainâs wild Costa de AlmerÃa are a handful of exquisite little towns and villages. San JosÃ© is probably the best known, put on the map by its most famous inhabitant, the late Joe Strummer, but 25 miles east is the real jewel of the AlmerÃa coast. Agua Amarga is a typical AndalucÃan fishing village moonlighting as a stylish low-key holiday destination, perfect for late-season sun-seekers. Its location, on a crescent bay, makes for spectacular sunrises and sunsets over the arid headlands that bookend the 500-metre-long beach. In the narrow, whitewashed streets, a lush palm grove and splashes of pink bougainvillaea remind you that north Africa is just a short hop across the Mediterranean. In the summer, Agua Amargaâs unspoilt sands and turquoise waters attract plenty of visitors, but the vibe remains relaxed. There are a handful of restaurants and bars around the main plaza, and a few eateries on the beach, including Los Tarahis, a traditional chiringuito (beach bar) where you can enjoy dishes such as arroz negro con bogavante (black rice with lobster) with your toes in the sand. In winter, the town goes into hibernation, but in autumn the sun and sea are still warm and the bars and restaurants are still open for business. Agua Amarga is not the place to go to party. Itâs a world away from the overdeveloped costas to the west and north, but it is the perfect base to immerse yourself in nature. Hiking trails lead from the village over the cliffs to a string of isolated coves and the ruins of 18th-century forts dotted along the headlands. And if you tire of following the shimmering sea, you can strike out inland to explore the Cabo de Gata nature reserve, with its winding ramblas (dry riverbeds), prickly pears and eerie abandoned goldmines. This corner of Spain is famous for its movie locations, notably Sergio Leoneâs spaghetti westerns and Hollywood blockbusters including Lawrence of Arabia and Conan the Barbarian. For UK cinephiles, British gangster classic Sexy Beast was filmed in Agua Amarga, and Ray Winstoneâs swanky villa is available as a holiday rental (minus the boulder in the swimming pool). The name Agua Amarga translates as âbitter waterâ, dating back to the 19th century and the contamination caused by mining iron ore. Those days are gone, and now Agua Amarga couldnât be sweeter.
As many of Portugalâs southern resorts prepare to hibernate for winter, Cascaisâs green-fingered municipal workers set to work on the townâs well-manicured flower beds, ensuring a seamless seasonal rotation. Violas, primroses and cyclamen furnish pops of purple, magenta and orange below tall palms lining a promenade punctuated with palatial homes and pockets of golden sand. Even in late autumn, the semi-tropical scene banishes the blues. My happy place when the off-season rolls around, Cascais has enough energy and atmosphere to entertain, and is arguably at its finest after summerâs beach throngs and Lisbon day trippers (Cascais lies 20 miles west of the city, a 30- to 40-minute train ride from Cais do SodrÃ© station) have receded. Once the summer retreat of Europeâs nobility, Cascais is now Portugalâs year-round crowd-pleaser â and come autumn, accommodation prices are far less aristocratic. There are stately manors and spa hotels aplenty, but my pick is Casa Vela, a surprisingly spacious sidestreet bolthole. Its sauna, shrouded in tropical gardens imported by the owner and his grandfather, brings joy even on the chilliest days. And if rains do come, there are a clutch of cultural attractions in the town, including the pyramid-shaped, terracotta-hued Casa das HistÃ³rias Paula Rego, featuring works by the acclaimed Portuguese-British artist. Still, with about 300 sunny days a year, Cascaisâs main off-season pull is for those who like to be active outdoors. Blue-sky mornings see waterfront joggers pass pretty squares carpeted in black-and-white calÃ§ada portuguesa (the distinctive patterned pavement mosaics), the hulking 15th-century citadel, and a mustard-hued palace overlooking a cove. Swimming is bracing, but kayaking on the calmer waters where the Tagus River meets the Atlantic more than compensates. Better still, hire a bicycle and trace the craggy coastline, which grows wilder as it arches north-west, with sheer cliffs appearing in the distant haze. Praia do Guincho is the star, a glorious dune-backed beach battered by winds that keep surfers of all stripes well sated. A half-hour bus ride from Cascais, Sintraâs iconic palaces and quintas unfurl across the forest-clad mountains. Summer in the town will test your patience. But with fewer crowds in the off-season, the essence of this former elite enclave and trove of European Romantic architecture returns. Hiking the hewn stairs to the Moorish Castle in thick fog is magical, while the vibrant burgundy-and-yellow facade of the fairytale National Palace of Pena brightens the greyest of days. As the nights start to draw in, you can chase the dwindling sunlight by heading to windswept Cabo da Roca at Portugalâs far western tip. Not only are the sunsets here spectacular, for much of autumn and winter they are the latest in mainland Europe â a sweetener for the shorter days.
Casa Vela has doubles from â¬79 room-only
Velvet Beach (Spiaggia di Velluto) is the alluring name for the miles of fine sand that fringe the town of Senigallia, in Italyâs Marche region. But from May to September, that golden loveliness all but disappears under the umbrellas and sunbeds of beach clubs. Italians love the place, some returning every summer for decades, but in high season it is probably best left to them. However, Senigallia has an allure beyond the beach that can be enjoyed year-round â and autumn is particularly rewarding. Itâs known in Italy as the âfive-star townâ for the number of Michelin stars its top two restaurants hold between them. At Uliassi (three stars) and Madonnina del Pescatore (two), ambitious locally born chefs have kept one another on their toes for decades, and their fame has encouraged other restaurateurs to up their game. If Uliassiâs famous â¬280 tasting menu is beyond your budget, Senigallia has plenty of innovative, quality places that are more affordable. Itâs hard to eat badly here, but fish fans will relish the exquisitely prepared raw stuff at Cuoco di Bordo (two courses from â¬34) on the seafront. The more rustic Rimante (two courses from â¬27), in the cobbled centre, offers super-friendly service, great pasta and a roast goose speciality. For pizza nights, nearby Oâsarracin has superlative margheritas (â¬8.50) and tasty ragÃ¹-filled arancini to start. Pizza al formaggio, by contrast, isnât pizza at all, but a sort of savoury panettone, flavoured with parmesan and pecorino cheese, maybe with chunks oozing out of a warm slice. Itâs usually an Easter treat, but bakery PandefrÃ makes it from October until May. Autumn in Senigallia also brings amazing fresh produce (chestnuts, persimmons, grapes and pomegranates; pumpkins, greens and radicchio) to chefs and market stalls. And, of course, it brings the olive harvest, with new oil to taste in local delis and at the Festa dellâOlio Nuovo (6-10 November) in Scapezzano, three miles inland, reached by a pleasant hourâs walk up the quiet Strada di Fontenuovo (thereâs a bus back). With so much eating, you do need to work up an appetite. Hiking the Heron Trail along the Misa River will help, and offers downy oaks in their autumn finery, but the best walk for me starts at the splendid Rotonda a Mare gallery on its 1930s pier, heads inland on quiet lanes to Gabriella and Montignano villages, then descends to the coast for a sunset stroll back along that â now peaceful â Velvet Beach.
Al Foro Annonario has doubles from â¬80 B&B
Tucked away in the corner of France just before the Basque coast runs into Spain, Saint-Jean-de-Luz hangs on to the warmth of summer a little longer than the rest of the west coast. Its enticing crescent beach is sheltered by two headlands and so, as the Atlantic crashes against the rest of the coast, you can dig your toes into the golden sand as the sea gently laps the shore and truly feel as if youâve escaped the world. The town makes for a great introduction to the French Basque Country, with its traditional red or green timber-framed architecture, adorned in many cases with strings of the local espelette chilli pepper â its gentle heat infuses many of the local dishes. Pick up a pot at the local market hall, which is a good place to find other hero products of the local cuisine, such as Ossau-Iraty cheese and black cherry jam. Elsewhere, the patisserie Maison Adam is the place to find the local almond macaron called the pare gabea (it means incomparable in Basque), which was first made in 1660 to celebrate the marriage of King Louis XIV and Marie-ThÃ©rÃ¨se of Spain. Their nuptials took place just round the corner at the Saint-Jean-de-Baptiste church â half-built at the time â which has an extraordinarily detailed gilt altarpiece that was installed in 1669, as well as a three-tiered gallery for the congregation. Meanwhile, a votive ship hanging from the ceiling is a nod to the townâs close relationship to the sea, with small fishing boats departing the neat harbour to fish for hake, a local speciality. You can venture out on to the seas too, with a boat trip on the small cruiser Nivelle V (â¬20), which goes along the coast towards Spain, first passing the 17th-century cylindrical fort at Socoa and its sea wall that juts across the bay. As you cruise past the Flysch cliffs, which look like layers of diagonally stacked cardboard, you might spot a few silver flying fish jumping out of the steely blue Atlantic. On arrival back at port, take the short walk across the bridge that spans the River Nivelle to the neighbouring village of Ciboure. Itâs a warren of red and green Basque townhouses that overlook narrow streets winding up the hill. Between them sits the restaurant Chez Mattin (mains from â¬28), a local institution, where chef Michel Niquet serves his signature dish, ttorro, a fish stew that was invented by his grandfather.
The Madison has doubles from â¬125. For more information, see saint-jean-de-luz.com
All accommodation prices are for October/November and were correct at the time of publication

item.title: The 10 best things to do in London this weekend
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
When searching for the best things to do in London this weekend, it’s hard not to end up more confused and indecisive than when you started. While it’s never a bad idea to secure a booking at one of the best restaurants in the capital, spend an evening in one of the latest innovative bars on the scene or even explore an iconic London attraction, we’re always on the lookout for new, exciting pop-ups, openings and events. Each week, we get the inside track on exciting things to do in London for the upcoming weekend to help us discover a new area of the city or explore a new address in a neighbourhood we thought we’d already uncovered. Things to do in London this weekend (16 - 18 October) Pulitzer Prize-winning opera Angel's Bone arrives at the London Coliseum following its UK premiere at Manchester’s Aviva Studio in spring. The run is part of the English National Opera's dual-centre model, bringing opera to audiences in both Greater Manchester and London – with productions shaped by the venues in which they’re performed. Angel’s Bone tells the story of Mr and Mrs X.E., a desperate couple longing for a better life who discover two wounded angels in their garden. However, what begins as an act of compassion takes a darker turn, highlighting human greed and socially relevant issues. Address: London Coliseum, St Martin's Lane, London WC2N 4ES Argentine bakery Madre is the latest business to take residency in King’s Cross – and the treats are well worth making time for. The coffee shop at Fabrica X is part of The Mills Fabrica, a platform that supports innovation across techstyle and agrifood, with a focus on sustainability and social impact. Think small-batch, indulgent bites that pair fabulously well with their usual coffee offering. Address: The Mills Fabrica, 36-40 York Way, London N1 9AB A handful of new drinking dens have opened across the capital recently, just in time for cosy autumn evenings spent nursing a pint (or stronger concoction, should you so choose). The Last Exchange is the city’s newest pub, having opened its doors in Exchange Square, a stone’s throw from Liverpool Street Station. The team is determined to ‘pub properly’, with all the tipples you can imagine and a menu of elevated classics. Sip on a pint of The City Scribbler, the pub’s own house beer, and feel the stresses of city life fizzle away. Elsewhere, Bar Buah has started welcoming thirsty foodies at The White Horse, Peckham. Ex-Oranj chef Elies Salvà Ruiz de Villegas is in charge, so expect dishes such as crab caldereta and oxtail croquetas to go down very well with a glass of wine. Address: The Last Exchange, 11 Exchange Square, Broadgate, London EC2A 2BR; Bar Buah at The White Horse Peckham Website: publicanestate.com; whitehorsepeckham.co.uk 4. Have a laugh at the Leicester Square Theatre Enjoy an evening of laughs as man of many talents – comedian, writer, director and novelist among them – Andy Hamilton takes to the stage at the Leicester Square Theatre this Sunday. Cackle away as he explores the wonders and the weaknesses of human memory, touching on the nights he’ll never forget along the way. Address: Leicester Square Theatre, 6 Leicester Place, London WC2H 7BX BREW//LDN goes Bavarian for its first-ever Oktoberfest celebration this weekend, uniting 18 breweries in the same space for two days of beer-sloshing. More than 35 beers are available on tap at the site, found at Riverside East in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, plus a live oompah band, DJs and street food stalls. Address: Riverside East, Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, 5 Thornton St, London E20 2AD 6. Pick up affordable pieces in Battersea Aesthetes and art lovers come together under one roof as the Affordable Art Fair Battersea returns for its autumn edition this week. The fair offers an accessible introduction to collecting with thousands of works priced under £10,000 across multiple spaces – with more than 100 galleries participating. Address: Battersea Evolution, Battersea Park, Queenstown Road, London SW11 4NJ Celebrate six years of Michelin-starred Kol, recognised as one of the best restaurants in the world, as the team throw a one-night-only celebration this Sunday. Chef and founder Santiago Lastra is transforming the restaurant into a dynamic culinary festival as four of the city’s most celebrated chefs, including Margo Henderson and Jeremy Lee, interpret iconic Mexican dishes in their own way. Tickets cost £135 per person and include a glass of biodynamic wine Gut Oggau, five dishes, and a cocktail. Address: KOL, 9 Seymour Street, London W1H 7BA 8. Experience the art of French patisserie Claridge’s Art Café has been one of London’s sleekest addresses for a sweet treat since it opened its doors. However, following a rebranding that sees Thibault Hauchard front and centre of the operation, there’s never been a better time to check out the selection on offer. Think artisan coffees, boiled eggs with truffle cheese soldiers and avo toast in the morning, before heartier lunch dishes and an array of spectacular patisserie options until close. Address: Art Café By Thibault Hauchard, Brook's Mews, London W1K 4HR 9. Find hidden treasure at a vintage market As if its array of viral street food stalls, thrift shops and various secret hideouts weren’t reason enough to visit, Camden Market welcomes a new open-air market on Saturdays this autumn in collaboration with Bootyfull Car Boot. Expect curated stalls filled with vintage fashion, retro accessories, rare vinyl records, original art and jewellery – or sell your own wares by securing a stall for £40. Address: Market Place, Hawley Wharf, NW1 10. Get soulful at Soho’s latest live music series Where better to spend an autumn evening than up high in one of the city’s glitziest rooftop bars? On select midweek nights throughout the rest of October, Flute at Broadwick Soho presents a series of live music events in collaboration with Johnnie Walker. Savour a range of limited-edition cocktails as performers including Madeleine (13 October) and Kianja (21 October) bring the soul above the colourful chaos of Soho. Address: Flute Bar, 7th floor, 20 Broadwick Street, London W1F 8TH

item.title: Old-school glamour, new-school luxury: Inside the reborn Delano Miami Beach
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Old-school glamour, new-school luxury: Inside the reborn Delano Miami Beach Dating back to 1947, Delano is a hotel synonymous with Miami glamour, South Florida celebrity culture and striking art deco architecture. A playground for the rich and famous throughout its years, the original hotel hosted presidents and dignitaries before being reborn in the 1990s under the groundbreaking guidance of Ian Schrager and Philippe Starck. At one point, Delano was home to a restaurant co-owned by Madonna and a nightclub from Lenny Kravitz. But when the COVID-19 pandemic crippled the hospitality industry in 2020, the famed Delano closed its doors. Now, the hotel is back, this time simply dubbed Delano Miami Beach, and it's as gorgeous and glamorous as ever after reopening this summer. Touted to "[honor] the legacy of its predecessor while redefining it for a new era," it was clear from the get-go that the newest iteration of the legendary hotel had big shoes to fill. So I went down to South Florida to check in and check it out myself. Here's what it was like staying at Delano Miami Beach. The vibe: Chic, airy and flat-out cool. The new Delano Miami Beach is both a living gallery and place to see and be seen. The location: Situated on the iconic Collins Avenue in Miami Beach, the hotel is located in the heart of all the action. Getting there: Delano Miami Beach is about 12 miles from Miami International Airport. Expect to pay between $25-45 for a cab or rideshare. Parking: Overnight valet parking costs $65 per night. Size: The hotel has 171 rooms and suites, multiple pools, beach access, a fitness center and a soon-to-open spa. Food and drink: There are two popular restaurants, plus a buzzy lobby-adjacent bar, pool and beach service, and a cafe. Pet policy: Dogs and cats up to 50 pounds are allowed to stay at Delano Miami Beach for a fee of $250. Delano Miami Beach offers rooms, suites and two-story bungalows with direct access to the pool. During my stay, I was placed in a partial ocean-view king suite that had a living room area, a hallway with closet space and beautiful bathroom and a large bedroom. The very chic living room had a massive TV (with streaming capabilities); a well-stocked minibar with snacks, top-shelf liquors and Noam Beer (a German beer in a truly gorgeous bottle); and a coffee maker. There was also a lounge-style couch, an armchair and a small table with two chairs. From one small sliver of the window in the living room, I could see the ocean, but the view put the emphasis on "partial" in my partial ocean view. If you're serious about having direct views of the water, be sure to book an ocean-view room. The hallway served as both a corridor between rooms and a closet, thanks to a curtained-off area with plush robes, hangers, a luggage rack and other areas to organize clothes, luggage and everything else you might be carrying. For a suite, the bathroom was compact, but the design was beautiful. Illuminated, abstract mirrors blended with a bold white dual vanity and a large soaking tub. The bathroom was stocked with Byredo Gypsy Water products and soft towels — and the shower's water pressure was great. The head-to-toe white and beige bedroom felt like sleeping in a cloud. In the headboard, a built-in switch controlled the lights and blinds, though I enjoyed the views of Collins Avenue's iconic art deco building when the blinds were up. The room also had a large TV (once again, with streaming capabilities), reading lights built into the headboard and an armchair with a small table. I really enjoyed the suite, especially the sleek design of the lamps and furniture. It was a great home-away-from-home for my two-night stay. Delano Miami Beach's food and drink scene was buzzing before it opened, thanks to the first U.S. outposts of famed restaurants Gigi Rigolatto and Mimi Kakushi. To put it bluntly: Gigi Rigolatto Miami is a scene in the best possible way. For my Friday night dinner, the restaurant was bustling and full of life. The famed Paris restaurant serving Italian dishes was also full of delicious flavors. For my meal, I started with fiori di zucchine, or fried zucchini flowers with ricotta and truffle ($38), which were lightly and beautifully fried, and could have served as meal itself. But, as multiple people told me, I couldn't go to Gigi without trying the spaghetti limone e caviale, spaghetti with a lemon sauce and 30 grams of Oscietra caviar ($135). The pasta was rich, citrusy-sweet and balanced well with the salty caviar. The dish was plentiful enough for a small group of people, but let's just say I was feeling selfish that night (and luckily, I was dining alone). In Dubai, Mimi Kakushi has been a trendy staple of the restaurant scene since 2021. Now open in Miami, the restaurant serves a menu of Japanese dishes from fresh nigiri to gyoza, Wagyu steaks, miso black cod and everything in between. I could eat Japanese food for every meal, so I tried a nice sampling of my favorites: an earthy, bold miso soup with truffle ($12), perfectly crafted pieces of freshwater eel nigiri and tuna nigiri ($17 for two pieces, each) and black cod and tiger prawns gyoza with citrus miso ($28). The well-crafted, umami-packed miso set the bar high for the rest of the meal, and the nigiri was as light and fresh as I've had. In fact, I was tempted to order more nigiri, but after packing in all of the delicious gyoza, I decided to call it and appreciate the great meal I had. But not without dessert! To end the meal, I tucked away a piece of Hokkaido cheesecake with strawberries and an earthy matcha sauce ($18). The subtle sweetness of the cheesecake was the perfect base for the rich matcha, and after I said I was done, I went back in for "just one more bite" multiple times. As I told people I was heading to Mimi Kakushi, everyone I talked to insisted I order "the world's coldest martini." Well, I love martinis, so it was an obvious must. Dubbed the Nara Nara ($38), the martini consists of Botanist Gin being chiseled from a giant block of ice (kept at a freezing –4°F) tableside, making for a show as cool as the drink itself. Adjacent to the lobby, Rose Bar is open nightly for drinks. The menu has an interesting cocktail menu with options like the Rose old fashioned with Macallan 12, banana, salted caramel and chocolate ($35) and the chamomile penicillin made with Johnnie Walker Black Label, chamomile, ginger, carrot, honey and Campari ($23). Delano Miami Beach also has an Italian-style coffee shop with classic coffee drinks, upscale pours like an iced pistachio milk shakerato ($15), juices, pastries, breakfast items and fruit bowls. Various food menus from the different restaurants are also available for order at the pool and beach. Service throughout the hotel was near exceptional, and it seemed like most of the people working at Delano Miami Beach were truly happy to be there — and happy to assist. Especially at Rose Bar, the outdoor bar at Gigi and the pool. The only mishap I experienced was a manager berating a bartender about one foot in front of me, while I was the only person at the bar trying to listen to the live music. Luckily, the pool staff over the course of my stay made up for it, and I can't thank Malou, Tania and Arian for their incredible hospitality. Here's what else is on offer: - A pool with lounge chairs and cabanas (available for a fee) - Direct beach access with lounge chairs and food-for-order from Gigi - The Source By Delano spa (scheduled to open later in the year) - The Nothing Finer shop offers a curated selection of lifestyle products, clothes and more for purchase Cash rates at Delano Miami Beach start around $600 per night. As an Accor property, members of its loyalty program can trade in multiples of 2,000 points for 40 euros (about $44) off a stay. Delano Miami Beach also participates in The Edit by Chase Travel, allowing eligible cardholders to receive elite-like benefits like daily breakfast for two, property credits and more. Delano Miami Beach has all the expected accessibility features travelers should anticipate in the United States, including dedicated accessible rooms and public spaces, and a pool with a lift. As always, TPG recommends calling the hotel before booking to ensure they can meet your needs. Miami Beach has no shortage of incredible luxury hotels, but few are as storied as Delano. All in all, I thoroughly enjoyed my two-night stay, and my only regret is that I couldn't stay longer. From mouthwatering nigiri at Mimi to salty caviar at Gigi, and the best pool attendants I've ever encountered, the all-new Delano Miami Beach really brought back to life a true Miami legend. item.title: The Volpi FastPack 30 Might Just Convince Me to Ditch My Hipbelt
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Hipbeltless packs are normally not part of how I hike. As a Backpacker editor, I’m blessed with a pretty deep gear closet, and I use most of the packs in there regularly: Burly conventional packs for gear-intensive winter and family trips, frameless ones for personal outings where I can pack as light as I want, and lightweight backpacks with a frame for anything in between. But like leaving my shelter at home or using my spork to dig a cathole, ditching the hipbelt always seemed like one of those cuts that took things a step too far. After taking Volpi’s FastPack 30 on the trail, though, I’m reconsidering my stance. This lightweight pack—a pound flat for the Ultra version—sat comfortably on my shoulders thanks to its vest-style carry and had enough organization that I was always able to find what I needed without fumbling. Hipbeltless packs still have their downsides, and we’re looking forward to testing the FastPack 30 more. In the meantime, here are my thoughts after my first trip with it; stay tuned for our full review. I like to go light, but I’m not the kind of person who will cut weight at any cost. There are certain things I’m not usually willing to give up when I go backpacking, and one of them is a hipbelt. I’ve used frameless packs in the past and liked them, but I haven’t used many packs without a hipbelt that I’ve really been willing to take out on my own time. But right now, I’m on the Ice Age Trail in Wisconsin, and I am trying out a pack that I think, for one of the first times, I would use on a personal trip, and that is the Volpi FastPack. Volpi is a company from Mexico. It was made by a couple of thru-hikers who wanted to make the kind of gear that they’d like to use. And the FastPack is a really good example of that. It’s a fairly compact, frameless pack. It’s got a vest-style carry, but no hipbelt. And I found it really comfortable to use so far, surprisingly comfortable for a pack with no hipbelt. Because it has a vest-style carry, it has pretty good storage on the shoulder straps. I’ve got a water bottle, a soft flask, in each pocket. It has a generous stuff pocket in the back where I’ve put some of the stuff I expect to need today, I’ve stuck my extra layers. And it has some side pockets good for carrying whatever. It sits fairly high on your back because it is on your shoulders rather than sitting on your hips. There are obviously a couple of tradeoffs. With no hipbelt, it gets a little harder to carry weight, since it’s all on your shoulders. These wide straps distribute it well, but there’s a limit to how much they can do. There’s the capacity issue—this would not be a great pack for long carries. We’re out for three days, so I haven’t had to bring too much. And we also, critically, have pretty abundant water. I probably wouldn’t bring this pack to the desert or anywhere where I expected to have to carry a lot. I’ve carried two gallons of water at a time in a frameless pack, and that’s pretty rough even with a hipbelt. I wouldn’t necessarily want to do it with this one. But for trips where you’re prioritizing moving fast and don’t have to carry a lot, this is a pretty comfortable option. One downside of using this pack is it does have a roll-top closure. It can be really inconvenient to get stuff in and out, so it’s best if your strategy is generally to pack your pack in the morning and not really open it the rest of the day. I’m hiking with a hip pack, where I’ve got my lunch and most of the stuff I expect to need. The stuff pocket in the back is where I’ve kept my rain jacket, my grid fleece, stuff I may need, but I’m probably not going to need constantly or quickly. Obviously, as a frameless pack, you’re going to want to be really careful in how you pack this. I took the time to arrange my stuff pretty carefully to avoid barreling, and used my sleep system to eat up the extra space, so it’s sitting pretty comfortably on me right now. There are some good attachment points on the pack for keeping some gear that you may not want to put inside the pack. You can see I’ve got my sleeping pad sitting on the top. There’s a really easy buckle and strap closure to put it there. And I’m not using it right now, but there are also nice attachment points for trekking poles, if you don’t want to use your trekking poles for a while. All in all, this is a really nice pack with good organization, and it sits more comfortably than you would think.

item.title: Why You Should Always Read the Label on Your Cleaning Spray
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Until I started reviewing kitchen gear five years ago, I rarely read product manuals or user guides. Iâm sure thatâs due in large part to my ADHD, as my brain tends to move more quickly than step-by-step instructions allow. Plus, I like to figure things out on my own, thank you very much! But my rogue, DIY, quick-start method hasnât always worked out in my favor. I inadvertently killed my first Dyson stick vacuum (that I saved for months to buy) because I failed to educate myself on proper filter maintenance. And Iâve owned my car for a decade and still have no clue what a couple of the buttons actually do. While user error can make for a funny punchline, it can also get expensive. For example, it might seem silly to read the manual for a nonstick frying pan or enameled cast-iron Dutch oven, but thatâs where youâd learn that putting it in the dishwasher or using metal utensils can destroy or degrade the cooking surface. In the case of cleaning products, the stakes can be even higherâespecially in this era of, er, less restrictive food safety regulations. Cleaning spray versus disinfecting spray Before you get to the instructions on the back of a cleaning spray bottle, you need to pay close attention to whatâs on the front, because not all kitchen cleaning sprays (no, not even all all-purpose cleaning sprays) are created equally. Though they might have some very minimal, naturally occurring disinfecting properties from ingredients like vinegar or essential oils, basic cleaning sprays like Mrs. Meyerâs and Aunt Fannieâs have one jobâand that is to clean the surfaces in your kitchen. And by âclean,â I mean they contain surfactants, which help to dislodge grease and gunk so you can more easily wipe away a mess. But simply removing discernible debris wonât leave you with a germ-free countertop, which is why you also need a disinfectant to kill bacteria and viruses (not to be confused with a sanitizer, which only kills bacteria). And if you want to ensure your counters are so clean you could eat off of them, I recommend using both. If you spray a disinfecting solution on top of a spill, itâs not disinfecting the counter underneath the spillâitâs sanitizing the surface of whatever is stuck to your counter. What is dwell time? Hereâs the real kicker, and the reason itâs important to read the instructions on the back of your disinfecting (or sanitizing) spray: In order for the product to kill the number of germs the label claims, it needs to sit on the surface in question for anywhere from about two to 10 minutes. This period is called the âdwell timeâ or âcontact time,â and the product needs to remain visibly wet for however long it takes to be truly effective. For example, Lysol's All-Purpose Cleaner (which is truly all-purpose when used properly), is a sanitizer at 10 seconds, but it only "kills 99.9% of viruses and bacteria" as the front of the label claims, if itâs left to sit for 10 minutes. The little asterisks after that claim lead you to the back label, which details the dwell time along with the common bacteria and viruses it kills. âUse as directedâ shows up four times in the online product description for Cloroxâs Multi-Surface Disinfecting Mist, which also claims to kill 99.9% of viruses and bacteria. It even has a specific instruction for kitchens (to rinse off of any food-prep surfaces after a 10-minute dwell time). The moral of the story? Use your cleaning products as directed, which unfortunately does require reading the fine print on the label. While youâre at it, you might want to consider replacing your microfiber cleaning cloths after a 2010 study found that microfiber becomes less effective at removing contaminants from surfaces the more it gets used.

item.title: Canada's bizarre mummified toe cocktail
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
On my second night in Canada's northern Yukon Territory, a bartender at the Eldorado Hotel pulled out a pair of tongs, plucked a mummified toe from a silver tray, plunged it into a glass of alcohol and dropped it into my glass of Yukon Jack whisky with a plunk. "Whose toe is that?" I asked. "And which toe is it?" "Not really sure," he said, with a sly smile. "It's a gnarly one, though." The dehydrated, salt-preserved digit was black and shrivelled. In its heyday, it may have been a well-kept pinky. Or perhaps one of the less celebrated middle toes, finally getting their spotlight. Warning: This article contains images and descriptions that some may find upsetting. I was in Dawson City, a 2,300-person former gold mining hub located 330 miles (531km) from the nearest actual city, about to try the famous Sourtoe Cocktail. This two-ingredient drink (a shot of whisky and… a toe) has been a tradition here for more than 50 years. It just might be the world's most unusual libation. A laminated white flyer on the worn wooden table explained the "Sourtoe Rules", noting that my membership to the Sourtoe Cocktail Club would be voided if I chewed, sucked, bit or otherwise ingested the severed digit. It also exclaimed, in extra-large letters, that there was a $2,500 (£1,884) fine for swallowing it. I was happy to limit toe contact as much as humanly possible. Most patrons feel the same way. However, there have been accidental swallowings in the past, plus a notorious incident in 2013 where a man downed the toe on purpose and was reportedly run out of town for unsportsmanlike conduct. "Are you ready to join the club?" the bartender, who identified himself as the official "Toe Captain", asked me. It was too late to back out now. I nodded. He then recited the official "Sourtoe chant", adding to the romance of it all: "You can drink it fast, you can drink it slow, but your lips must touch this gnarly toe!" And with that, I dutifully took my shot of whisky through clenched teeth as someone's former toe kicked me in the mouth. Before Dawson City was famous for its toe-garnished cocktail, it was famous for its gold. When the mineral was discovered nearby in 1896, it became the epicentre of the international Klondike Gold Rush. Within two years, tens of thousands of people descended into the area in search of fortune. The town grew from a network of prospector tents to include saloons, hotels and restaurants – many of which still stand today. But when gold was struck elsewhere a few years later, the prospectors moved on and the town's population plummeted, leaving the few remaining hardy residents to eke out a living in Dawson City's harsh landscape, 60 miles (96km) from the Alaska border. : The Sourtoe's origins go back to US Prohibition (1920 – 1933), when two rumrunner brothers, Louie and Otto Linken, got stranded in a blizzard while smuggling booze across the border to Alaska via dogsled in the 1920s. Louie stepped into icy water and soon suffered frostbite. According to legend, they journeyed on, but when it became clear Louie needed an amputation, Otto took out an axe and hacked off his brother's toe in their remote cabin. The brothers kept the toe in a jar of alcohol for posterity. In the early 1970s, Dawson resident Dick Stevenson (locally known as Captain Dick) found the jar while cleaning out the brothers' abandoned cabin, and for unknown reasons, decided it would make for a great cocktail garnish. Thus, the Sourtoe Cocktail was born in 1973. As the story goes, Captain Dick thought it would be fun to let people become honorary "sourdoughs" (Gold Rush slang for locals) by drinking the Sourtoe. Initially, he dared some friends and saloon patrons to try it. Dawson City's isolated location and history of colourful, rough-and-tumble characters played into the legend of the Sourtoe nicely. Word soon spread, and before long, visitors started sidling up to the bar to taste the toe-flavoured tipple. Today, the Sourtoe has become something of a must-do for visitors who make the long journey to experience Dawson City's Gold Rush history and rugged frontier culture, and some 140,000 people have downed the daunting drink. All automatically become members of the Sourtoe Cocktail Club, and their names are proudly written in a hefty ledger book post-sip. Terry Lee has served as the main Toe Captain – the bartender tasked with serving the mummified toe to patrons and presiding over the ceremony – for 13 years. During the busy summer season, he works five days a week, making 75 to 100 Sourtoes a night during his four-hour shift. The Sourtoe is served between May and September at the Sourdough Saloon (in the Downtown Hotel), then the rest of the year at the Eldorado Hotel's Sluice Box Lounge. "It's considered somewhat of a rite of passage. A lot of the locals have done it," said Lee. Since Captain Dick (the original Toe Captain) passed away in 2019, several other people have been trained as Toe Captains, but Lee is the modern face of the toe. Lee first tried a Sourtoe in 1980 with Captain Dick and immediately fell in love with the history. A few months into his Toe Captain tenure, a customer accidentally swallowed Louie's original frostbitten toe, so Lee was one of the last people to drink with the original appendage. Over the years, the catalog of toes has grown from one to around 25, which are used in rotation today. The toes arrive in a variety of ways. Captain Stevens donated all 10 of his toes when he died in 2019. A British athlete who suffered frostbite in the Yukon Arctic Ultra marathon donated three of his digits in 2018. An untold number of people have willed their toes to the Downtown Hotel (including the tourist who swallowed one, in an effort to make amends). Sometimes, toes show up in the post unannounced. Like much of Dawson City, the Sourdough Saloon looks like it's straight out of the Gold Rush era, with its wooden tables, red wallpaper and swinging doors. The Sluice Box Lounge has a similar vibe, with velvet swivel barrel bar stools emblazoned with the hotel's name. The town still has no traffic lights or crosswalks. Many of the buildings have been standing since the 1890s. Colourful false-front facades dot the streets advertising businesses like the Diamond Tooth Gerties Gambling Hall, The Dawson City General Store and Bonanza Market. In summer months, there's nearly 24 hours of light. In winter, the Yukon River freezes over and part of it becomes an official government-maintained ice bridge. "Because the weather and the environment are so extreme here, it attracts people that are extreme in other ways. You get a lot a big characters," said Tara Kehoe, the exhibit curator at the Dawson City Museum. "Dawson is a weird intersection of people who love living in nature and are artistically inclined, so you get a lot of people with big, strange ideas because of that." This toe-garnished cocktail is the kind of offbeat creativity Dawson City is now known for. The town has also hosted annual events like the Great Klondike International Outhouse Race, a town-wide Easter egg fight on the frozen river and a spring carnival called Thaw Di Gras. "The Sourtoe has become a weird sort of bragging right. Everyone here loves it, even if they haven't tried it. If you have friends coming to town, you have to take them to at least watch other people drinking it," said Kehoe. She added: "The Sourtoe is so odd that it really sticks in your mind. Even when I've travelled overseas, when I tell people I'm from Dawson City there's always a person or two who says, 'Wait, isn't there a drink with a human toe?'". In a weird way, the cocktail has become a community bonding experience – and the toe's grip on tourists is only getting stronger. In June this year, The Sourdough Saloon set a new record, serving 156 toes in a single night, the crowds joining in on the iconic chant. You can drink it fast, you can drink it slow… Having now done it, I'd suggest drinking it fast.

item.title: This Bryce Canyon Hike Rivals the Grand Canyon’s Rim-to-Rim Trail—and No One’s on It
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Group of hikers trekking through Bryce Canyon National Park, Utah, with rugged red rock formations in view. (Photo: Alex Moliski) Bryce Canyon might be America’s most spectacular drive-through national park. Visitors pull into an overlook, admire a thousand orange hoodoos, snap a photo, and drive to the next viewpoint. It’s fast food for the eyes: beautiful, looks great on your feed, and over in minutes. But I wanted more than the Happy Meal. So I shouldered my pack at Bryce Point and headed down the Under-the-Rim Trail, leaving the overlooks and crowded dayhikes behind for an overnight adventure. What I found was another Bryce Canyon entirely, where the landscape becomes something you walk through rather than look down upon. I expected more of the same orange hoodoos that made Bryce famous. Instead, I wandered through pine forests, sandy hills, and open meadows. The towering formations hadn’t disappeared. They were just above me now, casting unfamiliar shadows across the landscape. Beneath the rim, Bryce felt less like a geological spectacle and more like a wilderness. Trailhead: Start: Bryce Point, End: Rainbow Point Distance: 23.60 miles (my GPS numbers) Elevation: 5,167 feet (my GPS numbers) Permits: Required for all overnight trips The first surprise came barely two miles in. The “Hat Shop” is a collection of odd hoodoos resembling people wearing oversized hats, with enormous boulders balanced on skinny pillars. Whoever named it deserves a raise. But don’t forget to turn around: You’ve already dropped almost a thousand feet below Bryce Point, and the view looking back is one most visitors will never see. That initial descent is deceiving. About four miles in, you’re at the bottom of the first big drop, but the trail is far from finished climbing. The remaining miles are full of what our backpacking group calls “PUDs,” or pointless ups and downs. Stunning, certainly, but brutal on the legs. Those PUDs led to an ongoing debate amongst our group: Which is harder, the Grand Canyon’s (currently closed) Rim-to-Rim or Bryce’s Under-the-Rim Trail? I’ve now hiked both, and the similarities are surprising. Both cover more than 20 miles, demand thousands of feet of elevation change, and reward you with spectacular Southwest scenery. Opinions are split, but I give the difficulty crown to Bryce. Those relentless ups and downs really add up, and so do the endless changing views. The Grand Canyon might be the undisputed king of desert backpacking, but I think Bryce deserves a place in the same conversation. With flooding, fire damage, and construction disrupting the Grand Canyon’s famous Rim-to-Rim route, this is another adventure worth considering just a few hours north. It’s not the Grand Canyon, and that’s exactly the point. My favorite stretch came between the Swamp Canyon and Whiteman Bench connecting trails. For roughly two miles, the trail passes through an old burn scar where the forest is slowly reclaiming the landscape. Normally, walking through burned trees feels somber. Here, fresh green growth fills the gaps, and the thinned forest opens up enormous views that the living trees once concealed. Swamp Canyon Butte and Mud Canyon Butte tower above you, with Bryce’s massive walls rising on your opposite side. Buttes look better from below, if you ask me. This is where you start feeling small—where the park’s big crowds become a distant memory, and the wilderness really creeps in. I thought about the Southern Paiute story of how the hoodoos were formed. “Legend People,” whom the trickster god Coyote turned to stone, were forever frozen in time. Looking up at those towering formations, it wasn’t hard to imagine those figures watching us pass. Bryce Canyon itself was named for Ebenezer Bryce, an early settler who reportedly described the rugged landscape as “a helluva place to lose a cow.” After navigating its maze of drainages and forests, I understood his frustration—though getting lost in the scenery was precisely why I’d come. Fortunately, getting an overnight permit is easier than finding Ebenezer’s missing livestock. When we arrived at the packed visitor center, the ranger perked up at the mention of backpacking, apparently excited to discuss something other than the Navajo Loop. They told us we were the only backpackers heading out that week. You can reserve permits on Recreation.gov up to three months ahead, with an in-person ranger check-in required before departure. Bear-resistant canisters are also required, and the park lends them out for free (yes, there are black bears in Bryce). The whole process is very easy, since the trail is still overshadowed by other “bucket list” hiking and backpacking routes in the area. Campsites are designated, and spacing makes planning important. Swamp Canyon and Natural Bridge are good options for breaking up the route, though neither guarantees equal mileage. You could make this a two-night trip and camp at both, but we were only permitted for a single night. At Swamp Canyon, we found flat tent pads and a designated cooking area. Water is the bigger headache. Unlike canyon hikes that follow a river, Under-the-Rim crosses long, usually dry washes that finger down from the tall wall. On our trip, the reliable stops were Yellow Creek early on and Iron Spring much closer to the finish. That meant carrying extra water across all those PUDs. Seasonal sources vary, so check with a ranger, treat everything you collect, and consider caching water at permitted trail junctions. Both Yellow Creek and Iron Spring dry up entirely by mid-summer. Timing is equally tricky. I hiked on April 27, hoping for green forests without the summer heat. I wish I’d waited another week for spring to wake up. Late spring and early fall offer appealing windows, but snow, freezing nights, and summer thunderstorms all deserve consideration. Bring layers, sun protection, and plenty of water. It was hot during the day and freezing at night. It made for the kinds of mornings where I really didn’t want to get out of my sleeping bag. Finally, remember that Under-the-Rim is a point-to-point hike from Bryce Point to Rainbow Point. The regular park shuttle doesn’t serve Rainbow Point, so arrange transportation ahead of time. We parked a car at both trailheads to make it easy. NPS offers other options for shuttling from Rainbow Point on its website. And here’s the funny part: Getting back means driving the same scenic road I’d spent the whole trip trying to escape. There I was, dusty and tired, sitting in national park traffic with everyone else, admiring those same orange hoodoos from the comfort of a car. Only now, I’d also seen them from below. On the trail, I was a backpacker. On the drive back, I was a tourist. And you know what? There’s nothing wrong with being both. Bryce is a damn beautiful place, no matter which angle you look at it from.

item.title: A Greece for all seasons: my autumn roadtrip through the Peloponnese
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
As I drove across the causeway which links the tiny fortress island of Monemvasia to the south-eastern coast of the Peloponnese, the Aegean sparkling on all sides, I recalled a line by Yiannis Ritsos, one of Greece’s greatest 20th-century poets. Ritsos lived in Monemvasia, in a house that is today a museum on a cobble-stretch by the tawny castle walls. A favourite passage goes: “The voyage is neither a leave-taking nor a home-coming – an ethereal bridge …” The excuse for my trip to the Peloponnese’s deep south – Messinia, the Mani, and Laconia – fell between those two ideas. My mother has roots in the Peloponnese – a sort-of homecoming that I’ve long wanted to explore – and with the summer over and greedy for an adventure to myself, I set out by car, leaving Kalamata, the leafy port city and gateway to the area, on a coastal road circuit. Autumn in the Peloponnese is another Greece. Forget the Cycladic white and blue; mountain valleys are carpeted in pine forests and wildflowers, a great stretch of green studded with rustic limestone houses. These villages, relieved by the end of a scorching summer, celebrate boisterous harvest festivals for wines, oranges and chestnuts in Laconia, figs in Messinia, and olives near Kalamata. This is the Greece the diaspora yearns for: the chorio – a word that snaps us back to our relatives and Greek rural life, villages where the air is healthy, eating depends on what is grown metres away, and tavernas are alive with locals rather than tourists. In the shoulder season, the weather is cool enough for long walks along the region’s spectacular trails but, at about 25C, is also still good for swimming. The two-hour drive to Monemvasia began with the Taygetus pass, winding through villages and cliffside tunnels as golden eagles soared above the firs. On the far side of the Taygetus, the road opened to Mystras, an archaeological Byzantine site stacked up its hillside. I climbed to the Paleologian Palace and its chapels, then descended, hungry, to the village of Parori, where Taverna Ores was serving syglino, the local cured pork, and an okra stew. I practised my flimsy Greek with the waitress and her mother, who kept one eye on a television gameshow while stirring the stew pots. After lunch I stopped at Sparta – site of the ancient city state and modern metropolis. Beneath the Taygetus, in the spectral hush of the olive groves, there is an acropolis, an agora and little else. Yet the air carries something over the ruins, and it’s a short but necessary stop. A statue of Leonidas, hero of Thermopylae, stands facing the new city with the ruins at his back. This is still the Greece of the Spartans: locals remain fiercely attached to their ancient ancestry. Monemvasia has a thrilling connection: in AD600, a bishop is said to have led the Spartan population to the rock to fortify themselves against invading tribes. Set on to a slope inside the castle walls is a town of tight passages and medieval Orthodox churches. It is a vivid encounter with Byzantine Greek architecture, as well as traces of Venetian trade: the sweet, fortified wine malvasia was once a prized export. Even my guesthouse, Kelia (rooms from €70), began as a monks’ residence on the sea-facing Chryssafitissa Square. Leaving Monemvasia, I took a detour south for the golden sand dune beaches in Elafonisos. Reaching this island requires taking a 10-minute ferry ride from Pounta. The turquoise waters of Simos beach are deserted in the off-season – a necessary respite before my hour drive north-west to spend a night in Gythio. This working harbour town has neoclassical pastel mansions and waterfront restaurants provisioned by local fishers. Here the Mani begins. “Victory or death” reads the Maniot banner, above the Spartan motto “With the shield, or on the shield”. The region has a reputation for a conservative way of life that might seem unfashionable in modern Greece, but I find it seductive. The Mani’s beauty comes partly from its insularity. Driving an hour to Vathia, rugged mountains are crowned by labyrinthine stone tower villages that Maniot clans built to protect themselves during periods of vendetta or skirmishes with the Ottomans. Some are now ghost towns. Others have been converted into guesthouses. But it was in Gerolimenas that a Greek friend suggested I stay for a few nights. The seaside village is an easy base for touring both western and eastern coasts. Along the latter, I hiked to mainland Greece’s southernmost point, Cape Tainaron lighthouse and went for an impromptu dip. The Mani’s water is so gin-clear the boats appear to hover above the surface. The Akroyiali hotel (doubles from €80 B&B) opened in the 1970s, before most of the region’s roads. It is built on Gerolimenas’s shore, so I dozed to the pulse of waves and chatter from the hotel’s taverna below, where owner Mr Theodorakakis and his family entertained guests. “The Mani is changing at its own rhythm,” Theodorakakis told me. “This is a special place. We can’t keep hiding from the world.” Most Greeks prefer to visit off-season, he said. “You can actually explore the region without burning. But be careful of the north-eastern wind. It cuts through!” Leaving Gerolimenas, I drove 30 minutes up the western coastal route, entering the busy town of Areopoli, where I shopped for hand-harvested sea salt and wild oregano. Pretty Limeni and Kardamyli – the home of British writer Patrick Leigh Fermor (who popularised the region) – get the Mani day-trip overspill from Kalamata. Regardless, it’s quieter in autumn. Every hairpin bend opens on to sea views, flowers and limestone. I was lunching over one such view of a grassy cape when the taverna owner mentioned a woman in the village who knew miralogia. These are wailing Maniot lamentations sung at funerals, which are heard rarely these days. After two days of asking around, I found Kaiti Braimi in a small chapel where she agreed to sing. “In a way, they’re less necessary,” the octogenarian told me. “No more vendettas.” The haunting rhythms of the miralogia were in mind as I left the Mani to enter Messinia – cutting through Kalamata again, but this time heading west. Here, the villagers were celebrating. Clarinets hummed in taverna gardens at Sunday family parties and relatives joined hands in circles to dance the kalamatianos. Passersby stood and clapped before being dragged in. On the hour drive from Kalamata to Pylos – which would be my base – the Maniot mountains flattened into lush forests. Wildflowers bloomed on the roadside. Yet in Messinia’s expansive green are traces of ancient civilisations, including the bronze age palace of Nestor, north of Pylos. My route sidetracked to the Polylimnio waterfalls. You can sidetrack easily in Messinia; there are unspoiled beaches (like Tsapi on the south coast, where mountains tumble into the sea), as well as areas for canyoning, cycling and kayaking. After a small hike, I bathed in clear pools surrounded by pines, alone mostly, apart from an Athenian couple. “We’re here for my birthday,” the man said. “Messinia is the best place in Greece for outdoor activities.” They pointed me to a canyoning trail north of the Bay of Navarino – a tip for my next visit. That evening in Pylos’s port, only an hour from where I began my voyage in Kalamata, I paused for an ouzo at a kafenion. A group of lads were watching Greece play Germany at football on the television. They wailed their own miralogia with every missed shot, but when the game ended in a win the cafes along the harbour roared. I thought back on my drive through the Peloponnese’s deep south, a journey that revealed a rural Greece I’d grown up romanticising from family, and believed was slowly disappearing. But not here. In the mountains and shores of Messinia, the Mani and Laconia, I found a Greece for all seasons.

item.title: This Cookbook Author Explores Cemeteries for Recipes To Die For
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
A recipe quite literally taken to the grave? Thatâs the foundation for creator Rosie Grantâs ongoing archival project turned cookbook To Die For. And itâs exactly how it sounds. Apropos for Spooky Season, the book collects âgravestone recipesâ so synonymous with departed loved ones theyâre immortalized on their headstones. It celebrates the legacies of ordinary folks who did extraordinary things. They were teachers or coaches, the local dentist, the neighbor everybody knew, and they all showed love through cooking for their communities. What began as a light curiosity turned into a larger, more emotional realization around identity, place, and what we leave behind. Over the past five and a half years since starting her TikTok and Instagram accounts under the username ghostly.archive during a digital archives internship at the Congressional Cemetery in Washington, DC, Grantâs travels have taken her across the United Statesâas far as Nome, Alaskaâas well as Nova Scotia, to visit their final resting places and families to learn their stories. To Die For features many baked goods that yield dozens per batch, evoking comforting funeral foods. Cookies and cakes adapting mostly traditional Americana nostalgia (spritz cookies, brownies, carrot cake) appear alongside more surprising inclusions like a WWIIâera guava cobbler; glazed, no-bake blueberry pie; and the little-known true story behind the beloved Irish coffee. Other recipes list ingredients for a Jack Danielâs marinade, easy cheese and ranch dips, rustic breads, and savories like meatloaf (âTexasâ best,â per the engraving), fried ripe tomato, spaghetti chicken casserole and kasha varnishkes, to name a few. Itâs an almost feel-good way to get into the topics of mortality and death, Grant assesses, as sitting around the table to share a meal or stepping into a memory-filled kitchen disintegrates conversational barriers. Though she was raised by parents who gave ghost tours at local cemeteries in Alexandria, Virginia, she says her family was much more comfortable with the idea of hauntings than discussing and planning for the inevitable themselves. âSomething like a recipe feels so life-giving,â Grant expresses, adding that these conversations could also encompass music or travel. âTalking about these many life-filling moments might be an easier way to talk about tough topics.â The 40 recipes were all approved by family members of the deceased, whom Grant tracked down mostly through internet sleuthing (obituaries and social media) to ask permission to publish. Richard Dawson and his daughter, Nailah, set the tone for the book when Grant met them two years after she first found out about Dawsonâs mother. Naomi Odessa Miller-Dawsonâs headstone is outfitted with a recipe book open to her famous spritz cookies atop her epitaph in Brooklynâs Green-Wood Cemetery. Her fierce but quiet passion for baking has been exalted by the family since her passing in 2009, making Naomiâs one of the most well-known gravestone recipes in country through online chats and Reddit threads. Initially Grant tried to separate the recipe from its provider and solely focus on the food itself, but the process didnât feel quite right. âThe way Richard talked about waiting by the oven for the cookies to come out, recalling smells from when he was a little kid, trying to eat them right off the tray even though itâs still a little hot,â Grant recalls. âIt really changed the project in the sense that it made the project.â Grant has since cooked with seven families highlighted in To Die For, and has shared her pilgrimages to the gravesites with the goods themselves to pay respect. With her years of research and immersion, Grant notes that burials and grave markers have become so much more personal over the course of time. Granite headstones have allowed for almost any customization after mass-industrialization made the tools to work on it more accessible, and are much more durable compared to the formerly used wood, slate, or marble, making for lasting memorials. Proof cemeteries are beautiful grounds still vibrating with life and knowledge, if youâre open to it. Her approach to keeping such individual histories alive has deeply resonated, furthering her relationship to the Death Positive Movement: formed by hospice workers, death doulas and other care workers who advocate that discussions around mortality and afterlife planning make for a healthier society; and establishing a more intimate sense of collectivity amongst strangers across the globe. While sheâs gotten her share of detractors for various reasons (mainly self-identified Mediums claiming the deceased, and in one caseâone participant still living, didnât appreciate their culinary secrets being shared), many folks have found inspiration as they consider their own gravestone recipe. Some commenters, meanwhile, express regret around not asking their own loved ones for recipes or helpful tips that most instructions donât leave nuance for when they had the chance. âI thought I could just have this on socials and do a PDF format online,â Grant says. â[The families] were like âWe like the idea of a physical book. Something thatâs precious.â Even the visual style of it is meant to be something youâd inherit from a grandparent.â The most underrated section of her book offers a thoughtful list of questions to begin documenting oneâs own familial food legacies. âIt can feel really morbid to be like âHey mom, can you write down your recipe because youâre gonna die someday?ââ Grant says jokingly. âThat can look like a lot things. Take pictures of the recipe box and text it to all the cousins or the family group chat and save it to a drive somewhere. Cook with your family member. Teach me how to do it, letâs cook it together. Passing down that knowledge, thereâs something very powerful about that shared experience.â Sentiments from both participants in the book and Grantâs audience echo how revisiting these recipes offers sensory catharsis in addition to talking about their grief. What started as a nerdy food adventure manifested into an exploration of what it means to be remembered for how people made us feel when we were with them; highlighting turn-of-the-century attitudes toward heritage, family and home life, and serving as a ârite of passageâ or way to pass the torch to the next generation. Grant reminds us of observing and maintaining such rituals. âIf we donât do it, nobody else will.â
